Joe decided that he would try to make some extra money by raking the leaves in his neighbors' yards. Joe figured he would need approximately seven bags per yard in which to collect the leaves. The bags are sold 10 to a box, and Joe is planning on raking 14 yards. How many boxes of bags must he buy?

solutions.title: Count bags, then boxes
solutions.body:
Bags needed: $7 \times 14 = 98$. Boxes: $98 \div 10 = 9.8$, so 9 boxes (90 bags) are not enough; he must buy **10** boxes.

**Answer: 10 boxes**

solutions.title: Check 9 vs 10 boxes
solutions.body:
9 boxes hold 90 bags, which covers only $90 \div 7 \approx 12.9$ yards — fewer than 14. 10 boxes hold 100 bags, enough for $14 \times 7 = 98$.

**Answer: 10 boxes**

prompt: Heather noticed that the high temperature on October 21st was 66 degrees, the high temperature on October 26th was 63 degrees and the high temperature on October 31st was 60 degrees. It appears that the high temperatures on every fifth day are forming an arithmetic sequence. If this sequence were to continue, on what date would the high temperature be 33 degrees?

solutions.title: Count the steps
solutions.body:
The temperature drops 3 degrees every 5 days. From 60° (October 31) to 33° is a drop of $27$ degrees, i.e. $27 \div 3 = 9$ steps, which is $9 \times 5 = 45$ days after October 31.

November has 30 days, so 30 days after October 31 is November 30, and 15 more days is **December 15**.

**Answer: December 15**

solutions.title: List the sequence
solutions.body:
Oct 31: 60, Nov 5: 57, Nov 10: 54, Nov 15: 51, Nov 20: 48, Nov 25: 45, Nov 30: 42, Dec 5: 39, Dec 10: 36, Dec 15: 33.

**Answer: December 15**

prompt: Lou promised himself he would exercise at least four days of every calendar week (every Sunday through Saturday period). If Lou never wants to skip exercising on consecutive days within a calendar week, and he exercises exactly four days out of the seven, how many different workout schedules are possible for a calendar week?

solutions.title: List the skipped days
solutions.body:
Lou skips exactly 3 of the 7 days, and no two skipped days may be next to each other. Write the days as S, M, T, W, R, F, Q (Sunday … Saturday) and list the skipped triples:

- Starting with S: (S,T,R), (S,T,F), (S,T,Q), (S,W,F), (S,W,Q), (S,R,Q) — 6
- Starting with M: (M,W,F), (M,W,Q), (M,R,Q) — 3
- Starting with T: (T,R,Q) — 1

Total: $6 + 3 + 1 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: Gaps between workout days
solutions.body:
Line up the 4 workout days: X X X X. They create 5 gaps (before, between, after). Each skipped day goes into a different gap so that no two skipped days touch. Choosing 3 of the 5 gaps: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: The Zappone family has a rectangular table that seats eight people: three people on each of the longer sides and one person on each of the shorter sides. Eight people will sit down to Thanksgiving dinner. Grady, who is 3 years old and can't read yet, is asked to place a pre-printed name card at each table setting to indicate where everyone should sit. What is the probability that Uncle Rob's name card will be placed at a table setting along one of the two shorter sides of the table? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Favorable seats over all seats
solutions.body:
Since Grady can't read, Uncle Rob's card is equally likely to land at any of the 8 settings. Two of them are on the short sides, so the probability is $\frac{2}{8} = \frac14$.

**Answer: $\frac14$**

solutions.title: Complement
solutions.body:
The chance his card is on a long side is $\frac{6}{8} = \frac34$, so the chance it is on a short side is $1 - \frac34 = \frac14$.

**Answer: $\frac14$**

prompt: For Thanksgiving dinner, Mrs. Zappone is preparing a huge turkey, as well as potatoes, carrots, green beans, cranberry salad and dinner rolls. Grandpa Curt takes a little bit of everything, while Grady sticks to turkey and dinner rolls. How many distinct combinations of food items are possible at the Zappone family feast, assuming everyone takes some turkey?

solutions.title: Yes/no for each side dish
solutions.body:
Turkey is always taken. Each of the 5 side dishes is either taken or not, so there are $2^5 = 32$ combinations (including turkey alone).

**Answer: 32**

solutions.title: Count by number of side dishes
solutions.body:
Choosing 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 of the 5 sides: $1 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 = 32$.

**Answer: 32**

prompt: Mrs. Zappone baked a round apple pie. Eight equal slices (sectors) of the pie are cut and one piece is distributed to each person at dinner. After this is done, there is exactly $\frac13$ of the pie left. How many degrees are in the central angle of each person's slice of pie?

solutions.title: Angle of the eaten part
solutions.body:
The 8 slices make up $1 - \frac13 = \frac23$ of the pie, which is $\frac23 \times 360° = 240°$. Each slice: $240° \div 8 = 30°$.

**Answer: 30 degrees**

solutions.title: Fraction per slice
solutions.body:
Each slice is $\frac23 \div 8 = \frac{1}{12}$ of the pie, and $\frac{1}{12}$ of $360°$ is $30°$.

**Answer: 30 degrees**

prompt: The ratio of 7th graders to 8th graders in Mrs. Franks' homeroom is $\frac34$. On Monday, 4 7th graders and 6 8th graders got to go on a special field trip for honor roll students. Since no other students were absent on Monday, the ratio of 7th graders remaining in homeroom to 8th graders remaining in homeroom was $\frac45$. How many students are in Mrs. Franks' homeroom when everyone is present?

solutions.title: Set up a proportion
solutions.body:
Let the class have $3x$ 7th graders and $4x$ 8th graders. After the trip:
$$\frac{3x-4}{4x-6} = \frac45 \;\Rightarrow\; 5(3x-4) = 4(4x-6) \;\Rightarrow\; 15x - 20 = 16x - 24 \;\Rightarrow\; x = 4.$$
So there are $12$ 7th graders and $16$ 8th graders: $12 + 16 = 28$ students.

**Answer: 28**

prompt: On a field trip, Abbey, Bethany, Christine and Darcy bought a total of 4 hot dogs and 3 sodas, which cost them \$17.00 before tax. Edward bought 2 hot dogs and 1 soda from the same lunch stand and it cost him \$7.80 before tax. How much would 1 hot dog and 1 soda cost at the lunch stand before tax?

solutions.title: Subtract the orders
solutions.body:
Let $h$ and $s$ be the prices. $4h + 3s = 17.00$ and $2h + s = 7.80$. Subtracting: $2h + 2s = 9.20$, so $h + s = 4.60$.

**Answer: \$4.60**

solutions.title: Solve for each price
solutions.body:
Double Edward's order: $4h + 2s = 15.60$. Compare with $4h + 3s = 17.00$: one soda costs $1.40$. Then $2h = 7.80 - 1.40 = 6.40$, so $h = 3.20$, and $h + s = 3.20 + 1.40 = 4.60$.

**Answer: \$4.60**

prompt: 32 students from the 6th grade went on a field trip to the zoo. Afterward, each was asked, "Which animal did you like best, the elephants or the lions?" When all of the surveys had been turned in, 20 students had selected elephants and 22 had selected lions. If all of the students selected at least one of the two choices, how many students selected both lions and elephants?

solutions.title: Count the overlap
solutions.body:
There were $20 + 22 = 42$ selections from only 32 students, so the extra $42 - 32 = 10$ selections come from students who chose both.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: Venn diagram
solutions.body:
Let $b$ chose both. Elephants only: $20 - b$; lions only: $22 - b$. Everyone is counted once: $(20 - b) + (22 - b) + b = 32$, so $42 - b = 32$ and $b = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: The first winter snowstorm in Middle Town, USA deposits, on average, 18.7 inches of snow. According to the public works department, the time to remove the snow is directly proportional to the number of inches of fallen snow. For the town's fleet of snowplows to clear all the roads after a storm leaving 10 inches of fresh snow on the ground it takes 25 minutes. It takes one hour to clear the town's roads of 24 inches of freshly fallen snow. If the rate of snow removal remains constant, how many minutes will it take to clear all the roads in the town after the first winter snowstorm, assuming it deposits 18.7 inches of snow? Express your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.title: Proportion
solutions.body:
$\frac{10 \text{ in}}{25 \text{ min}} = \frac{18.7 \text{ in}}{M}$, so $10M = 467.5$ and $M = 46.75 \approx 47$ minutes.

**Answer: 47 minutes**

solutions.title: Minutes per inch
solutions.body:
$25 \div 10 = 2.5$ minutes per inch (and $60 \div 24 = 2.5$ too). Then $18.7 \times 2.5 = 46.75 \approx 47$ minutes.

**Answer: 47 minutes**

prompt: After each snowstorm in Big City, USA, plows remove snow from 762 lane miles of road, which is equivalent to about 48,000,000 square feet. The snowfall total was 34.2 inches in Big City, USA last winter. Suppose every snowfall evenly blanketed all road surfaces. How many cubic feet of snow were plowed last winter in Big City, USA?

solutions.title: Compute in inch-feet, then convert
solutions.body:
$48{,}000{,}000 \times 34.2 = 1{,}641{,}600{,}000$ (square feet × inches). Dividing by 12 inches per foot gives $136{,}800{,}000$ cubic feet.

**Answer: 136,800,000 cubic feet**

prompt: After each snowstorm in Big City, USA, plows remove snow from road surfaces with a total area of about 48,000,000 square feet. The snowfall total was 34.2 inches last winter, and every snowfall evenly blanketed all road surfaces. If 1 cubic foot of snow weighs about 15 pounds, approximately how many tons of snow were plowed in Big City, USA last winter?

solutions.title: Tons per cubic foot
solutions.body:
One cubic foot weighs $15 \div 2000 = 0.0075$ ton, so the snow weighs $136{,}800{,}000 \times 0.0075 = 1{,}026{,}000$ tons.

**Answer: 1,026,000 tons**

prompt: Twin brothers, Kenny and Isaiah, take turns shoveling the walkway after each snowfall. Kenny can shovel the walkway in 22 minutes, while it takes Isaiah only 14 minutes to shovel the same walkway. How many minutes will it take to shovel the walkway if they work together? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Add the rates
solutions.body:
Per minute, Kenny does $\frac1{22}$ of the job and Isaiah $\frac1{14}$. Together: $\frac1{22} + \frac1{14} = \frac{7 + 11}{154} = \frac{18}{154} = \frac{9}{77}$ of the job per minute. Time $= \frac{77}{9} \approx 8.56 \approx 8.6$ minutes.

**Answer: 8.6 minutes**

solutions.title: Harmonic formula
solutions.body:
For two workers taking $a$ and $b$ minutes, together they take $\frac{ab}{a+b} = \frac{22 \times 14}{36} = \frac{308}{36} \approx 8.56$ minutes, which is 8.6 to the nearest tenth.

**Answer: 8.6 minutes**

prompt: Every year, during the holiday season, Mary knits gifts for several of her relatives. This year, she plans to make a hat for her cousin, a scarf and hat for her grandmother, two pairs of socks for her grandfather, two hats and a scarf for her mother, and a hat and two pairs of socks for her father. Each hat requires 1 ball of yarn, each scarf requires 3 balls of yarn, and each pair of socks requires 1.5 balls of yarn. What is the minimum number of balls of yarn Mary must have to complete all the knitted gifts she intends to make?

solutions.title: Person by person
solutions.body:
Cousin 1; grandmother $3 + 1 = 4$; grandfather $2 \times 1.5 = 3$; mother $2 + 3 = 5$; father $1 + 3 = 4$. Total $1 + 4 + 3 + 5 + 4 = 17$.

**Answer: 17**

prompt: Mary wants to make a very special holiday blanket. This blanket requires 1300 yards of yarn. Two hundred of these yards should be one color, 800 yards should be a second color, and the remaining should be a third color. The balls of yarn sold at her local craft store contain 150 yards of yarn. If yarn is only sold in whole balls (and each ball is a single color), how many balls of yarn will she need to complete this project?

solutions.title: Round up each color
solutions.body:
- Color 1: $200 \div 150 \approx 1.33$ → 2 balls.
- Color 2: $800 \div 150 \approx 5.33$ → 6 balls.
- Color 3: $1300 - 1000 = 300$ yards, $300 \div 150 = 2$ balls.

Total $2 + 6 + 2 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: Why not 9?
solutions.body:
$1300 \div 150 \approx 8.67$ would suggest 9 balls, but each color must be bought separately in whole balls. Colors 1 and 2 each leave part of a ball unused, so 10 balls are needed.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: Mary bought 18 balls of yarn at a sale. She will make at least one hat, one scarf and one pair of socks from this yarn. Each hat requires 1 ball of yarn, each scarf requires 3 balls of yarn, and each pair of socks requires 1.5 balls of yarn. If she only uses the 18 balls of yarn purchased at the sale and doesn't want to have any yarn left over, what is the largest number of scarves she can knit?

solutions.title: Try the largest scarf counts
solutions.body:
With $h \ge 1$ hats, $p \ge 1$ pairs of socks and $s$ scarves: $h + 1.5p + 3s = 18$.

- $s = 5$: $h + 1.5p = 3$. $p = 1$ gives $h = 1.5$ (not whole); $p = 2$ gives $h = 0$ (not allowed). ✗
- $s = 4$: $h + 1.5p = 6$. $p = 2$, $h = 3$ works ✓.

So the largest number is **4** scarves (with 3 hats and 2 pairs of socks).

**Answer: 4**

solutions.title: Parity argument
solutions.body:
Socks must come in an even number of pairs (otherwise the half ball can't be used up), so socks use a multiple of 3 balls; with at least 2 pairs that is at least 3 balls. Scarves also use multiples of 3. So hats use $18 - (\text{multiple of }3)$, a multiple of 3, which is at least 3. That leaves at most $18 - 3 - 3 = 12$ balls for scarves: $12 \div 3 = 4$.

**Answer: 4**

prompt: Kathryn realized that she is in a time-crunch to get some of her holiday shopping completed. She needs to have all of it done by this time tomorrow. As she looks over her schedule for the next 24 hours, she sees that she will be spending $\frac13$ of it sleeping, $\frac13$ of it at school and $\frac18$ of it working at her part-time job. How much of the next 24 hours is left over for shopping? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Use hours
solutions.body:
Sleep 8 h, school 8 h, work 3 h: 19 hours. That leaves 5 of the 24 hours, i.e. $\frac{5}{24}$.

**Answer: $\frac{5}{24}$**

prompt: Kathryn was given a \$25 gift certificate to the music store. She decides to use it to buy her brother a CD. The tax on her purchase will be 4.5%. If Kathryn wants to ensure that her gift certificate covers her entire purchase (including the tax), what is the most amount of dollars that can be in the price of her purchase before the tax is added? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Solve an inequality
solutions.body:
With price $x$, the total is $1.045x \le 25$, so $x \le 25 \div 1.045 \approx 23.923$. The largest price in cents that works is **\$23.92** (check: $23.92 \times 1.045 \approx 24.996 \le 25$; while $23.93 \times 1.045 \approx 25.007$ is too much).

**Answer: \$23.92**

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
The \$25 must be 104.5% of the price. 1% of the price is $25 \div 104.5 \approx 0.23923$, so 100% is about \$23.92.

**Answer: \$23.92**

prompt: Kathryn saw her mother put 4 teaspoons of baking soda into a bowl. The cookie recipe only calls for $1\frac13$ teaspoons of baking soda, but her mother explained that she was making more than one batch at a time. If the recipe calls for $\frac12$ teaspoon of vanilla, how many teaspoons of vanilla does Kathryn now expect her mother to put into the bowl?

solutions.title: Count the batches
solutions.body:
Batches: $4 \div 1\frac13 = 4 \div \frac43 = 4 \times \frac34 = 3$. Vanilla: $3 \times \frac12 = 1\frac12$ teaspoons.

**Answer: $1\frac12$ teaspoons**

solutions.title: Ratio
solutions.body:
Vanilla to baking soda is $\frac12 : \frac43 = 3 : 8$. With 4 teaspoons of baking soda: $4 \times \frac38 = \frac32 = 1\frac12$ teaspoons.

**Answer: $1\frac12$ teaspoons**

prompt: Peitlyn decided that she would like to read more in 2026, so she made a resolution to read 30 minutes each day, starting January 1. If Peitlyn reads an average of 1 page every 2 minutes and she finishes her 6th book at the end of her reading session on March 31, 2026, what is the average number of pages per book for these six books?

solutions.title: Pages per day × days
solutions.body:
She reads $30 \div 2 = 15$ pages a day. January 1 through March 31, 2026 is $31 + 28 + 31 = 90$ days (2026 is not a leap year). Total pages $= 15 \times 90 = 1350$, so the average is $1350 \div 6 = 225$ pages per book.

**Answer: 225 pages**

solutions.title: Minutes first
solutions.body:
Total reading time: $90 \times 30 = 2700$ minutes, which is $2700 \div 2 = 1350$ pages. Per book: $1350 \div 6 = 225$.

**Answer: 225 pages**

prompt: Nora's resolution is to get more exercise. She decided that starting with the first full week in 2026, she will do a 45-minute workout four times each week (four days during every seven-day period). This means she will have to exercise four of the days during the week of Jan. 1 through Jan. 7, and then four of the days during the week of Jan. 8 through Jan. 14, etc. If Nora sticks to her resolution, what is the first possible date on which she could reach a total of 25 hours of exercise for the year?

solutions.title: Hours per week
solutions.body:
Each week she exercises $4 \times 45 = 180$ minutes $= 3$ hours. After 8 full weeks (starting Jan 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, Feb 5, 12, 19) she has 24 hours. The 9th week starts on February 26. To reach 25 hours as early as possible she works out on Feb 26 (24 h 45 min) and Feb 27 (25 h 30 min).

**Answer: February 27**

solutions.title: Count workouts
solutions.body:
25 hours $= 1500$ minutes, and $1500 \div 45 = 33\frac13$, so she needs 34 workouts. 8 weeks give 32 workouts, ending by Feb 25. Workouts 33 and 34 can be at the earliest on the first two days of the next week: Feb 26 and Feb 27.

**Answer: February 27**

prompt: Riley decided to cut back on the time that she spends watching television. During the first week of 2026 she will allow herself to watch her usual 22 hours of television. However, during each successive week of 2026, she will only allow herself to watch 90% of the time that she watched during the previous week. During which week (first, second, third, etc.) will her viewing time first be under 5 hours?

solutions.title: Geometric sequence
solutions.body:
Week $n$ allows $22 \times 0.9^{\,n-1}$ hours. We need $22 \times 0.9^{\,n-1} < 5$, i.e. $0.9^{\,n-1} < \frac{5}{22} \approx 0.227$.
$0.9^{14} \approx 0.2288$ (gives about 5.03 hours) and $0.9^{15} \approx 0.2059$ (about 4.53 hours). So $n - 1 = 15$ and $n = 16$.

**Answer: the 16th week**

prompt: Ariana loves hats. Her favorite top hat is an 18-inch-tall right circular cylinder with a brim that goes all the way around the opening for her head. The top surface of the hat as well as the brim are covered in solid yellow fabric, while only the lateral surface of the cylinder is covered with patterned fabric, as shown. If the cylinder has a diameter of 7.5 inches, what is the lateral surface area of the cylinder? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Circumference × height
solutions.body:
Lateral area $=$ (circumference) $\times$ (height) $= 7.5\pi \times 18 = 135\pi$ in².

**Answer: $135\pi$ square inches**

solutions.title: Use the formula $2\pi r h$
solutions.body:
$r = 3.75$, so $2\pi r h = 2\pi(3.75)(18) = 7.5\pi \cdot 18 = 135\pi$ in².

**Answer: $135\pi$ square inches**

prompt: Ariana's favorite top hat is an 18-inch-tall right circular cylinder with a brim that goes all the way around the opening for her head. The cylinder has a diameter of 7.5 inches. The top surface of the hat as well as the brim are covered in solid yellow fabric, while only the lateral surface of the cylinder is covered with patterned fabric, as shown. If the brim on Ariana's top hat is 4.5 inches wide, what is the circumference of the outer edge of the brim? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Outer diameter
solutions.body:
The brim adds 4.5 inches on each side, so the outer diameter is $7.5 + 2(4.5) = 16.5$ inches and the circumference is $16.5\pi$ inches.

**Answer: $16.5\pi$ inches**

solutions.title: Using the radius
solutions.body:
Outer radius $= 3.75 + 4.5 = 8.25$ in, so $C = 2\pi(8.25) = 16.5\pi$ in.

**Answer: $16.5\pi$ inches**

prompt: Ariana's favorite top hat is an 18-inch-tall right circular cylinder with a brim that goes all the way around the opening for her head. The cylinder has a diameter of 7.5 inches. The top surface of the hat as well as the brim are covered in solid yellow fabric, while only the lateral surface of the cylinder is covered with patterned fabric, as shown. The brim is 4.5 inches wide. What is the area of the top surface of the brim on Ariana's top hat? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Big circle minus hole
solutions.body:
Outer radius $= 16.5 \div 2 = 8.25$ in; hole radius $= 7.5 \div 2 = 3.75$ in.
Area $= \pi(8.25^2 - 3.75^2) = \pi(68.0625 - 14.0625) = 54\pi$ in².

**Answer: $54\pi$ square inches**

solutions.title: Difference of squares
solutions.body:
$8.25^2 - 3.75^2 = (8.25 - 3.75)(8.25 + 3.75) = 4.5 \times 12 = 54$, so the brim's area is $54\pi$ in².

**Answer: $54\pi$ square inches**

prompt: On January 13, 1979, a 15-cent stamp honoring Martin Luther King, Jr. was issued by the United States Postal Service as part of the Black Heritage Series of commemorative stamps. In 1979, it cost 15¢ to mail a first class letter weighing up to 1 ounce, and the current cost to mail a first class letter weighing no more than 1 ounce is 78¢. Suppose \$24,965,253 worth of the Black Heritage King stamps have been issued by the USPS. Using only those 15-cent commemorative King stamps that have been issued, how many first class letters weighing up to 1 ounce each could be mailed today?

solutions.title: Stamps per letter
solutions.body:
A letter needs at least 78¢, and 15-cent stamps give 75¢ (too little) with 5 stamps, so 6 stamps = 90¢ are needed per letter. Letters: $\$24{,}965{,}253 \div \$0.90 = 27{,}739{,}170$.

**Answer: 27,739,170 letters**

prompt: On January 13, 1979, a 15-cent stamp honoring Martin Luther King, Jr. was issued by the United States Postal Service as part of the Black Heritage Series of commemorative stamps. In 1979, it cost 15¢ to mail a first class letter weighing up to 1 ounce, and the current cost to mail a first class letter weighing no more than 1 ounce is 78¢. Suppose \$24,965,253 worth of the Black Heritage King stamps have been issued by the USPS. Using only the 15-cent King stamps, each 1-ounce letter needs 6 stamps (90¢), and these stamps can mail 27,739,170 letters. What is the total amount of money that would be saved by instead using a combination of commemorative 15-cent King stamps, 10-cent stamps and 1-cent stamps to mail the same number of first class letters weighing up to 1 ounce each?

In 1979, it cost 15¢ to mail a first class letter weighing up to 1 ounce, and the current cost to mail a first class letter weighing no more than 1 ounce is 78¢. Suppose \$24,965,253 worth of the Black Heritage King stamps have been issued by the USPS. What is the percent decrease in the total number of first class letters that can be mailed using \$24,965,253 worth of first class postage today compared to 1979, when the commemorative King stamp was first issued? Express your answer as a percent to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Use the price ratio
solutions.body:
The number of letters is the money divided by the price, so today's count is $\frac{15}{78}$ of 1979's count. Percent decrease $= 1 - \frac{15}{78} = \frac{63}{78} \approx 0.8077 = 80.8\%$.

**Answer: 80.8%**

prompt: Warren is throwing a pie party for his entire school to celebrate National Pie Day. He figures out that to feed all his guests and have a good variety of pie flavors, he should make 15 pies. The recipe he is using calls for $2\frac14$ cups of flour per pie crust. He only has 1 cup of flour in his kitchen, so he will need to buy more. Flour is sold in 5-pound bags. To figure out how many bags of flour he needs to buy, he weighs the 1 cup of flour he has. The 1 cup weighs 4.8 ounces. To make all 15 pies, how many bags of flour does Warren need to buy?

solutions.title: Cups → ounces → pounds
solutions.body:
Flour needed: $15 \times 2\frac14 = 33\frac34$ cups; to buy: $33\frac34 - 1 = 32\frac34$ cups.
Weight: $32.75 \times 4.8 = 157.2$ oz $= 157.2 \div 16 = 9.825$ lb. One 5-lb bag is not enough, two bags (10 lb) are.

**Answer: 2 bags**

solutions.title: Cups per bag
solutions.body:
A 5-pound bag is $80$ ounces, which is $80 \div 4.8 = 16\frac23$ cups. Two bags give $33\frac13$ cups $\ge 32\frac34$ cups needed, while one bag is far too little.

**Answer: 2 bags**

prompt:
Warren is making 15 pies for a pie party. He asks all his guests what their favorite type of pie is and tallies all the answers. The responses are shown in this table.

| Type of Pie | Number of Favorites |
|---|---|
| Apple | 63 |
| Cherry | 18 |
| Blueberry | 18 |
| Pecan | 9 |
| Blackberry | 27 |

If he uses the ratios of his guests' responses to determine which flavors each of his 15 pies will be, how many cherry pies should he make?

solutions.title: Fraction of responses
solutions.body:
Total responses: $63 + 18 + 18 + 9 + 27 = 135$. Cherry's share: $\frac{18}{135} = \frac{2}{15}$. Of 15 pies, that is 2 cherry pies.

**Answer: 2**

solutions.title: Guests per pie
solutions.body:
$135 \div 15 = 9$ guests per pie. Cherry has $18 \div 9 = 2$ pies' worth of fans.

**Answer: 2**

prompt:
Warren is making 15 pies for a pie party. Every guest named a favorite pie, with these results:

| Type of Pie | Number of Favorites |
|---|---|
| Apple | 63 |
| Cherry | 18 |
| Blueberry | 18 |
| Pecan | 9 |

He wants to figure out how many slices to cut each pie into to make sure everyone gets at least one slice of pie. If all cuts are made across the diameter of the pie, and every pie is cut into the same number of slices, how many slices should he cut each pie into?

solutions.title: At least 9, and even
solutions.body:
There are $135$ guests and 15 pies, so each pie needs at least $135 \div 15 = 9$ slices. Each cut across a diameter adds 2 slices, so the number of slices is even. The smallest even number $\ge 9$ is 10.

**Answer: 10 slices**

solutions.title: Check 8 and 10
solutions.body:
4 diameter cuts give 8 slices: $15 \times 8 = 120 < 135$, too few. 5 cuts give 10 slices: $150 \ge 135$ ✓.

**Answer: 10 slices**

prompt: Three of the same small rectangles are put together to make a big rectangle, as shown. The big rectangle is 10 inches tall. How many inches wide is it?

solutions.title: Short side is half the long side
solutions.body:
The left rectangle stands upright, so its long side is the 10-inch height. On the right, two rectangles are stacked, so two short sides equal one long side: the short side is 5 inches. Width $=$ short side of the upright rectangle $+$ long side of a lying rectangle $= 5 + 10 = 15$ inches.

**Answer: 15 inches**

solutions.title: Area check
solutions.body:
Each small rectangle is $5 \times 10 = 50$ in², so the big rectangle has area $150$ in². With height 10, the width is $150 \div 10 = 15$ inches.

**Answer: 15 inches**

prompt:
What is the largest **odd** sum you can get by adding four of the numbers below?

$$4 \quad 5 \quad 7 \quad 9 \quad 10 \quad 11 \quad 12$$

solutions.title: One odd or three odd
solutions.body:
An odd sum of four numbers needs an odd count of odd numbers: 1 or 3.
- 1 odd + 3 even: $11 + 12 + 10 + 4 = 37$.
- 3 odd + 1 even: $11 + 9 + 7 + 12 = 39$.

The largest is **39**.

**Answer: 39**

solutions.title: Start from the biggest sum
solutions.body:
The four biggest numbers $12 + 11 + 10 + 9 = 42$ is even. To make it odd, swap one number for one of the other parity, losing as little as possible: swap 10 for 7 (lose 3) to get 39; other swaps (9→4, lose 5; 12→7, lose 5; …) lose more.

**Answer: 39**

prompt: Alex glues four cubes together to make this shape. How many square cube faces are on the outside of this shape, including the three on the bottom?

solutions.title: Count each cube
solutions.body:
Looking cube by cube, the three cubes that touch only one other cube each show 5 faces, and the bottom-front cube that touches the other three shows 3 faces: $5 + 5 + 5 + 3 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

solutions.title: Subtract hidden faces
solutions.body:
Four cubes have $4 \times 6 = 24$ faces. The shape has 3 places where two cubes are glued, and each hides 2 faces: $24 - 3 \times 2 = 18$.

**Answer: 18**

prompt: If June ate $\frac14$ of $\frac23$ of $\frac12$ of a pie, what fraction of the whole pie did she eat? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Multiply
solutions.body:
$\frac14 \times \frac23 \times \frac12 = \frac{2}{24} = \frac{1}{12}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{12}$**

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
$\frac23$ of $\frac12$ is $\frac13$ of the pie; $\frac14$ of $\frac13$ is $\frac{1}{12}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{12}$**

prompt: The top surface of a particular slice of pie is a sector of a circle with a vertex angle measuring 20 degrees, and the length of the arc is $\pi$ units. What is the circumference of the top surface of the whole pie? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Fraction of the circle
solutions.body:
The slice is $\frac{20}{360} = \frac{1}{18}$ of the pie, so its arc is $\frac{1}{18}$ of the circumference: $C = 18 \times \pi = 18\pi$.

**Answer: $18\pi$**

solutions.title: Arc length formula
solutions.body:
Arc $= \frac{20}{360} \cdot 2\pi r = \frac{\pi r}{9} = \pi$, so $r = 9$ and $C = 2\pi(9) = 18\pi$.

**Answer: $18\pi$**

prompt: The top surface of a round pie is a circle. One slice is removed; its top surface is a sector with a vertex angle of 20 degrees and an arc length of $\pi$ units. What is the perimeter of the top surface of the remaining portion of the pie? Express your answer in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Arc plus two radii
solutions.body:
The slice is $\frac{20}{360} = \frac1{18}$ of the pie, so the full circumference is $18\pi$ and the radius is $r = 18\pi \div 2\pi = 9$.
The remaining piece is bounded by the remaining arc, $18\pi - \pi = 17\pi$, and two radii (the cuts), $2 \times 9 = 18$. Perimeter: $18 + 17\pi$.

**Answer: $18 + 17\pi$ units**

solutions.title: Using the remaining angle
solutions.body:
The remaining sector has angle $340°$. From $\frac{20}{360}(2\pi r) = \pi$ we get $r = 9$. Arc $= \frac{340}{360} \cdot 18\pi = 17\pi$; add the two radii: $17\pi + 18$.

**Answer: $18 + 17\pi$ units**

prompt: Patrick has a leprechaun hat that looks like a tall, green top hat. The main portion of the hat is a cylinder that is 8 inches tall and has a 3-inch radius. He will fill this portion of the hat with chocolates wrapped to resemble small gold coins to pass out to all his friends. One bag of these chocolate "coins" takes up about 20 in³ of space. What is the minimum number of bags of chocolate that Patrick must get to completely fill his hat?

solutions.title: Volume, then divide
solutions.body:
$V = \pi r^2 h = \pi(3^2)(8) = 72\pi \approx 226.2$ in³. Bags: $226.2 \div 20 \approx 11.3$, so 11 bags aren't enough; he needs **12**.

**Answer: 12 bags**

solutions.title: Compare with 11 and 12 bags
solutions.body:
11 bags fill $220$ in³ and 12 bags fill $240$ in³. Since $72\pi \approx 226$ is between them, 12 bags are needed.

**Answer: 12 bags**

prompt: Margaret painted a mural for St. Patrick's Day and mixed her own green paint. She mixed 3 parts yellow paint with 2 parts blue paint to create green paint. Maureen wanted to also paint a mural with the same green color, but she currently has 8 cups of green paint that is a mixture of 40% yellow paint and 60% blue paint. To get the same shade of green as Margaret, how many cups of yellow paint must she add to her mixture?

solutions.title: Set up a proportion
solutions.body:
Maureen has $0.4 \times 8 = 3.2$ cups yellow and $0.6 \times 8 = 4.8$ cups blue. Adding $x$ cups yellow: $\frac{3.2 + x}{4.8} = \frac32$, so $3.2 + x = 7.2$ and $x = 4$.

**Answer: 4 cups**

solutions.title: Blue stays fixed
solutions.body:
Blue is 2 parts and there are 4.8 cups of it, so 1 part $= 2.4$ cups. Yellow should be 3 parts $= 7.2$ cups. She has 3.2 cups, so she adds $7.2 - 3.2 = 4$ cups.

**Answer: 4 cups**

prompt: How many ways can we arrange the five letters in the word GREEN, even if they don't form real words, if any arrangement must keep the two Es together?

solutions.title: Glue the Es
solutions.body:
Treat EE as one block. Then we arrange 4 distinct items: G, R, N, [EE]. That gives $4! = 24$ arrangements (swapping the two identical Es gives nothing new).

**Answer: 24**

solutions.title: Place the EE block
solutions.body:
The EE block can start in position 1, 2, 3 or 4 (4 choices). The other three distinct letters fill the remaining 3 spots in $3! = 6$ ways: $4 \times 6 = 24$.

**Answer: 24**

prompt:
There are three walls in Jordan's living room. The three walls, shown here, are 12 feet, 9 feet and 10 feet wide, respectively. Each wall has a height of 8 feet with a 6-inch baseboard along the bottom. The largest of the three walls contains a window that measures 5 feet by 6 feet. Jordan plans to paint the three walls of his living room by mixing together some paint he already has, which includes white #2, magenta #3, red #4, yellow #5 and green #6. Jordan has decided to paint two of the walls a pale goldenrod and the third wall will be painted burnt umber.

Suppose that 1 gallon of paint is used to cover 400 sq feet. Jordan plans to apply four coats of the goldenrod paint mixture to the 12-foot wall and the 9-foot wall leaving only the window and baseboard unpainted. How many gallons of the goldenrod paint mixture will he need? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Area of each wall
solutions.body:
Paintable height: $8 - 0.5 = 7.5$ ft.
- 12-ft wall: $12 \times 7.5 - 5 \times 6 = 90 - 30 = 60$ ft².
- 9-ft wall: $9 \times 7.5 = 67.5$ ft².

Total $127.5$ ft², four coats: $510$ ft². Paint: $510 \div 400 = 1.275 \approx 1.28$ gallons.

**Answer: 1.28 gallons**

solutions.title: Both walls together
solutions.body:
The two walls are $12 + 9 = 21$ ft wide, so without the baseboard they have $21 \times 7.5 = 157.5$ ft²; minus the 30-ft² window gives $127.5$ ft². Four coats is $4 \times 127.5 \div 400 = 1.275$ gallons ≈ 1.28.

**Answer: 1.28 gallons**

prompt: To apply two coats of a burnt umber paint mixture to a wall, Jordan determines that he will use 3 pints of paint. In order to create the burnt umber mixture, Jordan needs to mix magenta #3, yellow #5 and green #6 in the ratio of 4:9:2, respectively. What is the positive difference between the number of pints of magenta #3 and yellow #5 Jordan will use to create 3 pints of the burnt umber mixture?

solutions.title: Find each amount
solutions.body:
There are $4 + 9 + 2 = 15$ parts, so each part is $3 \div 15 = 0.2$ pint. Magenta: $4(0.2) = 0.8$; yellow: $9(0.2) = 1.8$. Difference: $1$ pint.

**Answer: 1 pint**

solutions.title: Difference in parts
solutions.body:
Yellow has $9 - 4 = 5$ more parts than magenta, which is $\frac{5}{15} = \frac13$ of the mixture: $\frac13 \times 3 = 1$ pint.

**Answer: 1 pint**

prompt: Jordan wants to create 2 gallons of a goldenrod paint mixture. The formulation for the goldenrod paint mixture calls for the use of white #2, red #4, yellow #5 and light green #9 in the ratio of 2:1:5:10, respectively. Jordan realizes that he does not have light green #9, but sees that he can create it using yellow #5 and green #6 in the ratio 14:1. Assuming Jordan creates the 2 gallons of goldenrod paint mixture correctly, what is the total amount of yellow #5 he used, in gallons? Express your answer as a mixed number.

solutions.title: Yellow in two places
solutions.body:
Total parts: $2 + 1 + 5 + 10 = 18$.
- Yellow directly: $\frac{5}{18} \times 2 = \frac59$ gallon.
- Light green: $\frac{10}{18} \times 2 = \frac{10}{9}$ gallons, of which $\frac{14}{15}$ is yellow: $\frac{14}{15} \times \frac{10}{9} = \frac{28}{27}$ gallon.

Total yellow: $\frac{15}{27} + \frac{28}{27} = \frac{43}{27} = 1\frac{16}{27}$ gallons.

**Answer: $1\frac{16}{27}$ gallons**

solutions.title: Rewrite the recipe with 15ths
solutions.body:
Split each of the 10 light-green parts into 15 sub-parts: light green = 150 sub-parts = 140 yellow + 10 green. Scaling the other colors by 15: white 30, red 15, yellow 75. Total $30 + 15 + 75 + 150 = 270$ sub-parts, of which yellow is $75 + 140 = 215$. Yellow $= \frac{215}{270} \times 2 = \frac{43}{27} = 1\frac{16}{27}$ gallons.

**Answer: $1\frac{16}{27}$ gallons**

prompt: The sum of any four consecutive odd integers is a multiple of eight. For example, $1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16$ and $5 + 7 + 9 + 11 = 32$. What is the product of the greatest and least of four consecutive odd integers whose sum is 64?

solutions.title: Use the average
solutions.body:
The average of the four numbers is $64 \div 4 = 16$, so they are centered on 16: $13, 15, 17, 19$. Product of greatest and least: $13 \times 19 = 247$.

**Answer: 247**

prompt: Unique mathematical expressions are created from the pattern $\underline{\quad}\ \square\ \underline{\quad}\ \square\ \underline{\quad}\ \square\ \underline{\quad}$ by replacing each blank with a different number from 2, 4, 6 and 8 and by replacing each box with a different operator from $+$, $-$ and $\div$ (using the usual order of operations). How many of these expressions, when evaluated, have an integer result?

solutions.title: Locate the division
solutions.body:
Every expression contains exactly one $\div$, so the result is an integer exactly when that quotient is an integer (the rest is adding/subtracting whole numbers). Integer quotients from distinct numbers: $8 \div 4$, $8 \div 2$, $6 \div 2$, $4 \div 2$ — 4 choices.

The quotient occupies one of 3 positions (first, middle or last pair of blanks). The other 2 numbers fill the other 2 blanks in 2 ways, and $+$, $-$ fill the other 2 boxes in 2 ways.

Total: $4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 2 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

solutions.title: Brute-force check
solutions.body:
There are $4! \times 3! = 144$ expressions in all. For the $\div$ in a given position, the pair of numbers around it is an ordered pair of distinct numbers: 12 possible pairs, of which 4 give integers ($8/4, 8/2, 6/2, 4/2$). So exactly $\frac{4}{12} = \frac13$ of the expressions give integers: $144 \div 3 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

prompt: Unique mathematical expressions are created from the pattern $\underline{\quad}\ \square\ \underline{\quad}\ \square\ \underline{\quad}\ \square\ \underline{\quad}$ by replacing each blank with a different number from 2, 4, 6 and 8 and by replacing each box with a different operator from $+$, $-$ and $\div$ (using the usual order of operations). What is the positive difference between the greatest and least possible integer results of these expressions?

solutions.title: List results by quotient
solutions.body:
An integer result needs an integer quotient. The expression then has three terms (the quotient and the two leftover numbers) joined by one $+$ and one $-$, so the result is (sum of the three terms) minus twice the subtracted term, where the subtracted term is any term except the first.
- With $8 \div 4 = 2$ (others 2 and 6): sum 10, results $10 - 4 = 6$ and $10 - 12 = -2$.
- With $8 \div 2 = 4$ (others 4, 6): sum 14, results $6$ and $2$.
- With $6 \div 2 = 3$ (others 4, 8): sum 15, results $9, 7, -1$.
- With $4 \div 2 = 2$ (others 6, 8): sum 16, results $12, 4, 0$.

All integer results: $-2, -1, 0, 2, 4, 6, 7, 9, 12$. Difference: $12 - (-2) = 14$.

**Answer: 14**

solutions.title: Aim for extremes
solutions.body:
The two other numbers $a, b$ and the quotient $q$ combine as $\pm$ terms with exactly one subtraction. The biggest result adds the two largest and subtracts the smallest: with $q = 4 \div 2 = 2$, $8 + 6 - 2 = 12$ (e.g. $8 + 6 - 4 \div 2$). The smallest subtracts the largest: with $q = 8 \div 4 = 2$, $2 + 2 - 6 = -2$ (e.g. $2 - 6 + 8 \div 4$). Checking the other quotients gives nothing beyond these. Difference: $12 - (-2) = 14$.

**Answer: 14**

prompt: The Grand Canyon Skywalk opened on March 28, 2007. It is owned and operated by the Hualapai Tribe at the Grand Canyon's western rim. The horseshoe shaped Skywalk extends 70 feet beyond the edge of the rim and is 4000 feet above the floor of the canyon. The Sears Tower, in Chicago, Illinois, is 1,450 feet in height. The height of a model of the Sears Tower is 9 feet 6 inches. A scale model of the Grand Canyon and the Skywalk is built to the same scale as the Sears Tower. What is the number of feet in the distance from the floor of the canyon to the Skywalk in the model? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Scale factor
solutions.body:
The model is $\frac{9.5}{1450}$ of real size. $4000 \times \frac{9.5}{1450} = \frac{38{,}000}{1450} \approx 26.21$ ft.

**Answer: 26.2 feet**

prompt: The Grand Canyon Skywalk is capable of supporting 71 million pounds. Assume the average weight per person on the Skywalk is 180 pounds and the maximum 120 people are on the Skywalk. What percent of the capable supporting weight is on the Skywalk? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Find 1% first
solutions.body:
1% of 71,000,000 is 710,000 lb, so 0.01% is 7,100 lb. 21,600 lb is about $21{,}600 \div 7{,}100 \approx 3.04$ hundredths of a percent, i.e. $0.03\%$.

**Answer: 0.03%**

prompt: The driving distance from Flagstaff, Arizona to the entrance to Grand Canyon West is 216 miles. The estimated travel time is 3 hours and 50 minutes. If a car is driven these 216 miles in that time, what is the average speed of the car in miles per hour? Express your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.title: Convert time to hours
solutions.body:
50 min $= \frac56$ h, so the time is $3\frac56 = \frac{23}{6}$ h. Speed $= 216 \div \frac{23}{6} = \frac{1296}{23} \approx 56.3 \approx 56$ mph.

**Answer: 56 mph**

solutions.title: Miles per minute
solutions.body:
Time $= 230$ minutes. $216 \div 230 \approx 0.939$ miles per minute, times 60 $\approx 56.3$ mph.

**Answer: 56 mph**

prompt: The cost to build the Grand Canyon Skywalk was \$40 million. When the Skywalk first opened, the entrance fee to walk out on the Skywalk was \$25 per person. If \$15 of each admission fee went towards paying for the construction of the Skywalk, and if the admission fee was never raised, how many visitors would need to pay the entrance fee to recover the cost of building the Skywalk? Express your answer to the nearest thousand.

solutions.title: Divide
solutions.body:
$40{,}000{,}000 \div 15 \approx 2{,}666{,}667$ visitors, which is about 2,667,000 to the nearest thousand.

**Answer: 2,667,000**

solutions.title: Thousands of visitors
solutions.body:
Each 1000 visitors pay \$15,000 toward construction. $40{,}000{,}000 \div 15{,}000 \approx 2666.7$ thousand visitors $\approx 2{,}667{,}000$.

**Answer: 2,667,000**

Marta recently started her own flower business. For creating floral arrangements, she ordered a dozen small, ceramic pots for \$40.00, a pack of plastic bags for \$5.99 and a roll of twine for \$4.75. solutions.title: Part over whole

Planting supplies: \$64.07. Total: \$114.81 (adding the arrangement materials, \$50.74). $\frac{64.07}{114.81} \approx 0.5581 = 55.8\%$.

solutions.title: Complement check

Arrangement materials are $\frac{50.74}{114.81} \approx 44.2\%$, so planting supplies are $100 - 44.2 = 55.8\%$.

prompt: Marta has a flower business. In her first six months of operation, Marta sold 3 mixed bouquets for \$13 each, 4 bouquets of lilies for \$15 each, and 5 bouquets of dahlias for \$12 each. She also sold 5 potted arrangements of marigolds and peonies for \$8 each. If Marta's business operates in a jurisdiction that has no sales tax, what was Marta's total revenue for the first six months her business was operational?

solutions.title: Group by count
solutions.body:
Lilies and dahlias each bring \$60 ($4 \times 15 = 5 \times 12$), so $120 + 39 + 40 = 199$.

**Answer: \$199**

Temi's analog clock, shown here, has an hour hand of length 9 in and a minute hand of length 15 in. When Temi's clock strikes 3 o'clock, what is the length of the segment drawn from the end of the minute hand to the end of the hour hand? Express your answer in simplest radical form.

solutions.title: Pythagorean theorem
solutions.body:
At 3:00 the hands are perpendicular, so the segment is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 9 and 15: $\sqrt{81 + 225} = \sqrt{306} = \sqrt{9 \cdot 34} = 3\sqrt{34}$ in.

**Answer: $3\sqrt{34}$ inches**

solutions.title: Factor first
solutions.body:
$9 = 3 \cdot 3$ and $15 = 3 \cdot 5$, so the triangle is 3 times a 3-5 right triangle, whose hypotenuse is $\sqrt{34}$. Hence $3\sqrt{34}$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt{34}$ inches**

prompt: Kari has an analog clock, shown here, with a minute hand of length 12 in. When Kari's clock strikes 2 o'clock, the segment drawn from the end of the minute hand to the end of the hour hand forms a right triangle with the two hands (as shown). What is the area of this right triangle? Express your answer in simplest radical form.

solutions.title: 30-60-90 triangle
solutions.body:
At 2:00 the hands are $2 \times 30° = 60°$ apart. The right angle is at the tip of the hour hand, so the minute hand (12 in) is the hypotenuse of a 30-60-90 triangle. The hour hand, next to the 60° angle, is the short leg: 6 in. The other leg is $6\sqrt3$ in. Area $= \frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 6\sqrt3 = 18\sqrt3$ in².

**Answer: $18\sqrt{3}$ square inches**

solutions.title: Area with sine
solutions.body:
Area $= \frac12 \cdot (\text{hour hand}) \cdot (\text{minute hand}) \cdot \sin 60°$. The hour hand is $12\cos 60° = 6$, so area $= \frac12 \cdot 6 \cdot 12 \cdot \frac{\sqrt3}{2} = 18\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $18\sqrt{3}$ square inches**

prompt: Mitch practices playing the violin every evening for 1 hour and 45 minutes. What is the positive difference between the total degrees traveled by the minute hand and the total degrees traveled by the hour hand of an analog clock during Mitch's practice? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Degrees per minute
solutions.body:
The minute hand turns $360° \div 60 = 6°$ per minute; the hour hand $360° \div 720 = 0.5°$ per minute. In 105 minutes: $630°$ and $52.5°$. Difference: $577.5°$.

**Answer: 577.5 degrees**

solutions.title: Relative speed
solutions.body:
The minute hand gains $6 - 0.5 = 5.5°$ per minute on the hour hand, so in 105 minutes it travels $5.5 \times 105 = 577.5°$ more.

**Answer: 577.5 degrees**

**Answer: 198**

prompt:
Ribbons are put on the name badges of attendees to designate the different ways they are helping the program. Suppose the details of one volunteer list (which shows who should get which ribbon(s)) are as follows:

1. There are only 4 types of ribbons on the list: Volunteer, Scorer, Monitor and Timer. (A person can have more than one ribbon attached to their name badge.)
2. Everyone has a Volunteer ribbon.
3. Only 3 people have exactly 3 ribbons.
4. There are 7 people with Monitor ribbons and 12 people with Scorer ribbons.
5. Only 2 people have exactly 4 ribbons.
6. There are an equal amount of Timers who are also Monitors as Timers who are not Monitors.
7. Exactly 5 people have Scorer and Monitor ribbons.
8. There are twice as many people that have exactly one ribbon as people who have multiple ribbons.

How many volunteers are on this list?

solutions.title: Work from 4 ribbons down
solutions.body:
- **4 ribbons:** 2 people (V, S, M, T).
- **3 ribbons:** 5 people have S and M; 2 are the 4-ribbon people, so 3 have exactly V, S, M. These are the only 3 people with 3 ribbons.
- **2 ribbons** (V + one other): Monitors: $7 - 5 = 2$ with V, M. Scorers: $12 - 5 = 7$ with V, S. Timers who are Monitors: just the 2 four-ribbon people, so 2 Timers are not Monitors; they can't have 3 ribbons, so they have V, T. Total $2 + 7 + 2 = 11$.
- **Multiple ribbons:** $2 + 3 + 11 = 16$. **One ribbon:** $2 \times 16 = 32$.

Total: $16 + 32 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

solutions.title: Venn-diagram bookkeeping
solutions.body:
Since everyone has V, look only at S, M, T. Regions: SMT = 2; exactly two of S, M, T = 3 people, and all must be SM (because S∩M has 5 = 2 + 3), so ST-only = MT-only = 0. Then M only $= 7 - 5 = 2$, S only $= 12 - 5 = 7$, T∩M $= 2$ so T only $= 2$. People with at least one of S, M, T: $2 + 3 + 2 + 7 + 2 = 16$; people with V only: 32. Total 48.

**Answer: 48**

prompt: Let's say that in the final round of the Countdown Round, the winner is the first competitor to get three questions correct. Assume no more than 5 questions are used and every question asked is answered correctly by one of the two competitors, A or B. How many different ways can the final round play out such that Competitor A wins the round? (Example I: Competitor A could get the first 3 questions correct (AAA). Example II: Competitor B could get only the second question correct (ABAA).)

solutions.title: Count by length
solutions.body:
A must answer the last question and have exactly 2 earlier correct answers.
- 3 questions: AAA — 1 way.
- 4 questions: one B among the first 3 — 3 ways.
- 5 questions: two Bs among the first 4 — $\binom42 = 6$ ways.

Total $1 + 3 + 6 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: List them all
solutions.body:
B can get 0, 1 or 2 questions before A's third correct answer:
- AAA
- BAAA, ABAA, AABA
- BBAAA, BABAA, BAABA, ABBAA, ABABA, AABBA

That is 10 ways.

**Answer: 10**
