prompt: Tasha is making 5 flowerpots for her mother for Mother's Day. Each flowerpot is a cylindrical can that has a diameter of 7 inches and a height of 8 inches. She fills each flowerpot $\frac34$ full with potting soil. What is the total number of cubic inches of potting soil she needs for the 5 flowerpots? Express your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.title: Volume of one pot
solutions.body:
$V = \pi (3.5)^2 (8) = 98\pi$ in³. Soil per pot: $\frac34 \cdot 98\pi = 73.5\pi$. Five pots: $367.5\pi \approx 1154.5 \to 1155$ in³.

**Answer: 1155 cubic inches**

solutions.title: Fill height
solutions.body:
$\frac34$ full means soil 6 inches deep: $\pi(3.5^2)(6) = 73.5\pi$ per pot; times 5 is $367.5\pi \approx 1155$ in³.

**Answer: 1155 cubic inches**

prompt: Richard is making a rectangular poster for his mother for Mother's Day. The poster is proportional to a rectangular 3-inch by 5-inch card that has the words "MOM, I LOVE YOU" written in letters that are 0.5 inches tall. The shortest side of the poster is 3 feet. What is the height in inches of each of the letters on the poster?

solutions.title: Scale factor
solutions.body:
The short side goes from 3 in to 3 ft $= 36$ in, a scale factor of 12. Letters: $0.5 \times 12 = 6$ in.

**Answer: 6 inches**

solutions.title: Proportion
solutions.body:
$\frac{0.5}{x} = \frac{3}{36}$, so $3x = 18$ and $x = 6$ in.

**Answer: 6 inches**

prompt: On May 20, 1873, Levi Strauss and David Jacobs received patent number 139,121 from the US Patent and Trademark Office for using rivets to strengthen the pockets of denim work pants. If each of the six digits in the patent number is placed on a separate card and 2 cards are selected at random without replacement, what is the probability that the sum of the numbers on the selected cards will be an even number? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Both odd
solutions.body:
The digits are 1, 3, 9, 1, 2, 1: five odd and one even. An even sum needs two odds (two evens is impossible). $P = \frac56 \times \frac45 = \frac46 = \frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

solutions.title: Count pairs
solutions.body:
There are $\binom62 = 15$ pairs of cards. The sum is odd only when the 2 is chosen with an odd card: 5 pairs. Even: $15 - 5 = 10$, so $P = \frac{10}{15} = \frac23$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

prompt: From one single bale of cotton measuring 54 in long, 20 in high and 32 in wide, 215 pairs of jeans can be produced. At this rate, approximately how many cubic inches of cotton are used to create one pair of jeans from a bale of cotton? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Volume ÷ pairs
solutions.body:
$54 \times 20 \times 32 = 34{,}560$ in³. $34{,}560 \div 215 \approx 160.74 \approx 160.7$ in³.

**Answer: 160.7 cubic inches**

solutions.title: Estimate and refine
solutions.body:
$215 \times 160 = 34{,}400$, leaving $160$ in³; $160 \div 215 \approx 0.74$. So about $160.7$ in³.

**Answer: 160.7 cubic inches**

prompt: A denim drive converts old denim into environmentally friendly insulation. If 70,000 sq ft of insulation is produced from 36,000 units of denim, how many square feet of insulation can be made from 15,500 units of denim? Express your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.title: Unit rate
solutions.body:
Each unit of denim makes $\frac{70}{36} \approx 1.9444$ sq ft. $15{,}500 \times \frac{35}{18} = \frac{542{,}500}{18} \approx 30{,}138.9$.

**Answer: 30,139 sq ft**

prompt: Joseph scored 76, 88, 96 and 98 on his 4 chapter tests this grading period. If the final exam will count twice as much as each of the chapter tests, and the 4 tests and the final exam are the only items contributing to this period's grade, what is the minimum score that Joseph must earn on the final to have an average of 94?

solutions.title: Weighted average
solutions.body:
The final counts as two tests, so there are 6 "test slots": $\frac{76 + 88 + 96 + 98 + 2x}{6} = 94$, so $358 + 2x = 564$, $2x = 206$, $x = 103$.

**Answer: 103**

solutions.title: Balance around 94
solutions.body:
Differences from 94: $-18, -6, +2, +4$, total $-18$. The final, counting twice, must make up $+18$, i.e. $+9$ each time: $94 + 9 = 103$.

**Answer: 103**

prompt: The final exam scores earned by the 16 students in Joseph's class are as follows: 80, 79, 96, 93, 94, 92, 88, 87, 90, 81, 83, 82, 89, 99, 91, 73. What is the positive difference between the median of these scores and the average (arithmetic mean) of these scores? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Deviations from 88.5
solutions.body:
Subtract 88.5 from each score and add: the total is $1397 - 16(88.5) = 1397 - 1416 = -19$. So the mean is $88.5 - \frac{19}{16} = 88.5 - 1.1875$, and the difference is $1.1875 \approx 1.19$.

**Answer: 1.19**

prompt: In another one of Joseph's classes the 14 8th graders averaged 94 on the final exam, while the 12 7th graders averaged 89 on the final exam. What was the average score for the entire class? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Weighted from 89
solutions.body:
The 8th graders are 5 points above 89, and they are $\frac{14}{26}$ of the class: $89 + 5 \cdot \frac{14}{26} = 89 + \frac{70}{26} \approx 89 + 2.692 = 91.69$.

**Answer: 91.69**

prompt: At Walter Whitman Middle School, to celebrate the last day of school, Mrs. Hanks brought in treats for her class. She has chocolate bars, lollipops and gumballs. Mrs. Hanks tells each student they can choose any combination of three treats from what she has. How many different combinations of three treats can one of her students choose?

solutions.title: List by type
solutions.body:
Call the treats A, B, C.
- All different: ABC — 1.
- All the same: AAA, BBB, CCC — 3.
- Two of one, one of another: AAB, AAC, BBA, BBC, CCA, CCB — 6.

Total $1 + 3 + 6 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: Stars and bars
solutions.body:
Choosing 3 treats from 3 types with repetition allowed: $\binom{3 + 3 - 1}{3} = \binom53 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: At the end-of-year assembly, WWMS holds a raffle, in which several lucky students will each win a gift certificate to the famous Giorgio's Gelato. There are 10 gift certificates to be raffled to the 6th graders, 15 gift certificates to be raffled to the 7th graders and 20 gift certificates to be raffled to the 8th graders. Each grade has 300 students. Junie is in 8th grade at WWMS. Junie's sister and brother also attend WWMS and are in 7th and 6th grade, respectively. What is the probability that at least one of the three siblings wins a gift certificate? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Complement
solutions.body:
Each grade's certificates go to different students, so the 6th-grade brother wins with probability $\frac{10}{300} = \frac1{30}$, the 7th-grade sister with $\frac{15}{300} = \frac1{20}$, and Junie with $\frac{20}{300} = \frac1{15}$. The three raffles are separate, so the events are independent.

$P(\text{nobody wins}) = \frac{29}{30} \cdot \frac{19}{20} \cdot \frac{14}{15} = \frac{7714}{9000}$.

$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - \frac{7714}{9000} = \frac{1286}{9000} = \frac{643}{4500} \approx 0.143$.

(Simply adding $\frac1{30} + \frac1{20} + \frac1{15} = \frac{3}{20}$ counts the cases where two or three of them win more than once.)

**Answer: $\frac{643}{4500}$**

reviewNote: The official solution gives 3/20 by adding 1/30 + 1/20 + 1/15, which double-counts outcomes where two or three siblings win (the events are not mutually exclusive). The correct probability 1 - (29/30)(19/20)(14/15) = 643/4500 is used here. Verified: the three grades are independent draws, so P(none) = 7714/9000.

prompt: Before WWMS students were officially released for summer vacation, the staff had to conduct an official check of all 900 lockers, numbered from 1 to 900. Once the locker check was completed, all 900 lockers remained open. As students exited in an orderly fashion, walking down the hallway single file, the 1st student closed all the lockers. The 2nd student then opened every even numbered locker. The 3rd student changed the status of every locker whose number was a multiple of three – opened it if closed or closed it if opened. The 4th student then did the same for every locker whose number was a multiple of four, and so on through the 900th student who changed the status of locker number 900. When all of the students had left the school, how many lockers were closed?

solutions.title: Count the toggles
solutions.body:
Locker $n$ is toggled once by each student whose number divides $n$. Starting open, it ends closed after an odd number of toggles, i.e. when $n$ has an odd number of divisors. Divisors pair up ($d$ with $n/d$) except when $d = n/d$, so only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors. The squares from 1 to 900 are $1^2, 2^2, \dots, 30^2$: **30** lockers.

**Answer: 30**

solutions.title: Small case check
solutions.body:
Try lockers 1–10: locker 1 (divisor 1) closed; 2 (1,2) open; 3 open; 4 (1,2,4) closed; 5–8 open; 9 (1,3,9) closed; 10 open. Closed lockers are 1, 4, 9 — the squares. Up to 900 there are 30 squares.

**Answer: 30**

prompt: Summer Fun Camp enrollment costs 85 dollars each week per camper. Each camper may register for up to three of the optional workshops offered for an additional charge of \$5.50 a week per workshop, or 15 dollars per week for three workshops. The total charge for Chloe's enrollment to attend Summer Fun Camp for $n$ weeks this summer is 768 dollars. If Chloe has registered to participate in two workshops each week, what is the value of $n$?

solutions.title: Weekly cost
solutions.body:
Each week costs $85 + 2(5.50) = 96$ dollars. $96n = 768$, so $n = 8$.

**Answer: 8**

prompt: Summer Fun Camp enrollment costs 85 dollars each week per camper. Each camper may register for up to three of the optional workshops offered for an additional charge of \$5.50 a week per workshop, or 15 dollars per week for three workshops. This summer, Lailan will attend Summer Fun Camp for six weeks and participate in the soccer, band and cheerleading workshops. If Lailan registered to participate in these three workshops each week, what is her total charge for six weeks of Summer Fun Camp and workshops?

solutions.title: Per week
solutions.body:
Each week: $85 + 15 = 100$ dollars (three workshops cost the 15-dollar package price, cheaper than $3 \times 5.50 = 16.50$). Six weeks: $600$ dollars.

**Answer: 600 dollars**

solutions.title: Separate totals
solutions.body:
Camp: $85 \times 6 = 510$. Workshops: $15 \times 6 = 90$. Total $600$.

**Answer: 600 dollars**

prompt: Summer Fun Camp enrollment costs 85 dollars each week per camper. Each camper may register for up to three of the optional workshops offered for an additional charge of \$5.50 a week per workshop, or 15 dollars per week for three workshops. Lailan will attend Summer Fun Camp for six weeks with the three-workshop package each week. This summer, Ailee plans to attend three different camps – a two-week soccer camp, followed by a two-week band camp, followed by a two-week cheerleading camp. The total cost for Ailee's band camp enrollment is 100 dollars more than the total cost of her soccer camp enrollment, and the total cost of her cheerleading camp enrollment is one-fourth the combined total costs for her enrollment in all three camps. If the combined total costs for Ailee's enrollment in all three camps is equal to Lailan's total charge for six weeks of Summer Fun Camp and workshops, what is the total cost of Ailee's band camp enrollment?

solutions.title: Set up equations
solutions.body:
Lailan pays $6(85 + 15) = 600$ dollars, so Ailee's camps total $s + b + c = 600$. Cheerleading is one-fourth: $c = 150$, so $s + b = 450$. With $b = s + 100$: $2s + 100 = 450$, $s = 175$, $b = 275$.

**Answer: 275 dollars**

solutions.title: Half-difference trick
solutions.body:
Soccer and band together cost $600 - \frac14(600) = 450$ and differ by 100. The larger is $\frac{450 + 100}{2} = 275$.

**Answer: 275 dollars**

prompt: A stand at a local parade is selling flags for observers to wave. The small flags each cost $\frac23$ the price of each large flag, and each flag costs a whole number of dollars. If Frida bought 5 flags and spent \$24.00, how much do each of the small flags cost in dollars?

solutions.title: Guess and check
solutions.body:
The large price must be a multiple of 3. Try large \$6, small \$4: three small and two large cost $12 + 12 = 24$ ✓. (Large \$3/small \$2 gives at most \$15; large \$9/small \$6 gives at least \$30.)

**Answer: \$4**

solutions.title: Algebra
solutions.body:
Let large $= 3k$, small $= 2k$, with $a$ small and $5 - a$ large: $2ka + 3k(5 - a) = 24$, so $k(15 - a) = 24$. With $0 \le a \le 5$, $15 - a$ is between 10 and 15 and divides 24 only for $15 - a = 12$: $a = 3$, $k = 2$. Small flags cost $2k = 4$.

**Answer: \$4**

prompt: The American flag has 13 horizontal stripes of equal height. If the flag outside of Victor's house is 4 feet tall and 6 feet wide, how many inches tall is each of the 13 stripes? Express your answer as a mixed number.

solutions.title: Convert, then divide
solutions.body:
4 ft $= 48$ in. $48 \div 13 = 3\frac{9}{13}$ in.

**Answer: $3\frac{9}{13}$ inches**

solutions.title: Long division
solutions.body:
$13 \times 3 = 39$, remainder $48 - 39 = 9$, so $\frac{48}{13} = 3\frac{9}{13}$.

**Answer: $3\frac{9}{13}$ inches**

prompt: On a bright, sunny day, Janine is standing 6 feet 3 inches away from the base of a 20-foot-tall flagpole. She notices that her shadow just touches the base of the flagpole. If Janine is exactly 5 feet tall, how long is the shadow of the flagpole at this same time?

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
Janine's shadow is 6 ft 3 in $= 6.25$ ft long. Shadows are proportional to heights: $\frac{6.25}{5} = \frac{x}{20}$, so $x = 25$ ft.

**Answer: 25 feet**

solutions.title: Shadow ratio
solutions.body:
Her shadow is $6.25 \div 5 = 1.25$ times her height, so the pole's shadow is $1.25 \times 20 = 25$ ft.

**Answer: 25 feet**

prompt: Small Town Ice Cream Shoppe carries five kinds of ice cream: vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, lemon custard and caramel swirl. They also have three types of toppings: sprinkles, chopped nuts and hot fudge. A "Shoppe Supreme" consists of three scoops of ice cream, not necessarily distinct flavors, and three scoops of toppings, also not necessarily distinct. If the ice cream is always scooped before the toppings are added, in how many distinct ways can a Shoppe Supreme be assembled at the Small Town Ice Cream Shoppe?

solutions.title: Multiplication principle
solutions.body:
The six scoops are added in order. Each ice cream scoop has 5 choices and each topping scoop has 3 choices: $5^3 \times 3^3 = 125 \times 27 = 3375$ ways of assembling.

**Answer: 3375**

solutions.title: Same idea, grouped
solutions.body:
Ice cream sequences: $5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 125$. Topping sequences: $3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 27$. Each pair gives a different assembly: $125 \times 27 = 3375$. Equivalently, $(5 \times 3)^3 = 15^3 = 3375$.

**Answer: 3375**

prompt: In the Ice Cream Shoppe, there are stools at the counter. Janet, Mason, Renae, Steve and Trina are going to sit side-by-side at the counter so that there are no empty seats between them. If Trina and Mason must sit next to each other, in how many possible distinct orders can they sit?

solutions.title: Treat the pair as one
solutions.body:
Glue Trina and Mason into one unit: 4 units can be ordered in $4! = 24$ ways, and the pair can be TM or MT: $24 \times 2 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

solutions.title: Place the pair
solutions.body:
The adjacent pair occupies seats 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 or 4-5 (4 choices), in 2 orders, and the other 3 people fill the remaining seats in $3! = 6$ ways: $4 \times 2 \times 6 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

prompt: Janet, Mason, Renae, Steve and Trina each ordered a different drink, but the waitress has forgotten who ordered what (and she is too embarrassed to ask). If she randomly places the drinks down, one in front of each person, what is the probability that she sets each of the five drinks down in front of the person who ordered it? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: One correct arrangement
solutions.body:
There are $5! = 120$ equally likely ways to hand out the drinks, and exactly one is fully correct: $\frac{1}{120}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{120}$**

solutions.title: Drink by drink
solutions.body:
First drink correct: $\frac15$; then $\frac14$, $\frac13$, $\frac12$, $1$. Product: $\frac{1}{120}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{120}$**

prompt: While walking around at their town's Independence Day Festival, Latrease and Hannah decide to buy lunch. Latrease bought two hot dogs and a soda for a total of \$7.50. Hannah bought a hot dog, a soda, and a bag of chips for \$5.50. If a bag of chips costs \$1.00, how much does one hot dog cost?

solutions.title: Subtract the orders
solutions.body:
Hannah's hot dog and soda cost $5.50 - 1.00 = 4.50$. Latrease's order has one more hot dog: $7.50 - 4.50 = 3.00$.

**Answer: \$3.00**

prompt: Frank is going to put on a fireworks show for his neighborhood. He bought 15 different fireworks to set off. If he plans to end with a specific sequence of five fireworks and he only wants to set off one firework at a time, how many distinct orders are there in which he could set off the fireworks?

solutions.title: Only the first ten vary
solutions.body:
The last five are fixed, so only the other 10 fireworks can be arranged in the first 10 slots: $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$.

**Answer: 3,628,800**

solutions.title: Slot by slot
solutions.body:
Slot 1 has 10 choices, slot 2 has 9, …, slot 10 has 1, and slots 11–15 have 1 each: $10 \cdot 9 \cdots 1 = 3{,}628{,}800$.

**Answer: 3,628,800**

prompt: Victoria and Hugo bought 42 cups of lemonade for the 10 guests they expected to have at their 4th of July party plus themselves. If 13 guests end up coming to the party, what is the minimum number of additional cups of lemonade that Victoria and Hugo must buy in order to have the planned amount of lemonade available to each guest and themselves? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Cups per person
solutions.body:
Planned: $42 \div 12 = 3.5$ cups per person. 3 extra guests need $3 \times 3.5 = 10.5$ more cups.

**Answer: 10.5 cups**

solutions.title: New total
solutions.body:
15 people at 3.5 cups is $52.5$ cups; they have 42, so they need $10.5$ more.

**Answer: 10.5 cups**

prompt: Smalltown is having a half-marathon race for walkers and runners. The length is 13 miles. Assume Starla walks the race at a constant rate of 4 miles per hour and Striper runs the race at a constant rate of 10 miles per hour. If Starla starts at 8:00 am, at what time should Striper start so that Starla and Striper cross the finish line at the same time?

solutions.title: Compare finishing times
solutions.body:
Starla takes $13 \div 4 = 3.25$ h and Striper $13 \div 10 = 1.3$ h. Striper should start $3.25 - 1.3 = 1.95$ h later; $0.95$ h $= 57$ min. So Striper starts at $8{:}00 + 1{:}57 = $ **9:57 a.m.**

**Answer: 9:57 a.m.**

solutions.title: Work back from the finish
solutions.body:
Starla finishes $3$ h $15$ min after 8:00, at 11:15 a.m. Striper needs $1.3$ h $= 1$ h $18$ min, so he starts at $11{:}15 - 1{:}18 = 9{:}57$ a.m.

**Answer: 9:57 a.m.**

prompt: Smalltown is having a 13-mile half-marathon race for walkers and runners. Starla walks the race at a constant rate of 4 miles per hour and Striper runs the race at a constant rate of 10 miles per hour. Starla starts at 8:00 a.m., and Striper starts later so that they both cross the finish line at the same time. At what distance, in miles, from the starting line is Starla when Striper starts running? Express your answer as a decimal number.

solutions.title: Head start time × rate
solutions.body:
Head start: $\frac{13}{4} - \frac{13}{10} = 3.25 - 1.3 = 1.95$ h. Distance: $4 \times 1.95 = 7.8$ miles.

**Answer: 7.8 miles**

solutions.title: Distance left
solutions.body:
When Striper starts, Starla has exactly as much time left as Striper needs, 1.3 h, in which she walks $4 \times 1.3 = 5.2$ miles. So she is $13 - 5.2 = 7.8$ miles from the start.

**Answer: 7.8 miles**

prompt: Smalltown is having a 13-mile half-marathon race for walkers and runners. Starla walks the race at a constant rate of 4 miles per hour and Striper runs the race at a constant rate of 10 miles per hour. Starla starts at 8:00 a.m., and Striper starts later so that they both cross the finish line at the same time. What percent of the length of the race does Starla walk before Striper starts running?

solutions.title: Distance ÷ total
solutions.body:
Starla's head start is $3.25 - 1.3 = 1.95$ h, in which she walks $4 \times 1.95 = 7.8$ miles. $\frac{7.8}{13} = 0.6 = 60\%$.

**Answer: 60%**

solutions.title: Ratio of speeds
solutions.body:
When Striper starts, both have the same time left, so the distances left are in ratio $4 : 10$. Striper has all 13 miles left, so Starla has $\frac{4}{10} \times 13 = 40\%$ of the race left, i.e. she has walked $60\%$.

**Answer: 60%**

prompt: When the letters of the alphabet are assigned their integer values (A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, …, Z = 26), the word-product of a sequence of letters is the product of the letter-values of its letters. When the square root of JULY's word-product is put into its simplest radical form of $a\sqrt{b}$, where $b$ has no perfect-square factors greater than 1, what is the value of $b$?

solutions.title: Prime factorize
solutions.body:
J = 10, U = 21, L = 12, Y = 25. Product $= 10 \cdot 21 \cdot 12 \cdot 25 = (2 \cdot 5)(3 \cdot 7)(2^2 \cdot 3)(5^2) = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7$.
$\sqrt{2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7} = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5\sqrt{2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7} = 30\sqrt{70}$, so $b = 70$.

**Answer: 70**

solutions.title: Compute the product
solutions.body:
$10 \cdot 21 \cdot 12 \cdot 25 = 63{,}000 = 900 \times 70$, and $\sqrt{900} = 30$. 70 = $2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$ has no square factor, so $\sqrt{63000} = 30\sqrt{70}$ and $b = 70$.

**Answer: 70**

prompt: When the letters of the alphabet are assigned their integer values (A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, …, Z = 26), the word-product of a sequence of letters is the product of the letter-values of its letters. What sequence of letters has the same word-product as JULY, but (1) does not contain any of the letters in JULY, (2) contains the letter N, (3) does not contain any of its letters more than once and (4) has its letters in alphabetical order?

solutions.title: Use the prime factorization
solutions.body:
JULY's word-product is $2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^3 \cdot 7$. N = 14 $= 2 \cdot 7$, leaving $2^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5^3$.
Three factors of 5 must come from different letters whose values are multiples of 5, other than J (10) and Y (25): only E = 5, O = 15 and T = 20. Together they give $5 \cdot 15 \cdot 20 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^3$, leaving a factor $3$: C = 3.
Letters C, E, N, O, T in alphabetical order: **CENOT**. (Adding A = 1 would not change the product; ACENOT is also accepted.)

**Answer: CENOT**

solutions.title: Check the product
solutions.body:
$C \cdot E \cdot N \cdot O \cdot T = 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 14 \cdot 15 \cdot 20 = 63{,}000$ and $J \cdot U \cdot L \cdot Y = 10 \cdot 21 \cdot 12 \cdot 25 = 63{,}000$ ✓. No letters repeat or come from JULY.

**Answer: CENOT**

prompt: When the letters of the alphabet are assigned their integer values (A = 1, B = 2, C = 3, …, Z = 26), the word-sum of a sequence of letters is the sum of the letter-values of its letters. The values of the letters of a particular four-letter sequence form an arithmetic sequence and this sequence has the same word-sum as JULY. What is the least possible value of a letter in this four-letter sequence?

solutions.title: Center at the average
solutions.body:
JULY's word-sum is $10 + 21 + 12 + 25 = 68$, average 17. A four-term arithmetic sequence is symmetric about its average: $17 - \frac{3d}{2}, 17 - \frac{d}{2}, 17 + \frac{d}{2}, 17 + \frac{3d}{2}$. For whole numbers $d$ must be even: $d = 2$: 14, 16, 18, 20; $d = 4$: 11, 15, 19, 23; $d = 6$: 8, 14, 20, 26; $d = 8$ would need 29 > 26. Least value: **8**.

**Answer: 8**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
$a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + (a + 3d) = 4a + 6d = 68$, so $2a + 3d = 34$. To make $a$ small, make $d$ large, but $a + 3d \le 26$. $d = 6$: $a = 8$, largest term $26$ ✓; $d = 8$: $a = 5$, largest $29$ ✗. So the least value is 8.

**Answer: 8**

prompt: Darcy has two part-time jobs during her summer vacation: counselor at a local day camp and lifeguard at the community swimming pool. Darcy works a combined total of 40 hours every week between the two jobs. The first week working both jobs, it rained all but one day, so three-fourths of the hours she worked that week were at the day camp. How many hours did Darcy work at the pool the first week?

solutions.title: Remaining fraction
solutions.body:
The pool got $1 - \frac34 = \frac14$ of the hours: $\frac14 \times 40 = 10$ hours.

**Answer: 10 hours**

solutions.title: Subtract camp hours
solutions.body:
Camp: $\frac34 \times 40 = 30$ hours. Pool: $40 - 30 = 10$ hours.

**Answer: 10 hours**

prompt: Darcy has two part-time jobs during her summer vacation: counselor at a local day camp and lifeguard at the community swimming pool. Darcy works a combined total of 40 hours every week between the two jobs. The second week, the number of hours Darcy worked at the day camp was $\frac35$ the number of hours she worked at the swimming pool. What is the positive difference in the number of hours Darcy worked at the day camp and the number of hours she worked at the pool during the second week?

solutions.title: Ratio parts
solutions.body:
Camp : pool $= 3 : 5$, which is 8 parts for 40 hours, so 1 part $= 5$ hours. Camp 15, pool 25; difference $10$ hours.

**Answer: 10 hours**

prompt: Darcy has two part-time jobs during her summer vacation: counselor at a local day camp and lifeguard at the community swimming pool. Darcy works a combined total of 40 hours every week between the two jobs. In the first week, three-fourths of her hours were at the day camp. In the second week, her day-camp hours were $\frac35$ of her pool hours. Darcy earns \$8 per hour as a camp counselor and \$12 per hour as a lifeguard. What is the positive difference in the amount Darcy earned the first week and the amount she earned the second week?

solutions.title: Only the shift matters
solutions.body:
From week 1 to week 2, 15 hours moved from camp to pool (pool went from 10 to 25). Each moved hour pays $12 - 8 = 4$ dollars more: $15 \times 4 = 60$.

**Answer: \$60**

prompt: Darcy has two part-time jobs during her summer vacation: counselor at a local day camp and lifeguard at the community swimming pool. Darcy works a combined total of 40 hours every week between the two jobs. Darcy earns \$8 per hour as a camp counselor and \$12 per hour as a lifeguard. What is the total amount Darcy will earn during the third week if she earns the same amount working at the day camp as she earns working at the pool?

solutions.title: Set the earnings equal
solutions.body:
$8d = 12p$ gives $d = \frac32 p$. Then $\frac32 p + p = 40$, so $p = 16$ and $d = 24$. Each job pays $12 \times 16 = 192$, total $384$ dollars.

**Answer: \$384**

solutions.title: Inverse ratio
solutions.body:
Equal pay means hours are in the inverse ratio of wages: camp : pool $= 12 : 8 = 3 : 2$, so 24 h and 16 h. Earnings: $8(24) + 12(16) = 192 + 192 = 384$.

**Answer: \$384**

prompt: What is the greatest positive three-digit integer that is divisible by 5, 7 and 9?

solutions.title: Multiples of the LCM
solutions.body:
5, 7 and 9 are pairwise relatively prime, so the number must be a multiple of $5 \cdot 7 \cdot 9 = 315$. Multiples: 315, 630, 945, 1260. The greatest three-digit one is 945.

**Answer: 945**

solutions.title: Work down from 999
solutions.body:
A multiple of 5 and 9 ends in 0 or 5 and has digit sum divisible by 9: the largest three-digit ones are 990, 945, … $990 = 7 \cdot 141 + 3$ ✗; $945 = 7 \cdot 135$ ✓.

**Answer: 945**

prompt: What is the greatest possible product of a pair of two-digit integers, composed of the digits 8, 6, 4 and 2 if each digit is used exactly once?

solutions.title: Big digits in the tens place
solutions.body:
Put 8 and 6 in the tens places. The options are $84 \times 62 = 5208$ and $82 \times 64 = 5248$. The greatest product is 5248.

**Answer: 5248**

solutions.title: Keep the numbers close
solutions.body:
With a fixed sum ($80 + 60 + 4 + 2$ is always 146), a product is largest when the two factors are as close as possible. 82 and 64 (difference 18) are closer than 84 and 62 (difference 22), so $82 \times 64 = 5248$ wins.

**Answer: 5248**

prompt: A proper divisor of a number is a divisor of the number that is not the number itself. What is the smallest positive integer that is less than the sum of its positive proper divisors?

solutions.title: Check in order
solutions.body:
Primes have proper-divisor sum 1. Composites: 4 → 3; 6 → 6 (equal); 8 → 7; 9 → 4; 10 → 8; 12 → $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 16 > 12$ ✓.

**Answer: 12**

solutions.title: Abundant numbers
solutions.body:
Numbers whose proper divisors add to more than the number are called abundant. A number below 12 would need many divisors; only 6, 8 and 10 have 3 or more proper divisors, and their sums are 6, 7 and 8 — not enough. 12 is the smallest abundant number.

**Answer: 12**

prompt: For how many positive four-digit integers is the sum of its digits equal to the product of its digits?

solutions.title: Find the digits
solutions.body:
No digit can be 0 (product 0, sum positive). Testing small digit sets: $1,1,2,4$ gives sum $8$ and product $8$ ✓; others fail (e.g. $1,1,1,x$: $3 + x \ne x$; $1,1,3,3$: 8 vs 9; $1,2,2,2$: 7 vs 8; $1,1,2,5$: 9 vs 10). Arrangements of 1, 1, 2, 4: $\frac{4!}{2!} = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

solutions.title: Bound the digits
solutions.body:
No digit is 0. With digits $a \le b \le c \le d$, sum $\le 4d$, so the product $abc \cdot d \le 4d$ means $abc \le 4$. The options for $(a,b,c)$ are $(1,1,1), (1,1,2), (1,1,3), (1,1,4), (1,2,2)$. Solving $a + b + c + d = abcd$: $(1,1,1)$: $3 + d = d$ ✗; $(1,1,2)$: $4 + d = 2d \Rightarrow d = 4$ ✓; $(1,1,3)$: $5 + d = 3d \Rightarrow d = 2.5$ ✗; $(1,1,4)$: $6 + d = 4d \Rightarrow d = 2 < c$ ✗; $(1,2,2)$: $5 + d = 4d$ ✗. Only $\{1,1,2,4\}$, with 12 arrangements.

**Answer: 12**

solutions.title: Recompute

The mean of all ten is $1033 \div 10 = 103.3$. Removing 77: $(1033 - 77) \div 9 = 956 \div 9 \approx 106.2$°F. Difference: $106.2 - 103.3 = 2.9$.

$\frac{114}{125} = 0.912$, so 2026's high is 91.2% of the record — a decrease of $100 - 91.2 = 8.8\%$.

$T \times 1.082 = 106$, so $T = 106 \div 1.082 \approx 97.97 \approx 98$°F.

solutions.title: Check

$98 \times 1.082 = 106.04 \approx 106$ ✓, while $97 \times 1.082 \approx 104.95$ and $99 \times 1.082 \approx 107.1$ are farther off.

prompt:
In the video game Asteroid Blaster, there are a total of five rounds on the first level. During each round, asteroids appear on the screen and a player must blast as many asteroids as possible before time expires. This becomes more difficult because the number of asteroids increases with each round. The table shows the number of asteroids for each of the first three rounds.

| Round | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

| Asteroids | 1 | 8 | 27 | | |

If this pattern continues, how many asteroids will there be to destroy in Round 4?

solutions.title: Differences
solutions.body:
The differences are 7 and 19. For cubes the differences themselves grow by 12, 18, 24, … (6 more each time), so the next difference is $19 + 18 = 37$ and Round 4 has $27 + 37 = 64$.

prompt:
In the video game Asteroid Blaster, there are five rounds on the first level. The amount of time within which a player must blast all the asteroids increases each round. The table shows the time limit, in seconds, for each round.

Each time limit doubles, so Round 5 gets 32 seconds. Total: $2 + 4 + 8 + 16 + 32 = 62$ seconds.

prompt:
In the video game Asteroid Blaster, the first level has five rounds. The number of asteroids in Rounds 1, 2 and 3 is 1, 8 and 27, and this pattern continues for Rounds 4 and 5. The number of points awarded for blasting each asteroid also increases with each round, as shown in the table.

How many points will a player earn for blasting all the asteroids in Rounds 1 through 4 and blasting $\frac25$ of the asteroids in Round 5 before time expires?

solutions.title: Pattern $10n^4$
solutions.body:
In round $n$ there are $n^3$ asteroids worth $10n$ points each, so a full round is worth $10n^4$: $10(1 + 16 + 81 + 256) = 3540$ for rounds 1–4, plus $\frac25 \cdot 10 \cdot 625 = 2500$: total 6040.

**Answer: 6040 points**

prompt: At Summer's annual physical exam on May 31st, her height was determined to be 4 feet and 3 inches. Summer last visited the doctor the previous year on September 28th at which time her height was 3 feet and $11\frac12$ inches. Based on this data, on average, how many inches did Summer grow each day? (February had 28 days.) Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Growth ÷ days
solutions.body:
Growth: from 3 ft $11\frac12$ in to 4 ft 3 in is $\frac12 + 3 = 3\frac12$ inches.
Days: Sept 28 → 30 is 2 days, then Oct 31, Nov 30, Dec 31, Jan 31, Feb 28, Mar 31, Apr 30, May 31: $2 + 31 + 30 + 31 + 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 31 = 245$.
Rate: $\frac{7}{2} \div 245 = \frac{7}{490} = \frac{1}{70}$ inch per day.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{70}$ inch per day**

solutions.title: Count days backward
solutions.body:
A full year minus the days from May 31 to Sept 28: there are $30 + 31 + 31 + 28 = 120$ days from May 31 to Sept 28, so $365 - 120 = 245$ days from Sept 28 to May 31. Heights in inches: $47.5 \to 51$, a growth of 3.5. $\frac{3.5}{245} = \frac{1}{70}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{70}$ inch per day**

prompt: At Summer's last doctor visit on September 28 her height was 3 feet $11\frac12$ inches, and at her annual physical exam on May 31st (the following year, not a leap year) her height was 4 feet 3 inches. Summer wants to ride the Shocker roller coaster before returning to school. Unfortunately, this roller coaster has a minimum height restriction of $4\frac12$ ft. Summer measured herself on August 16th, and she is still not tall enough. If Summer maintained her average rate of growth between those two doctor visits since May 31st, how many inches does Summer need to grow during the rest of her summer break in order to meet the minimum height restriction and ride the Shocker? Express your answer as a mixed number in simplest form.

solutions.title: Growth since May 31
solutions.body:
Average rate: $3\frac12$ in over 245 days (Sept 28 to May 31) $= \frac1{70}$ in/day.
May 31 → Aug 16: $30 + 31 + 16 = 77$ days, growth $\frac{77}{70} = 1\frac1{10}$ in. Height: 4 ft $4\frac1{10}$ in. Needed: $4$ ft $6$ in, so $6 - 4\frac1{10} = 1\frac9{10}$ inches more.

**Answer: $1\frac{9}{10}$ inches**

solutions.title: All in inches
solutions.body:
Required height $54$ in. Height Aug 16: $51 + 77 \cdot \frac1{70} = 51 + 1.1 = 52.1$ in. Needed: $54 - 52.1 = 1.9 = 1\frac9{10}$ in.

**Answer: $1\frac{9}{10}$ inches**

prompt: At Summer's last doctor visit on September 28 her height was 3 feet $11\frac12$ inches, and at her annual physical exam on May 31st (the following year, not a leap year) her height was 4 feet 3 inches. The Shocker roller coaster has a minimum height restriction of $4\frac12$ ft. Assume Summer keeps growing at her average rate between those two doctor visits. Summer is determined to ride the Shocker before school begins on September 8th. Summer heard that practicing yoga makes you taller. In addition to the number of inches Summer expects to grow from August 16th to September 7th, by how many inches will Summer need to increase her height as a result of practicing yoga in order to meet the minimum height restriction and ride the Shocker before September 8th? Express your answer as a mixed number in simplest form.

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
Rate: $3\frac12$ in over 245 days $= \frac1{70}$ in/day.
Height on Aug 16: $51 + \frac{77}{70} = 52\frac1{10}$ in (77 days after May 31). She still needs $54 - 52\frac1{10} = 1\frac9{10}$ in.
Aug 16 → Sept 7: $15 + 7 = 22$ days, natural growth $\frac{22}{70} = \frac{11}{35}$ in.
Yoga must add $1\frac9{10} - \frac{11}{35} = \frac{133}{70} - \frac{22}{70} = \frac{111}{70} = 1\frac{41}{70}$ in.

**Answer: $1\frac{41}{70}$ inches**

solutions.title: Directly from May 31
solutions.body:
May 31 → Sept 7 is $30 + 31 + 31 + 7 = 99$ days, growth $\frac{99}{70}$ in. She needs $54 - 51 = 3$ in total, so yoga must add $3 - \frac{99}{70} = \frac{111}{70} = 1\frac{41}{70}$ in.

**Answer: $1\frac{41}{70}$ inches**

prompt: Sawyer's family took a road trip from Washington, DC to Duck, NC. On the way, they stopped for lunch in Richmond, VA, which was 106 miles from DC and 174 miles from Duck, NC. They traveled at an average speed of 58 mph from DC to Richmond, and after lunch it took them 3 hours and 12 minutes to get to Duck. What is Sawyer's family's average speed in miles per hour for the entire trip from Washington, DC to Duck, NC (disregard the time spent at rest stops, lunch, etc.)? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Total distance ÷ total time
solutions.body:
Distance: $106 + 174 = 280$ miles. Time: $\frac{106}{58} \approx 1.8276$ h plus $3.2$ h $= 5.0276$ h. Speed: $280 \div 5.0276 \approx 55.7$ mph.

**Answer: 55.7 mph**

prompt: Sawyer's family took a road trip from Washington, DC to Duck, NC. On the way, they stopped for lunch in Richmond, VA, which was 106 miles from DC and 174 miles from Duck, NC. They traveled at an average speed of 58 mph from DC to Richmond, and after lunch it took them 3 hours and 12 minutes to get to Duck. On the return trip, Sawyer's family decides to stop to take a break in Williamsburg, VA, which is 126 miles from Duck, NC and 153 miles from Washington, DC. If Sawyer's family drove at a speed of 54 mph from Duck to Williamsburg, what must their average speed, in mph, be for the rest of the trip so that their driving time from Duck to DC is the same as their total driving time from DC to Duck (disregard the time spent at rest stops, lunch, etc.)? Express your answer as an integer.

solutions.title: Time remaining
solutions.body:
DC → Duck took $\frac{106}{58} + 3.2 \approx 5.0276$ h. Duck → Williamsburg: $126 \div 54 \approx 2.3333$ h. Time left: $5.0276 - 2.3333 = 2.6943$ h. Speed: $153 \div 2.6943 \approx 56.8 \approx 57$ mph.

**Answer: 57 mph**

solutions.title: Fractions
solutions.body:
Total time $\frac{729}{145}$ h; first leg $\frac{7}{3}$ h. Remaining: $\frac{729}{145} - \frac73 = \frac{2187 - 1015}{435} = \frac{1172}{435}$ h. Speed $= 153 \cdot \frac{435}{1172} \approx 56.79 \approx 57$ mph.

**Answer: 57 mph**

prompt: Sawyer's family took a road trip from Washington, DC to Duck, NC. On the way, they stopped for lunch in Richmond, VA, which was 106 miles from DC and 174 miles from Duck, NC. They traveled at an average speed of 58 mph from DC to Richmond, and after lunch it took them 3 hours and 12 minutes to get to Duck. On the return trip, Sawyer's family stopped to take a break in Williamsburg, VA, which is 126 miles from Duck, NC and 153 miles from Washington, DC. They drove at a speed of 54 mph from Duck to Williamsburg, and planned to drive the rest of the way in exactly the time that would make their driving time from Duck to DC the same as their total driving time from DC to Duck, which requires an average speed of about 57 mph. There was road work between Williamsburg and DC. Sawyer's family had to reduce their speed to 45 mph for 20 miles and to 30 mph for 10 miles. If they were able to maintain 57 mph for the rest of the drive from Williamsburg to DC, how much time was added compared with their planned driving time from Williamsburg to DC (disregard the time spent at rest stops, lunch, etc.)? Express your answer in minutes to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Actual minus planned

Planned Williamsburg → DC time: total DC → Duck time $\frac{106}{58} + 3.2 \approx 5.0276$ h minus Duck → Williamsburg $126/54 \approx 2.3333$ h $= 2.6943$ h.

prompt: The MATHCOUNTS Club at your school is planning a pizza party for the club's 10 Mathletes. The local pizza place has medium and large as the two size options. An 8-slice medium pizza has a diameter of 11 inches and costs \$10.99. A 16-slice large pizza costs \$15.99 and has a diameter of $16\frac12$ inches. The restaurant currently has a special that if you purchase a pizza, each additional pizza of equal or smaller size is just \$5. What is the area of each size pizza? Express your answers as decimals to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Area formula
solutions.body:
Medium: $r = 5.5$, $A = \pi(5.5)^2 = 30.25\pi \approx 95.03$ in². Large: $r = 8.25$, $A = \pi(8.25)^2 = 68.0625\pi \approx 213.82$ in².

**Answer: medium ≈ 95.03 in², large ≈ 213.82 in²**

solutions.title: Scale the medium
solutions.body:
The large diameter is $16.5 \div 11 = 1.5$ times the medium's, so its area is $1.5^2 = 2.25$ times: $30.25\pi \times 2.25 = 68.0625\pi \approx 213.82$ in², with medium $30.25\pi \approx 95.03$ in².

**Answer: medium ≈ 95.03 in², large ≈ 213.82 in²**

prompt: The MATHCOUNTS Club at your school is planning a pizza party for the club's 10 Mathletes. The local pizza place has medium and large as the two size options. solutions.title: Area needed
solutions.body:
Large area $\approx 213.82$ in², so one large slice $\approx 13.36$ in². Twenty large slices (2 for each of 10 members) $\approx 267.28$ in². A medium has $\approx 95.03$ in²: $267.28 \div 95.03 \approx 2.81$, so **3 medium** pizzas. Large: 20 slices $\div$ 16 per pizza $= 1.25$, so **2 large** pizzas.

**Answer: 3 medium or 2 large**

solutions.title: Compare in large-pizza units
solutions.body:
They need $\frac{20}{16} = 1.25$ large pizzas' worth of area. A medium is $\left(\frac{11}{16.5}\right)^2 = \frac49$ of a large. Medium pizzas needed: $1.25 \div \frac49 = 2.8125$, so 3. Large: $1.25 \to 2$.

**Answer: 3 medium or 2 large**

prompt: Students at Sandstone Middle School have been welcomed back for the new school year. But it took Mr. Allen weeks to get all the classrooms ready. There are three classrooms along one hallway. The length and width of the classrooms increase proportionally. The 1st classroom measures 15 feet long by 18 feet wide. The 2nd classroom measures $18\frac34$ feet long by $22\frac12$ feet wide. The 3rd classroom is larger than the 2nd classroom. How many square feet of tile did Mr. Allen need to tile the floors in all three classrooms? Express your answer as a mixed number in simplest form.

solutions.title: Areas scale by the square
solutions.body:
Lengths scale by $\frac54$, so areas scale by $\frac{25}{16}$. The three areas are $270$, $270 \cdot \frac{25}{16}$, $270 \cdot \left(\frac{25}{16}\right)^2$:
$$270\left(1 + \frac{25}{16} + \frac{625}{256}\right) = 270 \cdot \frac{256 + 400 + 625}{256} = 270 \cdot \frac{1281}{256} = \frac{345870}{256} = \frac{172935}{128} = 1351\frac{7}{128}.$$

**Answer: $1351\frac{7}{128}$ square feet**

prompt: Mr. Allen is getting three classrooms along one hallway ready for the school year. The length and width of the classrooms increase proportionally: the 1st classroom measures 15 feet long by 18 feet wide, the 2nd classroom measures $18\frac34$ feet long by $22\frac12$ feet wide, and the 3rd classroom is larger than the 2nd, enlarged by the same scale factor. The height of each classroom is 10 feet. Each classroom has a doorway that is $6\frac34$ feet tall and $3\frac12$ feet wide and a window that is 5 feet tall and $11\frac12$ feet wide. He paints the walls (not the floors or ceilings), except the doorways and windows. How many square feet did Mr. Allen have to paint in all three classrooms? Express your answer as a mixed number in simplest form.

solutions.title: Room by room
solutions.body:
3rd room: $\frac{375}{16} = 23\frac7{16}$ ft by $\frac{225}{8} = 28\frac18$ ft (scale factor $\frac54$).
Wall area $= 10 \times$ perimeter:
- 1st: $10 \cdot 2(15 + 18) = 660$
- 2nd: $10 \cdot 2(18\frac34 + 22\frac12) = 825$
- 3rd: $10 \cdot 2(23\frac7{16} + 28\frac18) = 1031\frac14$

Door + window per room: $6\frac34 \cdot 3\frac12 + 5 \cdot 11\frac12 = 23\frac58 + 57\frac12 = 81\frac18$.
Paint: $(660 + 825 + 1031\frac14) - 3 \cdot 81\frac18 = 2516\frac14 - 243\frac38 = 2272\frac78$ ft².

**Answer: $2272\frac{7}{8}$ square feet**

solutions.title: Perimeters scale too
solutions.body:
Perimeters scale by $\frac54$: $66$, $82.5$, $103.125$ ft, total $251.625$ ft. Wall area $= 2516.25$ ft². Openings: $3 \times 81.125 = 243.375$ ft². Paint: $2516.25 - 243.375 = 2272.875 = 2272\frac78$ ft².

**Answer: $2272\frac{7}{8}$ square feet**

prompt: Mr. Allen is getting three classrooms along one hallway ready for the school year. When he only lays tile, Mr. Allen can lay 225 square feet of tile a day. When he only paints, Mr. Allen can paint 750 square feet a day. How many days did it take him to tile and paint all three classrooms? Express your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.title: Tile days + paint days
solutions.body:
Floor area (scale factor $\frac54$ per room): $270 + 421\frac78 + 659\frac{23}{128} = 1351\frac7{128}$ ft². Wall area to paint: $2272\frac78$ ft² (walls $10 \times$ perimeter, minus $81\frac18$ ft² of door and window per room).
Tile: $1351.05 \div 225 \approx 6.005$ days. Paint: $2272.875 \div 750 \approx 3.031$ days. Total $\approx 9.04 \approx 9$ days.

**Answer: 9 days**

solutions.title: Estimate
solutions.body:
Floor area $\approx 1351$ ft² is almost exactly $6 \times 225 = 1350$; wall area $\approx 2273$ ft² is about $3 \times 750 = 2250$. So about $6 + 3 = 9$ days (precisely 9.04).

**Answer: 9 days**

The figure shows a square inscribed in a circle with radius 2 cm. What is the ratio of the area of the circle to the area of the square? Express your answer as a common fraction in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Diagonal = diameter
solutions.body:
Circle area: $4\pi$. The square's diagonal is the diameter, 4 cm, so its side is $\frac{4}{\sqrt2} = 2\sqrt2$ and its area is $8$. Ratio: $\frac{4\pi}{8} = \frac{\pi}{2}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{2}$**

solutions.title: Square from its diagonal
solutions.body:
A square's area is half its diagonal squared: $\frac{4^2}{2} = 8$. Ratio $\frac{4\pi}{8} = \frac\pi2$ (this is true for every inscribed square: $\frac{\pi r^2}{2r^2}$).

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{2}$**

prompt: In this figure, a square is inscribed in a circle of radius 12 inches, and another circle is inscribed in that square. What is the ratio of the area of the smaller circle to the area of the larger circle? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Find the small radius
solutions.body:
The square's diagonal is 24, so its side is $12\sqrt2$, which is the small circle's diameter: radius $6\sqrt2$. Areas: $\pi(6\sqrt2)^2 = 72\pi$ and $144\pi$. Ratio $\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

solutions.title: Ratio of radii
solutions.body:
From the center, the big radius goes to a corner of the square and the small radius to the midpoint of a side; these form a 45-45-90 triangle, so small : big $= 1 : \sqrt2$. Areas are in ratio $1 : 2$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

prompt: This figure shows a circle inscribed in a rhombus with diagonals of length 6 cm and 8 cm. What is the ratio of the area of the circle to the area of the rhombus? Express your answer as a common fraction in terms of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Radius as an altitude
solutions.body:
The diagonals cut the rhombus into four right triangles with legs 3 and 4 and hypotenuse 5 (a side of the rhombus). Rhombus area: $4 \cdot \frac12 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 = 24$. The radius to a side is the altitude of a 3-4-5 triangle onto its hypotenuse: $\frac12 \cdot 5 \cdot r = 6$, so $r = \frac{12}{5}$. Circle area $= \frac{144\pi}{25}$. Ratio: $\frac{144\pi}{25 \cdot 24} = \frac{6\pi}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac{6\pi}{25}$**

solutions.title: Area = inradius × semiperimeter
solutions.body:
For any polygon with an inscribed circle, area $= r \times$ (half the perimeter). Rhombus area $= \frac{6 \cdot 8}{2} = 24$; side $= 5$, half-perimeter $= 10$. So $r = 2.4$ and the ratio is $\frac{\pi (2.4)^2}{24} = \frac{5.76\pi}{24} = 0.24\pi = \frac{6\pi}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac{6\pi}{25}$**

The mean weight of a crate of 9 pumpkins is 16 pounds. One of the pumpkins is removed. The mean weight of the remaining 8 pumpkins is 13 pounds. What is the weight, in pounds, of the pumpkin that was removed?

solutions.title: Totals
solutions.body:
$9 \times 16 = 144$ and $8 \times 13 = 104$. Removed: $144 - 104 = 40$ pounds.

**Answer: 40 pounds**

solutions.title: Effect on the mean
solutions.body:

solutions.body:
Haejin is at $(3, 2)$ and Harmoni at $(9, -3)$. Going from Harmoni to Haejin is 6 left and 5 up. A parallelogram with the town square west of Hallie needs the side from Hallie to the town square to match: $(6 - 6, -7 + 5) = (0, -2)$.

solutions.title: All three possible fourth vertices

For points $P$, $Q$, $R$, the fourth vertex of a parallelogram is $P + Q - R$ for some choice of $R$:
- Hallie + Haejin − Harmoni $= (0, -2)$
- Hallie + Harmoni − Haejin $= (12, -12)$
- Haejin + Harmoni − Hallie $= (6, 12)$

Only $(0, -2)$ is west of Hallie ($x < 6$).

**Answer: $(0, -2)$**

prompt: There is a fun divisibility rule for 11. For any integer, insert alternating minus (–) and plus (+) signs between the consecutive pairs of digits, starting with a minus sign between the left-most pair of digits. For example, the number 91,828 would be written $9 - 1 + 8 - 2 + 8$. Now, simplify the expression: $9 - 1 + 8 - 2 + 8 = 22$. Since this value, 22, is divisible by 11, the original number is divisible by 11. Using this rule, if the five-digit integer $76{,}9a2$ is a multiple of 11, what is the value of the digit $a$?

solutions.title: Apply the rule
solutions.body:
$7 - 6 + 9 - a + 2 = 12 - a$. For a digit $a$, $12 - a$ is between 3 and 12, and the only multiple of 11 there is 11, so $a = 1$. Check: $76{,}912 = 11 \times 6992$ ✓.

**Answer: 1**

solutions.title: Divide directly
solutions.body:
$76{,}902 = 11 \times 6991 + 1$, so $76{,}902$ leaves remainder 1. Adding $10a$ must fix this: $10a \equiv -1 \equiv 10 \pmod{11}$, so $a = 1$.

**Answer: 1**

prompt: When playing many games, players must roll a pair of dice and find the sum of the two numbers rolled. With two 6-sided dice, there are 11 possible sums ranging from 2 through 12. Of the $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely outcomes, a sum of 11 comes from (5, 6) and (6, 5): $\frac{2}{36} = \frac{1}{18}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{18}$**

solutions.title: First die then second

The first die must be 5 or 6 ($\frac26$), and then the second die must be the one number that makes 11 ($\frac16$): $\frac26 \cdot \frac16 = \frac1{18}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{18}$**

prompt: Eleven is a palindrome. A palindrome is an integer that reads the same backward and forward. The integer 12,321 is a palindrome since writing the numbers in reverse order is also 12,321. What is the greatest possible four-digit palindrome that is a multiple of 6?

solutions.title: Even, and digit sum divisible by 3
solutions.body:
A four-digit palindrome is $abba$. To be even, its last digit $a$ is even; the largest choice is $a = 8$. Its digit sum $2a + 2b = 16 + 2b$ must be divisible by 3, so $2b \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, i.e. $b \in \{1, 4, 7\}$. The largest is $b = 7$: **8778** ($= 6 \times 1463$).

**Answer: 8778**

solutions.title: Check from the top
solutions.body:
Palindromes starting with 9 end in 9 (odd), so try 8998, 8888, 8778, …: digit sums 34, 32, 30. Only 8778 has digit sum divisible by 3, so it is the first multiple of 6.

**Answer: 8778**

Area = length × width, so length $= 105 \div 7 = 15$ inches.

**Answer: 15 inches**

prompt: What integer is closest to $-7\pi$?

solutions.title: Estimate
solutions.body:
$\pi \approx 3.1416$, so $7\pi \approx 21.99$ and $-7\pi \approx -21.99$. The closest integer is $-22$.

**Answer: −22**

solutions.title: Bound it
solutions.body:
$3.14 < \pi < 3.15$ gives $21.98 < 7\pi < 22.05$, so $7\pi$ is within $0.05$ of 22, and $-7\pi$ is closest to $-22$.

**Answer: −22**

prompt: On Monday at 8 p.m., the temperature measured −17 degrees. Between 8 p.m. on Monday and 6 a.m. on Tuesday, the temperature increased 23 degrees. On Tuesday, between 6 a.m. and 3 p.m., the temperature decreased 5 degrees. What was the temperature on Tuesday at 3 p.m.?

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
$-17 + 23 = 6$ degrees at 6 a.m. Then $6 - 5 = 1$ degree at 3 p.m.

**Answer: 1 degree**

solutions.title: Net change
solutions.body:
The net change is $+23 - 5 = +18$ degrees, so the final temperature is $-17 + 18 = 1$ degree.

**Answer: 1 degree**

prompt: This table shows all five lunch options on Friday at a middle school and the number of students that ordered each. Based on this, what percent of the lunch orders on Friday were for spaghetti?

solutions.title: Scale to 100
solutions.body:
400 orders is 4 groups of 100; $44 \div 4 = 11$ spaghetti orders per 100 orders, so 11%.

**Answer: 11%**

prompt: What is the 40th positive odd integer?

solutions.title: Formula
solutions.body:
The $n$th positive odd integer is $2n - 1$. For $n = 40$: $2 \cdot 40 - 1 = 79$.

**Answer: 79**

solutions.title: Pair with even numbers
solutions.body:
The 40th positive even integer is 80; each odd integer is 1 less than the even integer in the same position, so the 40th odd integer is 79.

**Answer: 79**

prompt: What is the value of the expression $1 + \dfrac{2}{1 - \frac{2}{3}}$, in simplest form?
If $(x^2y^3)^2 = x^ay^b$, what is the value of $a + b$?

solutions.title: Shortcut
solutions.body:
Squaring doubles every exponent, so $a + b = 2(2 + 3) = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: For each rock-paper-scissors match, paper beats rock, rock beats scissors, scissors beat paper and two identical items result in a tie. Based on this table, which summarizes the results of Kalyani and Mark’s last 200 matches, how many matches did Kalyani win?

solutions.title: Find the winning cells
solutions.body:
Columns are Kalyani’s choice and rows are Mark’s. Kalyani wins when:
- Kalyani paper, Mark rock: 24
- Kalyani rock, Mark scissors: 20
- Kalyani scissors, Mark paper: 21

Total: $24 + 20 + 21 = 65$.

**Answer: 65 matches**

solutions.title: Subtract ties and losses
solutions.body:
Ties (diagonal): $30 + 21 + 18 = 69$. Mark wins (Mark rock vs scissors 20, Mark paper vs rock 26, Mark scissors vs paper 20): 66. Kalyani wins $200 - 69 - 66 = 65$.

**Answer: 65 matches**

prompt: Given that a mile equals 5280 feet, how many inches are in one-sixth of a mile?

solutions.title: Feet first
solutions.body:
One-sixth of a mile is $5280 \div 6 = 880$ feet, which is $880 \times 12 = 10{,}560$ inches.

**Answer: 10,560 inches**

solutions.title: Simplify first
solutions.body:
$\frac{5280 \times 12}{6} = 5280 \times 2 = 10{,}560$ inches.

**Answer: 10,560 inches**

prompt: Maria was born on January 1, 2000. Her mother was born on January 1, 1975 and her father was born on January 1, 1970. In what year was the sum of their ages 100?

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
In year $Y$ the ages are $Y - 2000$, $Y - 1975$, $Y - 1970$. Their sum is $3Y - 5945 = 100$, so $3Y = 6045$ and $Y = 2015$.

**Answer: 2015**

solutions.title: Start in 2000
solutions.body:
On January 1, 2000 the ages are 0, 25 and 30, sum 55. Each year adds 3 to the sum, and we need $100 - 55 = 45$ more, i.e. 15 years: 2015.

**Answer: 2015**

prompt: A bicycle that originally cost \$200 is on sale for \$140. By what percent was the price reduced?

solutions.title: Percent decrease
solutions.body:
The reduction is $200 - 140 = 60$ dollars, and $\frac{60}{200} = 30\%$.

**Answer: 30%**

solutions.title: Compare prices
solutions.body:
$\frac{140}{200} = 70\%$ of the original price, so the price was reduced by $100\% - 70\% = 30\%$.

**Answer: 30%**

prompt: Jay’s dog outgrew his rectangular pen that measured 10 feet by 14 feet. To make it larger, he increased each side length by the same amount, which increased the pen’s area by 81 square feet. What is the greater side length of the larger pen?

solutions.title: Look for factors
solutions.body:
The new area is $140 + 81 = 221$ sq ft, and the new sides differ by 4. Since $221 = 13 \times 17$, the new pen is 13 ft by 17 ft.

**Answer: 17 feet**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
Let $x$ be the increase: $(10 + x)(14 + x) = 221$, so $x^2 + 24x - 81 = 0$, $(x + 27)(x - 3) = 0$, $x = 3$. The greater side is $14 + 3 = 17$ ft.

**Answer: 17 feet**

prompt: Parker has three sons: Alfred, Beto and Dell. When Alfred turned 11 years old, Beto was 9 years old and Dell was 4 years old. What was the average of their ages when Alfred turned 37?

solutions.title: Find each age
solutions.body:
Alfred aged $37 - 11 = 26$ years, so Beto is $9 + 26 = 35$ and Dell is $4 + 26 = 30$. Average: $\frac{37 + 35 + 30}{3} = \frac{102}{3} = 34$.

**Answer: 34 years**

solutions.title: Shift the average
solutions.body:
The average was $\frac{11 + 9 + 4}{3} = 8$. Everyone is 26 years older, so the average is $8 + 26 = 34$.

**Answer: 34 years**

prompt: Triangle $ABC$ has an area of 40 units$^2$. Point $D$ is on side $AC$, and $AD:DC = 3:1$. What is the area of triangle $BDC$?

solutions.title: Same height
solutions.body:
Triangles $ABD$ and $BDC$ share the height from $B$ to line $AC$, so their areas are in the ratio of their bases $3:1$. Triangle $BDC$ gets $\frac14$ of 40, which is 10.

**Answer: 10 units²**

solutions.title: Formula
solutions.body:
Area of $BDC = \frac12 \cdot DC \cdot h = \frac12 \cdot \frac{AC}{4} \cdot h = \frac14 \left(\frac12 \cdot AC \cdot h\right) = \frac{40}{4} = 10$.

**Answer: 10 units²**

prompt: Kendra surveyed 100 people who own a dog or a cat, or both. Of those surveyed, 15 own both a dog and a cat, and the number of people who own a dog is four times the number of people who own a cat. How many people surveyed own a cat?

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
Let $c$ own a cat, so $4c$ own a dog. Then $4c + c - 15 = 100$, so $5c = 115$ and $c = 23$.

**Answer: 23 people**

solutions.title: Check with a Venn diagram
solutions.body:
With 23 cat owners and 92 dog owners: cat only $23 - 15 = 8$, dog only $92 - 15 = 77$, both 15. Total $8 + 77 + 15 = 100$ ✓.

**Answer: 23 people**

prompt: What is the area of the region in the first quadrant that lies between the lines $x + 3y = 12$ and $x + 3y = 18$?

solutions.title: Subtract triangles
solutions.body:
Each line cuts off a right triangle with the axes. $x + 3y = 18$ meets the axes at $(18, 0)$ and $(0, 6)$: area $\frac12 \cdot 18 \cdot 6 = 54$. $x + 3y = 12$ meets them at $(12, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$: area $\frac12 \cdot 12 \cdot 4 = 24$. The region between them has area $54 - 24 = 30$.

**Answer: 30 units²**

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
The two triangles are similar with ratio $12 : 18 = 2 : 3$, so their areas are in ratio $4 : 9$. The big one has area 54, the small one $\frac49 \cdot 54 = 24$, and the difference is 30.

**Answer: 30 units²**

prompt: What is the absolute difference between the mean and median of the first 100 positive integers?

solutions.title: Compute both
solutions.body:
Mean: $\frac{1 + 2 + \cdots + 100}{100} = \frac{5050}{100} = 50.5$. Median: average of the 50th and 51st values, $\frac{50 + 51}{2} = 50.5$. Difference: 0.

**Answer: 0**

solutions.title: Symmetry
solutions.body:
The numbers $1, \dots, 100$ are symmetric about $50.5$, so both the mean and the median equal $50.5$.

**Answer: 0**

prompt: The square labeled A has area 81 units$^2$. The square labeled B has area 16 units$^2$. The square labeled C has area 36 units$^2$. These three squares along with the shaded, non-overlapping rectangles labeled D, E and F are arranged to form a large square as shown. What is the area of rectangle D?

solutions.title: Find the side lengths
solutions.body:
The squares have sides 9 (A), 4 (B) and 6 (C). The bottom edge of the large square is A plus C: $9 + 6 = 15$, so the large square has side 15.

- D sits on top of A, so its height is $15 - 9 = 6$.
- B and F together span the width of C (6), so F has width $6 - 4 = 2$, and D spans A plus F: width $9 + 2 = 11$.

Area of D $= 11 \times 6 = 66$.

**Answer: 66 units²**

solutions.title: Subtract from the whole
solutions.body:
The large square (side 15) has area 225. The right column (width 6) has C (height 6) at the bottom, B (height 4) above it, and E on top with the same width as B: E is $4 \times (15 - 6 - 4) = 4 \times 5 = 20$. F fills the gap between the top of C (height 6) and the top of A (height 9) next to B: $2 \times 3 = 6$. So D $= 225 - 81 - 16 - 36 - 20 - 6 = 66$.

**Answer: 66 units²**

prompt: If a fair coin is tossed four times, what is the probability of it landing heads up at least three times? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Count outcomes
solutions.body:
There are $2^4 = 16$ equally likely outcomes. Exactly 3 heads: $\binom43 = 4$ outcomes; 4 heads: 1 outcome. Probability $\frac{5}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{5}{16}$**

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
HHHH, HHHT, HHTH, HTHH, THHH — 5 of the 16 sequences.

**Answer: $\frac{5}{16}$**

prompt: If $n$ is an integer for which the greatest common factor of $n$ and 18 is 6 and the least common multiple of $n$ and 9 is 126, what is the value of $n$?

solutions.title: Prime factorizations
solutions.body:
$126 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 7$ and $9 = 3^2$, so $n$ must contain $2 \cdot 7$ and at most $3^2$. Since $\gcd(n, 18) = 6 = 2 \cdot 3$, $n$ has exactly one factor of 3 (two would make the GCF 18). So $n = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7 = 42$.

**Answer: 42**

solutions.title: Check divisors of 126
solutions.body:
$n$ divides 126 and is a multiple of 6: candidates 6, 18, 42, 126. $\text{lcm}(6,9) = 18$, $\gcd(18,18) = 18$, $\gcd(126, 18) = 18$; only 42 works: $\gcd(42,18) = 6$, $\text{lcm}(42,9) = 126$.

**Answer: 42**

prompt: The lines given by the equations $y = 9 - \frac13 x$ and $y = mx + b$ are perpendicular and intersect at a point on the $x$-axis. What is the value of $b$?

solutions.title: Slope and point
solutions.body:
The first line has slope $-\frac13$, so $m = 3$. It meets the $x$-axis where $0 = 9 - \frac{x}{3}$, i.e. $x = 27$. The second line passes through $(27, 0)$: $0 = 3 \cdot 27 + b$, so $b = -81$.

**Answer: −81**

solutions.title: Point-slope form
solutions.body:
The second line is $y = 3(x - 27) = 3x - 81$, so $b = -81$.

**Answer: −81**

prompt: If two standard, fair 6-sided dice are rolled, what is the probability that the product of the two numbers rolled is a perfect square? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Doubles plus extras
solutions.body:
All 6 doubles give squares. Otherwise the two numbers must have the same square-free part; among 1–6 only 1 and 4 share one. That adds (1,4) and (4,1): $\frac{8}{36} = \frac29$.

**Answer: $\frac{2}{9}$**

prompt: Gracie has made 2 gallons of punch that contains 50% juice. After Gracie pours out some of her mixture and replaces it with an equal amount of pure 100% juice, she has 2 gallons of punch that contains 65% juice. How many gallons of the original mixture did Gracie pour out? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Track the juice
solutions.body:
Let $x$ gallons be replaced. Juice: $1 - 0.5x + x = 0.65 \cdot 2 = 1.3$, so $0.5x = 0.3$ and $x = \frac35$.

**Answer: $\frac35$ gallon**

solutions.title: Track the water
solutions.body:
Water starts at 1 gallon and must end at $0.35 \cdot 2 = 0.7$ gallon. Each gallon poured out removes 0.5 gallon of water, so she removes $\frac{0.3}{0.5} = \frac35$ gallon.

**Answer: $\frac35$ gallon**

prompt: Ursula’s starting location (green plus sign) is on the shore of a river that measures 8 km across. Her destination (red X) is 27 km downshore on the opposite side of the river. Ursula rows a boat in a straight line, at a speed of 5 km/h, to a point that is 6 km downshore on the opposite side, and then runs the remaining distance, at a speed of 14 km/h. How many hours will it take Ursula to reach her destination? Express your answer as a mixed number.

solutions.title: Pythagorean theorem
solutions.body:
The rowing path is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6: $\sqrt{64 + 36} = 10$ km, taking $10 \div 5 = 2$ hours. She then runs $27 - 6 = 21$ km, taking $21 \div 14 = 1\frac12$ hours. Total: $3\frac12$ hours.

**Answer: $3\frac12$ hours**

prompt: A cylinder whose height is 3 times its radius is inscribed in a cone whose height is 6 times its radius. What fraction of the cone’s volume lies inside the cylinder? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
Let the cone have radius $R$ and height $6R$, and the cylinder radius $r$ and height $3r$. Above the cylinder is a small cone similar to the big one, with radius $r$ and height $6R - 3r$. Its height is 6 times its radius: $6R - 3r = 6r$, so $r = \frac23R$ and the cylinder’s height is $2R$.

Cylinder: $\pi r^2 h = \pi \cdot \frac49R^2 \cdot 2R = \frac89\pi R^3$. Cone: $\frac13\pi R^2 \cdot 6R = 2\pi R^3$. Ratio: $\frac{8/9}{2} = \frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{9}$**

solutions.title: Pick numbers
solutions.body:
Take $R = 3$: cone height 18. The cylinder’s top rim lies on the cone’s side, where the radius at height $h$ is $3 - \frac{h}{6}$. With radius $r$ at height $3r$: $r = 3 - \frac{r}{2}$, so $r = 2$, height 6. Volumes: cylinder $\pi \cdot 4 \cdot 6 = 24\pi$, cone $\frac13 \pi \cdot 9 \cdot 18 = 54\pi$. Ratio $\frac{24}{54} = \frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{9}$**

prompt: What value of $x$ yields the minimum value of the sum $|x - 2^0| + |x - 2^1| + |x - 2^2| + |x - 2^3| + \cdots + |x - 2^{10}|$?

solutions.title: Median minimizes distance
solutions.body:
The sum of distances from $x$ to a list of points is smallest at the median of the points. The 11 points $2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{10}$ have median $2^5 = 32$.

**Answer: 32**

solutions.title: Pair the terms
solutions.body:
Pair $|x - 2^0| + |x - 2^{10}|$, $|x - 2^1| + |x - 2^9|$, …, $|x - 2^4| + |x - 2^6|$. Each pair is at least the distance between its two points, with equality when $x$ lies between them; all pairs achieve that for $2^4 \le x \le 2^6$. The leftover term $|x - 2^5|$ is smallest (0) at $x = 32$, which lies in that range.

**Answer: 32**

prompt: Charles has opened a service, called Charlie’s Chores, that performs various household chores for families in his neighborhood. The table shows the amount he charges for each chore and how many times he was hired to complete that chore in January. How much money in dollars did Charlie’s Chores earn in the month of January?

solutions.title: Multiply and add
solutions.body:
- Ironing: $10 \times 9.50 = 95$
- Dog walking: $12 \times 7.50 = 90$
- Kitchen cleaning: $7 \times 12 = 84$
- Snow shoveling: $5 \times 14 = 70$

Total: $95 + 90 + 84 + 70 = 339$ dollars.

**Answer: \$339**

prompt: Sunil draws a regular hexagon and a convex quadrilateral on a sheet of paper, so that no side of the quadrilateral lies on the same line as a side of the hexagon. What is the maximum total number of points in which the sides of the quadrilateral can intersect the sides of the hexagon?

solutions.title: Bound each side
solutions.body:
A line segment can cross the boundary of a convex polygon at most twice (once going in, once going out). The quadrilateral has 4 sides, so there are at most $4 \times 2 = 8$ intersection points. Eight is achievable: draw a square with the same center as the hexagon, with its corners just outside the hexagon but the midpoints of its sides inside it (for a hexagon with vertices at distance 1 from the center, a square with corners at distance 0.99 from the center works, as long as no corner points at a hexagon vertex). Each side of the square starts outside, passes through the hexagon and leaves again, crossing it twice.

**Answer: 8 points**

prompt: Penelope and George go trick-or-treating together. Penelope gets 152 pieces of candy and George gets 124 pieces of candy. Penelope eats 5 pieces of candy every day, and George eats 4 pieces of candy every day. After how many days will George have the same amount of candy as Penelope?

solutions.title: Close the gap
solutions.body:
Penelope starts with $152 - 124 = 28$ more pieces, and the gap shrinks by $5 - 4 = 1$ piece per day. It closes after 28 days (both then have $152 - 140 = 12 = 124 - 112$ pieces).

**Answer: 28 days**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
$152 - 5d = 124 - 4d \Rightarrow d = 28$.

**Answer: 28 days**

prompt: Rosie grows 160 bushels of corn per acre in a right triangular field, as shown, with perpendicular sides of lengths 660 feet and 1320 feet. Given that an acre equals 43,560 ft$^2$, what is the total number of bushels of corn that Rosie grows?

solutions.title: Area in acres
solutions.body:
Area $= \frac12 \cdot 660 \cdot 1320 = 435{,}600$ ft², which is $435{,}600 \div 43{,}560 = 10$ acres. Bushels: $10 \times 160 = 1600$.

**Answer: 1600 bushels**

prompt: A standard, six-sided die is rolled five times. What is the probability that the five rolls are either all the same or all different? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth of a percent.

solutions.title: Count outcomes
solutions.body:
Total outcomes: $6^5 = 7776$. All the same: 6. All different: $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 720$. Probability $\frac{726}{7776} \approx 0.093364$, i.e. $9.34\%$.

**Answer: 9.34%**

solutions.title: Multiply probabilities
solutions.body:
All same: $\left(\frac16\right)^4 \approx 0.000772$. All different: $\frac56 \cdot \frac46 \cdot \frac36 \cdot \frac26 \approx 0.092593$. Sum $\approx 0.093364 = 9.34\%$.

**Answer: 9.34%**

prompt: If $(0, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(-2, 6)$ and $(a, b)$ are the coordinates of the vertices of a parallelogram, what is the least possible value for $a + b$?

solutions.title: Three possible fourth vertices
solutions.body:
In a parallelogram the fourth vertex equals the sum of its two neighbors minus the opposite vertex. Choosing each given point as the one opposite $(a, b)$:
- $(6,2) + (-2,6) - (0,0) = (4, 8)$, sum 12
- $(0,0) + (6,2) - (-2,6) = (8, -4)$, sum 4
- $(0,0) + (-2,6) - (6,2) = (-8, 4)$, sum $-4$

The least value is $-4$.

**Answer: −4**

solutions.title: Shortcut with sums
solutions.body:
Let $s$ be the coordinate sum: the points have $s = 0, 8, 4$. The fourth vertex’s sum is (sum of two) − (third): $8 + 4 - 0 = 12$, $0 + 8 - 4 = 4$, $0 + 4 - 8 = -4$. Minimum $-4$.

**Answer: −4**

prompt: Alan, Ben and Craig, who have three distinct ages, are among five children running a race. Assuming there are no ties, in how many different orders can the five children finish the race with Alan, Ben and Craig in order from oldest to youngest?

solutions.title: Choose positions
solutions.body:
Choose which 3 of the 5 finishing places go to Alan, Ben and Craig: $\binom53 = 10$ ways; they must fill them in the one required order. The other two children fill the remaining 2 places in $2! = 2$ ways. Total $10 \times 2 = 20$.

**Answer: 20 orders**

solutions.title: Symmetry
solutions.body:
There are $5! = 120$ finishing orders. The three boys appear in each of their $3! = 6$ relative orders equally often, so exactly $\frac{120}{6} = 20$ have them oldest to youngest.

**Answer: 20 orders**

prompt: Let a *trime* be defined as a three-digit integer for which any two digits of the integer, ordered as they appear in the original integer, form a two-digit prime number. For example, 137 is a trime because 13, 17 and 37 are all prime numbers. However, 211 is not a trime because 21 is not prime. What is the greatest trime?

solutions.title: Search from the top
solutions.body:
For a trime $\overline{abc}$, the numbers $\overline{ab}$, $\overline{ac}$, $\overline{bc}$ are all prime, so $b$ and $c$ are odd and not 5.
- $a = 9$: the only prime in the 90s is 97, so $b = c = 7$, but 77 is not prime.
- $a = 8$: primes 83, 89 force $b, c \in \{3, 9\}$ with $\overline{bc}$ prime; 33, 39, 93, 99 are all composite.
- $a = 7$: primes 71, 73, 79. Try $b = 9$: $c \in \{1,3,9\}$ needs $\overline{9c}$ prime — none. Try $b = 3$: $c = 9$ gives 39 (no), $c = 3$ gives 33 (no), $c = 1$ gives 31 ✓. So 731 works (73, 71, 31 are prime).

**Answer: 731**

prompt: William counted all the animals he saw at the zoo. This graph shows the data he collected. Based on this, what percentage of the animals that William saw are mammals? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth.
How many ways are there to arrange the four integers 1, 2, 3 and 4 in a row so that no two adjacent numbers have a sum of 5?

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
The forbidden neighbors are $\{1,4\}$ and $\{2,3\}$. Of the $4! = 24$ arrangements, those with 1 and 4 adjacent: treat them as a block, $3! \cdot 2 = 12$. Likewise 12 with 2 and 3 adjacent. Both blocks: $2! \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$. Bad: $12 + 12 - 8 = 16$, good: $24 - 16 = 8$.

**Answer: 8 ways**

solutions.title: Build directly
solutions.body:
Start with 1: its neighbor can’t be 4, so the next is 2 or 3. 1-2-?: next can’t be 3, so 4, then 3: 1243. 1-3-?: next can’t be 2, so 4, then 2: 1342. So 2 arrangements start with 1; by symmetry 2 start with each digit: $4 \times 2 = 8$.

**Answer: 8 ways**

prompt: There are 93 sixth graders and 108 seventh graders entering a raffle. In each grade, the number of dog owners is twice the number of students who do not own a dog. What is the probability that a seventh grader who does not own a dog wins the raffle? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Count the group
solutions.body:
In seventh grade, $\frac13$ of students don’t own a dog: $108 \div 3 = 36$. There are $93 + 108 = 201$ entrants, so the probability is $\frac{36}{201} = \frac{12}{67}$.

**Answer: $\frac{12}{67}$**

prompt: In the $5 \times 5$ grid shown, each row and each column is to contain the integers 1 through 5 exactly once with one integer per cell. The sum of the two integers in each outlined pair of cells is 5. What is the product of the integers in the four corner cells that are shaded?

solutions.title: Fill the grid
solutions.body:
Each outlined pair is $\{1,4\}$ or $\{2,3\}$, so 5 never appears in a pair. Label cells (row, column) from the top left.

1. Row 5 has 3 in the corner, so its left pair is $\{1,4\}$; the remaining cells (5,3), (5,4) are 2 and 5. Cell (5,4) is in a pair, so it is 2 and (5,3) = 5; its partner (4,4) = 3.
2. Column 4 now has 3 and 2, so the pair (1,4)-(2,4) is $\{1,4\}$ and (3,4) = 5. Row 2 already has 1, so (2,4) = 4 and (1,4) = 1.
3. Row 2 then needs 2, 3, 5: the pair (2,2)-(2,3) is $\{2,3\}$ and (2,5) = 5. Column 3 has 2 at top, so (2,3) = 3, (2,2) = 2.
4. Column 5 has 1, 3, 5, so (1,5), (4,5) are 2, 4; row 1 has 2, so (1,5) = 4 and (4,5) = 2.
5. Row 3 has 5 and 1, so the pair (3,3)-(4,3) is (4, 1).
6. Column 1 has 1 in row 2, so (5,1) = 4 and (5,2) = 1. Row 1 needs 3 and 5 in (1,1), (1,2); row 4 needs 4 and 5 in (4,1), (4,2). Column 1 already has 4, so (4,1) = 5, which forces (1,1) = 3.

Corners: $3 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 144$.

**Answer: 144**

prompt: A satellite, located 400 km above Earth’s surface, travels at a speed of 28,000 km/h. For simplicity, assume that Earth is a perfect sphere with circumference 40,075 km. How many minutes does it take the satellite to orbit Earth one time? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Orbit circumference
solutions.body:
Increasing a circle’s radius by 400 km increases its circumference by $2\pi \cdot 400 \approx 2513.3$ km. The orbit is about $40{,}075 + 2513.3 = 42{,}588.3$ km long. Time: $\frac{42{,}588.3}{28{,}000} \approx 1.52101$ h $\times 60 \approx 91.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 91.3 minutes**

solutions.title: Via the radius
solutions.body:
Earth’s radius is $\frac{40{,}075}{2\pi} \approx 6378.1$ km, so the orbit radius is $\approx 6778.1$ km and its circumference $\approx 2\pi \cdot 6778.1 \approx 42{,}588$ km. At 28,000 km/h this takes $\approx 91.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 91.3 minutes**

prompt: Three children each live in one of three houses, equally spaced and arranged as shown. Each child is equally likely to live in any of the houses, and it is possible that a house has no children living in it. All three children will play in the house that minimizes the total distance they have to travel. What is the probability that they will play in house B?

solutions.title: Count the complement
solutions.body:
There are $3^3 = 27$ equally likely assignments. The best house is the one where the median child lives. They play at A exactly when at least two children live in A: all three in A (1 way) or exactly two ($3 \cdot 2 = 6$ ways), 7 in total. Likewise 7 for C. So house B is chosen in $27 - 14 = 13$ cases: probability $\frac{13}{27}$.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{27}$**

solutions.title: Count directly
solutions.body:
B is chosen when the median child is in B: either at least two children live in B ($1 + 3 \cdot 2 = 7$ ways), or exactly one lives in each house ($3! = 6$ ways). Total $13$ of 27.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{27}$**
