Repeat this process twice more, drawing a line through $P_5$ parallel to $P_2P_3$, intersecting the circle again at $P_6$, and finally drawing a line through $P_6$ parallel to $P_3P_4$, intersecting the circle again at $P_7$. Prove that $P_7$ is the same point as $P_1$.
answer: Parallel chords cut off equal arcs in opposite directions: in angle coordinates, chord $XY\parallel ZW$ iff $\theta_X+\theta_Y\equiv\theta_Z+\theta_W\pmod{2\pi}$, so $\theta_5=\theta_1+\theta_2-\theta_4$, $\theta_6=\theta_3+\theta_4-\theta_1$, $\theta_7=\theta_1$.

solutions.title: Angle coordinates on the circle
solutions.body:
Take the circle to be the unit circle and write each point as $P_k=(\cos\theta_k,\sin\theta_k)$.

**Lemma.** For two points $X,Y$ of the circle at angles $\alpha,\beta$, the line $XY$ (or, if $X=Y$, the tangent at $X$) is perpendicular to the direction at angle $\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$. Two such lines, for angle pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ and $(\gamma,\delta)$, are parallel exactly when $\alpha+\beta\equiv\gamma+\delta\pmod{2\pi}$.

*Proof.* If $\alpha\ne\beta$, then $Y-X=(\cos\beta-\cos\alpha,\ \sin\beta-\sin\alpha)=2\sin\frac{\beta-\alpha}{2}\left(-\sin\frac{\alpha+\beta}2,\ \cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\right)$, which is perpendicular to $\left(\cos\frac{\alpha+\beta}2,\sin\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\right)$. If $\alpha=\beta$, the tangent at $X$ is perpendicular to the radius, which has direction angle $\alpha=\frac{\alpha+\beta}2$. Two lines are parallel exactly when their normal directions agree up to a half-turn, i.e. $\frac{\alpha+\beta}2\equiv\frac{\gamma+\delta}2\pmod\pi$, i.e. $\alpha+\beta\equiv\gamma+\delta\pmod{2\pi}$. $\square$

**The construction.** The line through $P_4$ parallel to $P_1P_2$ meets the circle at $P_4$ and at the point $P_5$ whose angle satisfies $\theta_4+\theta_5\equiv\theta_1+\theta_2$. This determines $\theta_5$ uniquely mod $2\pi$, and it gives $P_5=P_4$ exactly in the tangent case, as the problem specifies. So
$$\theta_5\equiv\theta_1+\theta_2-\theta_4,\qquad \theta_6\equiv\theta_2+\theta_3-\theta_5\equiv\theta_3+\theta_4-\theta_1,\qquad \theta_7\equiv\theta_3+\theta_4-\theta_6\equiv\theta_1 \pmod{2\pi}.$$
Hence $P_7=P_1$. ∎

solutions.title: Equal arcs between parallel chords
solutions.body: Parallel chords $P_1P_2$ and $P_4P_5$ cut off equal arcs between them: $\angle P_1P_5P_4=\angle P_5P_1P_2$ (alternate angles), and these inscribed angles subtend the arcs $P_1P_4$ and $P_5P_2$, so the arcs are equal. Moreover they run in opposite directions: going from $P_1$ to $P_4$ is, say, clockwise, while going from $P_2$ to $P_5$ is counterclockwise (the reflection in the diameter perpendicular to the chords swaps the endpoints). Repeating, arc $P_3P_6$ equals arc $P_2P_5$ with the opposite direction (so the same direction as $P_1P_4$), and arc $P_4P_7$ equals arc $P_3P_6$ with the opposite direction. So moving from $P_4$ to $P_7$ goes the same distance as from $P_1$ to $P_4$, but backwards, which brings us back to $P_1$. (The tangent case is the limiting case of the same equalities, or is covered directly by the first solution.) ∎

prompt: Suppose that $2002$ numbers, each equal to $1$ or $-1$, are written around a circle. For every two adjacent numbers, their product is taken; it turns out that the sum of all $2002$ such products is negative. Prove that the sum of the original numbers has absolute value less than or equal to $1000$. (The absolute value of $x$ is usually denoted by $|x|$. It is equal to $x$ if $x\ge0$, and to $-x$ if $x<0$. For example, $|6|=6$, $|0|=0$, and $|-7|=7$.)
answer: More than $1001$ adjacent products are $-1$; each such pair contains one $+1$ and one $-1$, and each number is in two pairs, so there are at least $501$ of each sign, giving $|{\rm sum}|\le 2002-2\cdot501=1000$.

solutions.title: Count sign changes
solutions.body:
Let $n$ of the numbers be $+1$; the other $2002-n$ are $-1$, and the sum of the numbers is $n-(2002-n)=2n-2002$.

Let $m$ of the $2002$ adjacent products equal $-1$. The sum of the products is $(2002-m)-m=2002-2m<0$, so $m>1001$, i.e. $m\ge1002$.

A product equals $-1$ exactly when the two neighbors are one $+1$ and one $-1$. Each $-1$ on the circle belongs to exactly two adjacent pairs, so it is in at most two of these $m$ pairs. Hence the number of $-1$'s is at least $\frac m2\ge501$, so $2002-n\ge501$, $n\le1501$ and $2n-2002\le1000$.

In the same way, each of the $m$ pairs contains a $+1$, so $n\ge\frac m2\ge501$ and $2n-2002\ge-1000$.

Therefore $|2n-2002|\le1000$. ∎

prompt: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive whole numbers such that $\dfrac{4.5}{11}<\dfrac ab<\dfrac5{11}$. Find the fraction $\dfrac ab$ for which the sum $a+b$ is as small as possible. Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Try small numerators
solutions.body:
Multiply the inequality by $11b$: we need
$$4.5\,b<11a<5b,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{11a}{5}<b<\frac{11a}{4.5}.$$
- $a=1$: $2.2<b<2.44\ldots$, no whole number $b$.
- $a=2$: $4.4<b<4.88\ldots$, no whole number $b$.
- $a=3$: $6.6<b<7.33\ldots$, so $b=7$ works, giving $a+b=10$. Check: $\frac{4.5}{11}=\frac{31.5}{77}<\frac{33}{77}=\frac37<\frac{35}{77}=\frac5{11}$. ✓
- $a\ge4$: since $\frac ab<\frac5{11}<\frac12$, we have $b>2a$, so $a+b>3a\ge12>10$.

So the smallest possible sum is $10$, reached only by $\frac37$.

**Answer: $\dfrac37$**

prompt: In the figure, parallelograms $ABCD$ and $BFEC$ have areas $1234\text{ cm}^2$ and $2804\text{ cm}^2$, respectively. Points $M$ and $N$ are chosen on sides $AD$ and $FE$, respectively, so that segment $MN$ passes through $B$. Find the area of $\triangle MNC$.

solutions.title: Split along BC
solutions.body:
The segment $BC$ splits $\triangle MNC$ into $\triangle BCM$ and $\triangle BCN$: since $B$ lies on $MN$, the line $BC$ separates $M$ (on $AD$, on one side of $BC$) from $N$ (on $FE$, on the other side).

- $\triangle BCM$ has base $BC$, and $M$ lies on $AD$, which is parallel to $BC$. So its height equals the height of parallelogram $ABCD$ on base $BC$, and $[BCM]=\tfrac12[ABCD]=617$.
- In the same way, $N$ lies on $FE\parallel BC$, so $[BCN]=\tfrac12[BFEC]=1402$.

So $[MNC]=617+1402=2019\text{ cm}^2$, the average of the two parallelogram areas.

**Answer: $2019\text{ cm}^2$**

solutions.title: Slide M and N
solutions.body:
Moving $M$ along $AD$ or $N$ along $FE$ does not change the areas of $\triangle BCM$ and $\triangle BCN$ (same base $BC$, same height). Slide $M$ to $D$ and $N$ to $E$: then $\triangle BCD$ is half of $ABCD$ (cut by a diagonal), and $\triangle BCE$ is half of $BFEC$. So the area is $\tfrac12(1234+2804)=2019\text{ cm}^2$.

**Answer: $2019\text{ cm}^2$**

prompt:
You are traveling in a foreign country whose currency consists of five different-looking kinds of coins. You have several of each coin in your pocket. You remember that the coins are worth $1$, $2$, $5$, $10$, and $20$ florins, but you have no idea which coin is which and you don't speak the local language. You find a vending machine where a single candy can be bought for $1$ florin: you insert any kind of coin, and receive $1$ candy plus any change owed. You can only buy one candy at a time, but you can buy as many as you want, one after the other.

What is the least number of candies that you must buy to ensure that you can determine the values of all the coins? Prove that your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Three can fail; four always work
solutions.body:
**Three candies are not always enough.** Three purchases use at most three kinds of coins. Imagine that the coins you happen to insert are worth $1$, $2$ and $5$ florins (whatever you choose to insert, this is possible), and that the machine always pays change in $1$-florin coins. Then you never see a $10$- or $20$-florin coin used or returned. Swapping the values of those two kinds would not change anything you observed, so you cannot tell them apart.

**Four candies are enough.** Buy four candies, paying each time with a *different* kind of coin; one kind is left unused.

1. *The 1-florin coin.* Paying with a $1$ gives no change, and every other coin gives change. If some purchase gave no change, that coin is the $1$. Otherwise the unused kind is the $1$.
2. *The 2-florin coin.* Change for a $2$ is a single $1$-florin coin. Change for $5$, $10$ or $20$ is worth at least $4$, so it is never a single $1$. So the purchase whose change was a single $1$ (if any) used the $2$; otherwise the unused kind is the $2$.
3. *The 5-florin coin.* Change for a $5$ is worth $4$ and consists only of $1$s and $2$s, which we now recognize. Change for a $10$ or $20$ is worth $9$ or $19$, so it never consists of $1$s and $2$s worth $4$ in total. So we can recognize the purchase with the $5$, if it happened; otherwise the unused kind is the $5$.
4. *The 10-florin coin.* Change for a $10$ is worth $9$ and consists of $1$s, $2$s and $5$s, all known now. Change for a $20$ that consists only of known coins is worth $19$, not $9$. So again we recognize the $10$, or it is the unused kind.
5. The remaining kind is the $20$.

**Answer: 4**

prompt:
Initially, all the squares of an $8\times8$ grid are white. You start by choosing one of the squares and coloring it gray. After that, you may color additional squares gray one at a time, but you may only color a square gray if it has exactly $1$ or $3$ gray neighbors at that moment (where a neighbor is a square sharing an edge).

For example, the configuration in the picture (of a smaller $3\times4$ grid) shows a situation where six squares have been colored gray so far. The squares that can be colored at the next step are marked with a dot.

Is it possible to color all the squares gray? Justify your answer.

solutions.title: Perimeter of the gray region mod 4
solutions.body:
Let $L(t)$ be the perimeter (number of unit edges on the boundary) of the gray region after $t$ squares are gray. Then $L(1)=4$.

When we add a square with exactly one gray neighbor, the shared edge leaves the boundary and three new edges join it: $L$ increases by $2$. When we add a square with exactly three gray neighbors, three edges leave the boundary and one joins: $L$ decreases by $2$. So every move changes $L$ by $\pm2$, and therefore by $2\pmod 4$.

Starting from $L(1)=4\equiv0\pmod4$, we get $L(t)\equiv0$ for odd $t$ and $L(t)\equiv2\pmod4$ for even $t$. If all $64$ squares were gray, then $L(64)\equiv2\pmod 4$. But then the gray region is the whole board, whose perimeter is $32\equiv0\pmod4$. Contradiction.

**Answer: No.** ∎

prompt:
In triangle $\triangle ABC$, we have marked points $A_1$ on side $BC$, $B_1$ on side $AC$, and $C_1$ on side $AB$ so that $AA_1$ is an altitude, $BB_1$ is a median, and $CC_1$ is an angle bisector. It is known that $\triangle A_1B_1C_1$ is equilateral. Prove that $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral too.

(Note: A median connects a vertex of a triangle with the midpoint of the opposite side. Thus, for median $BB_1$ we know that $B_1$ is the midpoint of side $AC$ in $\triangle ABC$.)
answer: $B_1A=B_1C=B_1A_1=B_1C_1$, so $C_1$ is on the circle with diameter $AC$ and $CC_1\perp AB$; a bisector that is an altitude gives $CA=CB$, then $C_1$ is the midpoint of $AB$ and $AB=2A_1C_1=AC$.

solutions.title: The circle with diameter AC
solutions.body:
Let $s$ be the side of the equilateral triangle $A_1B_1C_1$.

**Step 1.** In the right triangle $AA_1C$ (right angle at $A_1$), the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse, so $B_1A_1=\tfrac12AC=B_1A=B_1C$. Hence
$$B_1A=B_1C=B_1A_1=s=B_1C_1,$$
so $A$, $C$, $A_1$, $C_1$ all lie on the circle with center $B_1$ and diameter $AC$.

**Step 2.** $C_1\ne A$: otherwise the bisector $CC_1$ would be the side $CA$, impossible. So $C_1$ is a point of this circle other than $A$ and $C$, and $\angle AC_1C=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). Thus $CC_1$ is both the angle bisector and the altitude from $C$. The triangles $ACC_1$ and $BCC_1$ then share $CC_1$ and have equal angles at $C$ and at $C_1$, so they are congruent (ASA). This gives $CA=CB$ and $AC_1=C_1B$, so $C_1$ is the midpoint of $AB$.

**Step 3.** In the right triangle $AA_1B$ (right angle at $A_1$), $A_1C_1$ is the median to the hypotenuse, so $A_1C_1=\tfrac12AB$. Therefore $AB=2s=AC$.

Together, $AB=AC=BC$, so $\triangle ABC$ is equilateral. ∎

prompt: A trapezoid is divided into seven strips of equal width as shown. What fraction of the trapezoid's area is shaded? Explain why your answer is correct.

solutions.title: Two copies make a parallelogram
solutions.body:
Take a second copy of the trapezoid, turn it upside down ($180^\circ$), and place it next to the first so that together they form a parallelogram (the short base of one copy lines up with the long base of the other). The strips of the two copies join up: strip $1$ (shaded) of one copy meets strip $7$ (shaded) of the other, strip $2$ (white) meets strip $6$ (white), and so on. So the parallelogram is cut into $7$ congruent strips, each a parallelogram with the same width and the same total length. Exactly $4$ of these $7$ strips are shaded, so the shading covers $\frac47$ of the parallelogram.

The shaded area of the parallelogram is twice the shaded area of one trapezoid, and the parallelogram's area is twice the trapezoid's area. So the shaded fraction of the trapezoid is also $\frac47$.

**Answer: $\dfrac47$**

solutions.title: Strip areas form an arithmetic sequence
solutions.body:
Let the strips have width $w$. The lengths of the horizontal lines across the trapezoid change linearly from top to bottom, so the midline lengths of the seven strips form an arithmetic sequence $m-3d,\,m-2d,\,\dots,\,m+3d$, and strip $k$ has area $w\cdot(\text{its midline})$. The shaded strips are numbers $1,3,5,7$ and the white ones are $2,4,6$. The shaded total is $w\big((m-3d)+(m-d)+(m+d)+(m+3d)\big)=4wm$, and the whole trapezoid is $w\cdot 7m$. So the shaded fraction is $\frac{4wm}{7wm}=\frac47$.

**Answer: $\dfrac47$**

prompt:
Four friends, Anna, Bob, Celia, and David, exchanged some money. For any two of these friends, exactly one gave some money to the other. For example, Celia could have given money to David but then David would not have given money to Celia. In the end, each person broke even (meaning that no one made or lost any money).

(a) Is it possible that the amounts of money given were \$10, \$20, \$30, \$40, \$50, and \$60?

(b) Is it possible that the amounts of money given were \$20, \$30, \$40, \$50, \$60, and \$70?

For each part, if your answer is yes, show that the situation is possible by describing who could have given what amounts to whom. If your answer is no, prove that the situation is not possible.

(Answer in the form: (a), (b).)

solutions.title: An example, and follow the biggest payment
solutions.body:
There are $\binom42=6$ pairs of friends, so each amount is used for exactly one pair.

**(a) Yes.** For example:
- Anna gives \$10 to Bob and \$30 to Celia; David gives \$40 to Anna.
- Bob gives \$60 to David; Celia gives \$50 to Bob.
- David gives \$20 to Celia.

Check: Anna gives $10+30=40$ and receives $40$. Bob receives $10+50=60$ and gives $60$. Celia receives $30+20=50$ and gives $50$. David receives $60$ and gives $40+20=60$. Everyone breaks even.

**(b) No.** Suppose it were possible, and say the \$60 went from $X$ to $Y$. Then $X$ has two other transactions, with amounts $u,v$ from $\{20,30,40,50,70\}$, which must bring in a net \$60.
- If $X$ receives both, then $u+v=60$, so $\{u,v\}=\{20,40\}$.
- If $X$ receives one and gives the other, then $u-v=60$, which is impossible with these amounts (the largest difference is $70-20=50$).
- $X$ cannot give both.

So $X$'s other two transactions are \$20 and \$40, both received. In the same way, $Y$ must *give away* a net \$60 in its two other transactions, so these must also be \$20 and \$40. But the four transactions of $X$ and $Y$ with the other two friends are four different pairs, so they need four different amounts, and \$20 and \$40 cannot both be used twice. Contradiction.

**Answer: (a) Yes; (b) No.**

prompt:
Find all real numbers $x$ that satisfy the equation
$$\frac{x-2020}{1}+\frac{x-2019}{2}+\cdots+\frac{x-2000}{21}=\frac{x-1}{2020}+\frac{x-2}{2019}+\cdots+\frac{x-21}{2000},$$
and simplify your answer(s) as much as possible. Justify your solution.

solutions.title: Subtract 1 from every fraction
solutions.body:
Each side has $21$ fractions. Subtract $21$ from both sides, i.e. subtract $1$ from each fraction. On the left, $\frac{x-(2021-k)}{k}-1=\frac{x-2021}{k}$ for $k=1,\dots,21$. On the right, $\frac{x-k}{2021-k}-1=\frac{x-2021}{2021-k}$. So the equation becomes
$$(x-2021)\left(\frac11+\frac12+\cdots+\frac1{21}\right)=(x-2021)\left(\frac1{2020}+\frac1{2019}+\cdots+\frac1{2000}\right).$$
The two sums are different: each of the $21$ terms on the left is at least $\frac1{21}$, and each term on the right is at most $\frac1{2000}$, so the left sum is larger. Hence $x-2021=0$.

**Answer: $x=2021$**

solutions.title: Guess, check, and use linearity
solutions.body:
For $x=2021$ every fraction on the left is $\frac{k}{k}=1$ and every fraction on the right is $\frac{2021-k}{2021-k}=1$, so both sides equal $21$. The equation is linear, $ax+b=0$ with
$$a=\left(1+\tfrac12+\cdots+\tfrac1{21}\right)-\left(\tfrac1{2020}+\cdots+\tfrac1{2000}\right)>0,$$
since every term of the first sum exceeds every term of the second. A linear equation with $a\ne0$ has exactly one solution, so $x=2021$ is the only one.

**Answer: $x=2021$**

prompt:
Consider a sheet of paper in the shape of an equilateral triangle creased along the dashed lines as in the figure on the left. Folding over each of the three corners along the dashed lines creates a new object which is uniformly four layers thick, as in the figure on the right. The number in each region indicates that region's thickness (in layers of paper).

We have just seen one example of how a plane figure can be folded into an object with a uniform thickness. This problem asks you to produce several other examples. In each case, you may fold along any lines. The different parts that are folded may or may not be congruent. Assume that paper may be folded any number of times without tearing or becoming too thick to fold. If needed, you can use any of the following tools:

- a magic ruler with which you can draw a line through any two given points and you can split any segment into as many equal parts as you wish; and
- a right triangle tool with which you can drop perpendiculars from points to lines and erect perpendiculars to lines from points on them.

Given these rules:

(a) Show how to fold an equilateral triangle into an object with a uniform thickness of $3$ layers.

(b) Show how to fold a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle into an object with a uniform thickness of $3$ layers.

(c) Show that every triangle can be folded into an object with a uniform thickness of $2020$ layers.
answer: (a) Trisect the sides to get $9$ small triangles, fold the $3$ corners in, then fold the hexagon in half along a long diagonal. (b) The perpendicular bisector of the hypotenuse and the segment from its foot on the long leg to the $60^\circ$ vertex cut it into $3$ congruent $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles; fold them onto each other. (c) With $AB$ longest, fold along the midline and the two perpendiculars from the midpoints to $AB$ to get a $2$-layer rectangle, then accordion-fold it into $1010$ strips.

solutions.title: Constructions
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let the triangle have side $3$. Trisect each side and join the trisection points by segments parallel to the sides. This cuts the triangle into $9$ small equilateral triangles of side $1$: three at the corners and six forming a regular hexagon in the middle. Going around the hexagon, its six small triangles alternate between "pointing up" and "pointing down".

Fold each corner triangle inward along its inner edge. Reflecting a small triangle in one of its edges gives the neighboring small triangle, so each corner lands exactly on one of the three hexagon triangles touching that edge, and these are every other triangle of the hexagon. The hexagon now has thicknesses $2,1,2,1,2,1$ going around.

Now fold the hexagon in half along one of its long diagonals (a line through two opposite vertices, which lies on one of the creases). This reflection pairs each triangle with its mirror image, and the mirror image of an up-triangle is a down-triangle and vice versa, so each pair has thicknesses $2+1=3$. The result is a trapezoid made of three small triangles, uniformly $3$ layers thick.

**(b)** Let the right angle be at $C$, with $\angle A=30^\circ$ and $\angle B=60^\circ$. Let $N$ be the midpoint of the hypotenuse $AB$, and let the perpendicular to $AB$ at $N$ meet the leg $AC$ at $P$. Draw $PB$.
- $P$ is on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$, so $PA=PB$ and $\angle PBA=\angle PAB=30^\circ$. Hence $\angle PBC=60^\circ-30^\circ=30^\circ$.
- Triangles $ANP$ and $BNP$ are congruent (right angles at $N$, $AN=NB$, common side $PN$).
- Triangles $BNP$ and $BCP$ are congruent: both have a right angle (at $N$ and at $C$), a $30^\circ$ angle at $B$, and the common hypotenuse $BP$.

So the triangle is cut into three congruent $30$-$60$-$90$ triangles. Fold $ANP$ over the crease $PN$ onto $BNP$, and fold $BCP$ over the crease $PB$ onto $BNP$. The result is triangle $BNP$, uniformly $3$ layers thick.

**(c)** Label the triangle so that $AB$ is the longest side; then $\angle A$ and $\angle B$ are acute, so the foot $H$ of the altitude from $C$ lies inside segment $AB$. Let $D$ and $E$ be the midpoints of $AC$ and $BC$, and let $F$ and $G$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $D$ and $E$ to $AB$. Then $DEGF$ is a rectangle.
- Fold along $DE$. Since $DE$ is parallel to $AB$ and halfway between $C$ and $AB$, the reflection of $C$ in $DE$ is $H$. So triangle $CDE$ lands on triangle $HDE$, which lies inside the rectangle.
- $DH=DC=DA$, so triangle $ADH$ is isosceles and its altitude $DF$ bisects it: $F$ is the midpoint of $AH$. Folding along $DF$ puts triangle $ADF$ exactly onto triangle $HDF$. Similarly, folding along $EG$ puts $BEG$ onto $HEG$.

The rectangle $DEGF$ is the union of the triangles $HDE$, $HDF$ and $HEG$, each now covered once by a folded flap, so the rectangle is uniformly $2$ layers thick. Finally divide $DE$ and $FG$ into $1010$ equal parts, join corresponding points (these segments are perpendicular to $AB$), and fold the rectangle like an accordion along these $1009$ lines. All $1010$ strips stack on top of each other, giving uniform thickness $2\cdot1010=2020$ layers. ∎

prompt: The integer $202020$ is a multiple of $91$. For every positive integer $n$, show how $n$ additional $2$'s may be inserted into the digits of $202020$ so that the resulting $(n+6)$-digit integer is also a multiple of $91$. For example, a possible way to do this when $n=5$ is $\underline{2}2020\underline{2}20\underline{222}$ (the inserted $2$'s are underlined).
answer: Insert all $n$ twos after the leading $202$: the numbers $a_n=202\underbrace{2\cdots2}_{n}020$ satisfy $a_n=10a_{n-1}+1820$ and $91\mid1820$, so $91\mid a_n$ by induction.

solutions.title: A recursion
solutions.body:
Let $R_k=\underbrace{22\cdots2}_{k}$ ($R_0=0$), and let
$$a_n=202\,\underbrace{2\cdots2}_{n}\,020=202\cdot10^{n+3}+R_n\cdot10^3+20,$$
which is $202020$ with $n$ twos inserted after the first three digits. We claim $91\mid a_n$ for all $n\ge0$.

For $n=0$: $a_0=202020=91\cdot2220$. For $n\ge1$, using $R_n=10R_{n-1}+2$:
$$10a_{n-1}+1820=202\cdot10^{n+3}+R_{n-1}\cdot10^4+200+1820=202\cdot10^{n+3}+(10R_{n-1}+2)\cdot10^3+20=a_n .$$
Since $1820=91\cdot20$, if $91\mid a_{n-1}$ then $91\mid a_n$. By induction, $91\mid a_n$ for every $n$. For example $a_1=2022020=91\cdot22220$ and $a_2=20222020=91\cdot222220$. ∎

solutions.title: Step by two
solutions.body:
With $a_n=202\cdot10^{n+3}+R_n\cdot10^3+20$ as in the first solution, compare $a_{n+2}$ and $a_n$:
$$a_{n+2}-100\,a_n=R_{n+2}\cdot10^3-100\,R_n\cdot10^3+20-2000=22\cdot10^3-1980=20020=91\cdot220,$$
because $R_{n+2}=100R_n+22$. So $91\mid a_n$ implies $91\mid a_{n+2}$. Checking $a_0=202020=91\cdot2220$ and $a_1=2022020=91\cdot22220$ starts the induction for even and odd $n$. ∎

prompt:
I have cards with whole numbers written on them. I can put them in various orders in a row, next to each other, to create a single long number. For example, if my cards were $3$, $6$, and $18$, some of the numbers I could make are $3618$, $6183$, and $1863$. However, $3861$ and $8136$ would not be allowable arrangements, as the number "$18$" is written on one card: it cannot be split up and its digits cannot be switched. Note that cards can only be arranged in a row; they may not be turned over or manipulated in other ways, and thus, $6318$ and $3918$ are not allowable arrangements of $3$, $6$, and $18$.

If I have $100$ cards with all the numbers $1$ through $100$ on them, how should I put them in order to create the largest possible number? Describe exactly how your answer is constructed. No formal proof is required.
answer: $9,99,98,\dots,90,\ 89,8,88,87,\dots,80,\ 79,78,7,77,76,\dots,\ \dots,\ 12,1,11,10,100$: for each leading digit $d$ (from $9$ down to $1$), the cards $d9,d8,\dots,d(d{+}1)$, then $d$ and $dd$ (either order), then $d(d{-}1),\dots,d0$; and $100$ last.

solutions.title: Greedy: make each next digit as large as possible
solutions.body:
Every arrangement gives a number with the same number of digits ($9\cdot1+90\cdot2+3=192$). For numbers of the same length, the larger one is the one with the larger digit at the first place where they differ, as in alphabetical order. So we choose cards from left to right, each time making the next digits as large as possible.

**Leading digit.** All cards starting with $9$ come first, then all starting with $8$, and so on down to $1$. (The card $100$ starts with $1$.)

**Order within a block.** Two cards $X$ and $Y$ should be placed as $XY$ rather than $YX$ when the string $XY$ is larger than $YX$. Within the block of cards starting with $d$:
- the two-digit cards go in decreasing order: $d9, d8, \dots, d0$;
- the one-digit card $d$ goes after $d(d+1)$ and before $d(d-1)$. For example $787>778$, so $78$ goes before $7$, and $776>767$, so $7$ goes before $76$;
- $d$ and $dd$ give the same string in either order ($777$).

So the block for digit $d$ is $d9,d8,\dots,d(d{+}1),\ d,\ dd,\ d(d{-}1),\dots,d0$ (with $d$ and $dd$ interchangeable). For $d=9$ the block is just $9,99,98,\dots,90$. For $d=1$ we must also place $100$. It belongs after every other card starting with $1$ (for example $10\,100>100\,10$ and $11\,100>100\,11$), so it goes last.

**Answer:**
$$9\ 99\ 98\cdots90\ \ 89\ 8\ 88\ 87\cdots80\ \ 79\ 78\ 7\ 77\ 76\cdots70\ \ \cdots\ \ 19\ 18\cdots12\ 1\ 11\ 10\ 100,$$
where each pair $d,\ dd$ may be swapped.

solutions.title: Sorting rule check
solutions.body:
A neat way to state the rule: put card $X$ before card $Y$ whenever the string $XY$ is larger than the string $YX$. This rule is consistent (it orders the cards like comparing their infinite repetitions $XXX\ldots$), and sorting by it gives the largest concatenation. If two neighbouring cards were in the wrong order, swapping them would increase the number. Sorting the cards $1,\dots,100$ by this rule gives exactly
$$9,99,98,\dots,90,89,8,88,87,\dots,80,79,78,7,77,\dots,23,2,22,21,\dots,12,1,11,10,100.$$

prompt: You are bargaining with a salesperson for the price of an item. Your first offer is \$$a$ and theirs is \$$b$. After you raise your offer by a certain percentage and they lower their offer by the same percentage, you arrive at an agreed price. What is that price, in terms of $a$ and $b$?

solutions.title: Solve for the percentage
solutions.body:
Let the percentage be $r$ written as a decimal (for $20\%$, $r=0.2$), and let $p$ be the agreed price. Then
$$p=a(1+r)=b(1-r).$$
From $a+ar=b-br$ we get $(a+b)r=b-a$, so $r=\dfrac{b-a}{a+b}$. Therefore
$$p=a\left(1+\frac{b-a}{a+b}\right)=a\cdot\frac{(a+b)+(b-a)}{a+b}=\frac{2ab}{a+b}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$ dollars** (the *harmonic mean* of $a$ and $b$).

solutions.title: Use reciprocals
solutions.body:
From $p=a(1+r)$ and $p=b(1-r)$:
$$\frac pa=1+r,\qquad \frac pb=1-r.$$
Adding eliminates $r$: $\dfrac pa+\dfrac pb=2$, so $p\left(\dfrac{a+b}{ab}\right)=2$ and $p=\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$.

(Check: $a=60$, $b=100$ gives $p=75$; that is $60$ raised by $25\%$, and $100$ lowered by $25\%$.)

**Answer: $\dfrac{2ab}{a+b}$**

prompt:
The game of pool includes $15$ balls that fit within a triangular rack as shown.

Seven of the balls are "striped" (not colored with a single color) and eight are "solid" (colored with a single color). Prove that no matter how the $15$ balls are arranged in the rack, there must always be a pair of striped balls adjacent to each other.
answer: Split the rack into $6$ groups of mutually touching balls (four triangles of $3$, one pair, one single ball); with $7$ striped balls, two striped balls share a group (pigeonhole).

solutions.title: Pigeonhole with six regions
Outer ring and inner triangle
solutions.body:
Suppose no two striped balls touch. The $3$ inner balls $(3,2),(4,2),(4,3)$ all touch each other, so at most one of them is striped. The $12$ outer balls form a closed ring in which consecutive balls touch, so at most $6$ of them can be striped, and exactly $6$ only if striped and solid balls alternate around the ring. Since $7$ balls are striped, exactly $6$ outer and $1$ inner ball are striped, and the outer ones alternate.

Each inner ball touches two outer balls that are neighbours in the ring: $(3,2)$ touches $(2,2),(3,3)$; $(4,2)$ touches $(3,1),(4,1)$; $(4,3)$ touches $(3,3),(4,4)$. In an alternating ring, one of any two neighbours is striped. So the striped inner ball touches a striped outer ball, a contradiction. ∎

prompt: Suppose that $p$, $p+d$, $p+2d$, $p+3d$, $p+4d$, and $p+5d$ are six prime numbers, where $p$ and $d$ are positive integers. Show that $d$ must be divisible by $2$, $3$, and $5$.
answer: If a prime $q\nmid d$, then any $q$ consecutive terms of the progression have different remainders mod $q$, so one is a multiple of $q$. For $q=2,3,5$ this produces a multiple of $q$ among the terms that is larger than $q$, which is not prime.

solutions.title: Remainders in an arithmetic progression
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** Let $q$ be a prime with $q\nmid d$. Then any $q$ consecutive terms $a, a+d,\dots,a+(q-1)d$ leave $q$ different remainders mod $q$, so exactly one of them is divisible by $q$.

*Proof.* If $a+id$ and $a+jd$ ($0\le i<j\le q-1$) had the same remainder, then $q\mid (j-i)d$. Since $q$ is prime, $q\mid j-i$ or $q\mid d$. But $0<j-i<q$ and $q\nmid d$. So the $q$ remainders are different, and they must be all of $0,1,\dots,q-1$. $\square$

The six terms are distinct, since $d>0$.

- **$2\mid d$.** If $d$ is odd, the terms alternate between even and odd, so three of them are even. At most one of them equals $2$, so another even term is larger than $2$ and not prime.
- **$3\mid d$.** If not, the lemma gives a multiple of $3$ among $p,p+d,p+2d$ and another among $p+3d,p+4d,p+5d$. At most one of them equals $3$, so the other is a multiple of $3$ larger than $3$, not prime.
- **$5\mid d$.** We now know $6\mid d$, so $d\ge 6$. If $5\nmid d$, the lemma gives a multiple of $5$ among $p+d,\dots,p+5d$. All of these are at least $2+6=8>5$, so it is not prime.

So $2$, $3$, and $5$ all divide $d$ (so $30\mid d$; e.g. $7,37,67,97,127,157$ works). ∎

prompt:
A polygon is called *convex* if all of its internal angles are smaller than $180^\circ$. Here are examples of nonconvex and convex polygons (see the figure).

Given a convex polygon, prove that one can find three distinct vertices $A$, $P$, and $Q$, where $PQ$ is a side of the polygon, such that the perpendicular from $A$ to the line $PQ$ meets the segment $PQ$ (possibly at $P$ or $Q$).
answer: Take $PQ$ to be a longest side. If no other vertex projected onto segment $PQ$, then going around the polygon from $Q$ to $P$, some side would have to jump from beyond $Q$ to beyond $P$, and that side would be longer than $PQ$.

solutions.title: Use a longest side
solutions.body:
Let $PQ$ be a side of maximal length $L$. Choose coordinates with $P=(0,0)$ and $Q=(L,0)$. For a point $V=(x,y)$, the perpendicular from $V$ to line $PQ$ meets the segment $PQ$ exactly when $0\le x\le L$. We must find a vertex other than $P,Q$ with $0\le x\le L$.

Suppose there is none. Walk around the polygon from $Q$ to $P$ the long way (not along side $PQ$): $Q=V_1,V_2,\dots,V_m=P$ with $m\ge3$. Every intermediate vertex $V_2,\dots,V_{m-1}$ has $x<0$ or $x>L$. Let $i$ be the last index with $x(V_i)\ge L$ (it exists since $x(V_1)=L$). Then $i<m$, and $V_{i+1}$ has $x\le 0$: either $V_{i+1}=P$, or it is an intermediate vertex with $x<L$, hence $x<0$.

The side $V_iV_{i+1}$ has length at least its horizontal extent $x(V_i)-x(V_{i+1})\ge L$. Equality would need $x(V_i)=L$ and $x(V_{i+1})=0$, i.e. $V_i=Q$ and $V_{i+1}=P$. That is impossible: $V_{i+1}=V_2\ne P$ when $i=1$, because $m\ge3$. So the side $V_iV_{i+1}$ is longer than $L$, which contradicts the choice of $PQ$.

Hence some vertex $A\ne P,Q$ has $0\le x(A)\le L$, and the perpendicular from $A$ to line $PQ$ meets the segment $PQ$. ∎

prompt:
A *tangent line* to a circle is a line that intersects the circle in exactly one point. A *common tangent line* to two circles is a line that is tangent to both circles. As an example, in the figure, line $a$ is a common tangent to both circles, but line $b$ is only tangent to the larger circle.

Given two distinct circles in the plane, let $n$ be the number of common tangent lines that can be drawn to these two circles. What are all possible values of $n$? Your answer should include drawings with explanations.
answer: $n\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$: one circle inside the other ($0$), internally tangent ($1$), crossing at two points ($2$), externally tangent ($3$), separate and outside each other ($4$).

solutions.title: Go through the relative positions
solutions.body:
Let the circles have centers $O_1,O_2$ and radii $r_1\ge r_2$, and let $d=O_1O_2$. (If $d=0$ and $r_1=r_2$, the circles would be equal, so this does not happen.) Every common tangent touches each circle at one point and has each circle entirely on one side. It is either *external* (both circles on the same side) or *internal* (the circles on opposite sides, so the line passes between them).

- **$n=0$: one circle strictly inside the other** ($d<r_1-r_2$). Any line tangent to the inner circle passes through an interior point of the outer circle, so it cuts the outer circle in two points. No common tangents.
- **$n=1$: internally tangent** ($d=r_1-r_2>0$). The tangent line at the point of contact touches both circles. Any other tangent line of the small circle passes inside the big circle, as in the previous case. Exactly $1$.
- **$n=2$: crossing at two points** ($r_1-r_2<d<r_1+r_2$). No line can pass between the circles, since they overlap, so there are no internal tangents. There are two external tangents, one on each side of the line of centers. Exactly $2$.
- **$n=3$: externally tangent** ($d=r_1+r_2$). The two external tangents, plus the common tangent at the point of contact, which separates the circles. Exactly $3$.
- **$n=4$: separate, neither inside the other** ($d>r_1+r_2$). Two external tangents and two internal tangents, the latter crossing between the circles. Exactly $4$.

These cases cover every pair of distinct circles. (Draw one picture for each case: a small circle inside a big one; a small circle touching a big one from inside; two overlapping circles with the two tangents along the "outside"; two touching circles with three tangents; two separate circles with four tangents forming an X between them.)

**Answer: $n$ can be $0, 1, 2, 3$, or $4$.**

prompt:
Ara and Bea play a game where they take turns putting numbers from $1$ to $5$ into the cells of the X-shaped diagram shown. Each number must be played exactly once, and a cell cannot have more than one number placed in it. Ara's goal is for the two diagonals of the X diagram to have the same sum when the game is over; Bea's goal is for these two sums to be unequal.

(a) Show that Ara can always win if he goes first.

(b) Show that Bea can always win if she goes first.
answer: (a) Ara puts $5$ in the center, then answers Bea's $n$ in a corner with $5-n$ in the opposite corner; both diagonals then sum to $10$. (b) Bea puts $2$ in the center; the two diagonal sums then total $17$, which is odd, so they cannot be equal.

solutions.title: Control the center
solutions.body:
The center cell lies on both diagonals and the four corners each lie on one. So at the end,
$$(\text{sum of diagonal 1})+(\text{sum of diagonal 2})=(1+2+3+4+5)+(\text{center})=15+(\text{center}).$$

**(a)** Ara first places $5$ in the center. Then the two diagonal sums will total $15+5=20$. Bea must now put some number $n\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ in a corner. Ara answers with $5-n$ in the opposite corner of the same diagonal. This is possible because $5-n$ is also in $\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $5-n\ne n$ (as $n\ne\tfrac52$), so it has not been used yet, and the opposite corner is empty. That diagonal now has sum $5+n+(5-n)=10$. Whatever happens with the last two numbers, the other diagonal has sum $20-10=10$ too. Ara wins.

**(b)** Bea first places $2$ in the center. The two diagonal sums will total $15+2=17$, an odd number. Two equal integers have an even total, so the sums can never be equal, whatever the remaining moves. Bea wins. (Placing $4$ in the center also works.) ∎

prompt:
Mr. Murgatroyd decides to throw his class a pizza party, but he's going to make them hunt for it first. He chooses eleven locations in the school, which we'll call $1, 2, \dots, 11$. His plan is to tell students to start at location $1$, and at each location $n$ from $1$ to $10$, they will find a message directing them to go to location $n+1$; at location $11$, there's pizza!

Mr. Murgatroyd sends his teaching assistant to post the ten messages in locations $1$ to $10$. Unfortunately, the assistant jumbles up the message cards at random before posting them. If the students begin at location $1$ as planned and follow the directions at each location, show that they will still get to the pizza.
answer: Each of the locations $2,\dots,11$ is named on exactly one message and location $1$ on none. So the students can never return to a location they have already visited (the first repeat would have to be location $1$), and they must reach $11$ within $10$ moves.

solutions.title: No location can be entered twice
solutions.body:
The ten messages say "go to $2$", "go to $3$", …, "go to $11$", one of each, posted in locations $1$ through $10$. So **each of the locations $2,\dots,11$ is the target of exactly one message, and location $1$ is the target of none.**

Let the locations visited be $v_0=1, v_1, v_2,\dots$, where each $v_{m}$ ($m\ge1$) is the target of the message at $v_{m-1}$. Suppose some location is visited twice, and pick the repeat $v_i=v_j$ ($i<j$) with $j$ as small as possible.

- If $i=0$, then $v_j=1$ is the target of a message, which is impossible.
- If $i\ge1$, then $v_i=v_j$ is the target of the messages at $v_{i-1}$ and at $v_{j-1}$. Only one message points to this location, and it hangs in one place, so $v_{i-1}=v_{j-1}$. That is an earlier repeat (since $j-1<j$), which contradicts the choice of $j$.

So the students never visit any location twice. There are only $11$ locations, so after at most $10$ moves the walk must end, and it can only end at location $11$, where there is no message. They get to the pizza. ∎

prompt:
Given a positive integer $N$ (written in base $10$), define its *integer substrings* to be integers that are equal to strings of one or more consecutive digits from $N$, including $N$ itself. For example, the integer substrings of $3208$ are $3$, $2$, $0$, $8$, $32$, $20$, $320$, $208$, and $3208$. (The substring $08$ is omitted from this list because it is the same integer as the substring $8$, which is already listed.)

What is the greatest integer $N$ such that no integer substring of $N$ is a multiple of $9$? (Note: $0$ is a multiple of $9$.)

solutions.title: Prefix sums and the pigeonhole principle
solutions.body:
Recall that an integer is divisible by $9$ exactly when its digit sum is. (Reason: $10^k-1=99\dots9$ is a multiple of $9$, so $\overline{d_k\dots d_1d_0}=\sum d_i10^i$ differs from $\sum d_i$ by a multiple of $9$.)

**$88{,}888{,}888$ works.** Its integer substrings are made of $k$ eights ($1\le k\le8$), with digit sum $8k$, and $9\nmid 8k$ for $1\le k\le 8$.

**Every larger $N$ fails.** If $N>88{,}888{,}888$ has $8$ digits, one of its digits is $9$, and that single digit is a substring divisible by $9$. Otherwise $N$ has at least $9$ digits. Let $s_0=0$ and let $s_k$ be the sum of the first $k$ digits of $N$, for $k=1,\dots,9$. These are $10$ numbers, but there are only $9$ possible remainders mod $9$. So by the pigeonhole principle, $s_j\equiv s_k\pmod 9$ for some $j<k$. Then $s_k-s_j$, the digit sum of the block of digits in positions $j+1,\dots,k$, is a multiple of $9$, so that block is an integer substring divisible by $9$. (If the block starts with zeros it is still a multiple of $9$, possibly $0$.)

**Answer: $88{,}888{,}888$**

prompt: In the following figure—not drawn to scale!—$E$ is the midpoint of $BC$, triangle $FEC$ has area $7$, and quadrilateral $DBEG$ has area $27$. Triangles $ADG$ and $GEF$ have the same area, $x$. Find $x$.

solutions.title: Chase areas with equal bases
solutions.body:
Write $[\,\cdot\,]$ for area. In the figure, $D$ is on $AB$, $G=AE\cap DC$, and $F$ is on $GC$.

1. Draw $GB$. Triangles $GBE$ and $GEC$ have equal bases $BE=EC$ and the same height from $G$, so $[GBE]=[GEC]=x+7$. Then $[GDB]=[DBEG]-[GBE]=27-(x+7)=20-x$.
2. Draw $AC$. Triangles $ABE$ and $AEC$ have equal bases and the same height from $A$, and $[ABE]=[ADG]+[DBEG]=x+27$. So $[AEC]=x+27$, $[AGC]=[AEC]-[GEC]=20$, and $[CAD]=[AGC]+[ADG]=20+x$. Also $[CDB]=[DBEG]+[GEC]=34+x$.
3. Triangles $GAD$ and $GDB$ share the height from $G$ to line $AB$, so $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{x}{20-x}$. Triangles $CAD$ and $CDB$ share the height from $C$, so $\dfrac{AD}{DB}=\dfrac{20+x}{34+x}$.

Hence $x(34+x)=(20-x)(20+x)$, i.e. $2x^2+34x-400=0$, i.e. $x^2+17x-200=(x-8)(x+25)=0$. Since $x>0$, $x=8$.

**Answer: $x=8$**

solutions.title: Check with a concrete figure

prompt:
A school needs to elect its president. The school has $121$ students, each of whom belongs to one of two tribes: Geometers or Algebraists. Two candidates are running for president: one Geometer and one Algebraist. The Geometers vote only for Geometers and the Algebraists only for Algebraists. There are more Algebraists than Geometers, but the Geometers are resourceful. They convince the school that the following two-step procedure is fairer:

(a) The school is divided into $11$ groups, with $11$ students in each group. Each group elects a representative for step 2.

(b) The $11$ elected representatives elect a president.

Not only do the Geometers manage to have this two-step procedure approved, they also volunteer to assign the students to groups for step 1. What is the minimum number of Geometers in the school that guarantees they can elect a Geometer as president? (In any stage of voting, the majority wins.)

solutions.title: Work backwards from the final vote
solutions.body:
**Step 2.** A Geometer becomes president exactly when at least $6$ of the $11$ representatives are Geometers.

**Step 1.** A group of $11$ elects a Geometer exactly when it contains at least $6$ Geometers.

**Enough.** With $36$ Geometers, put $6$ Geometers (and $5$ Algebraists) in each of $6$ groups, and fill the other $5$ groups with the remaining $85-30=55$ Algebraists. Six groups elect Geometers, and the Geometer wins $6$ to $5$.

**Necessary.** To win, the Geometers need $6$ groups with at least $6$ Geometers each, so at least $6\cdot 6=36$ Geometers. With $35$ or fewer, at most $5$ groups can have a Geometer majority, and the Algebraist wins.

**Answer: 36**

prompt:
Amelia's mother proposes a game. "Pick two of the shapes below," she says to Amelia. (The shapes are an equilateral triangle, a parallelogram, an isosceles trapezoid, a kite, and an ellipse. These shapes are drawn to scale.) Amelia's mother continues: "I will draw those two shapes on a sheet of paper, in whatever position and orientation I choose, without overlapping them. Then you draw a straight line that cuts both shapes, so that each shape is divided into two congruent halves."

Which two of the shapes should Amelia choose to guarantee that she can succeed? Given that choice of shapes, explain how Amelia can draw her line, what property of those shapes makes it possible for her to do so, and why this would not work with any other pair of these shapes.

solutions.title: Half-turn symmetry
solutions.body:
**The winning choice: the parallelogram and the ellipse.** Both shapes have a *center* $O$: a half-turn ($180^\circ$ rotation) about $O$ maps the shape onto itself. If a line passes through $O$, the half-turn about $O$ maps the line to itself and swaps the two sides of it. So it maps one half of the shape onto the other, and the two halves are congruent. So whatever positions her mother chooses, Amelia draws the line through the centers of the two shapes (the intersection of the parallelogram's diagonals and the center of the ellipse). It cuts each shape into two congruent halves.

**Why no other pair works.** Two congruent halves have equal areas, so a good line must split the area of each shape in half. For a shape with a center $O$, an area-halving line must pass through $O$: a line not through $O$ and its half-turn image are two different parallel lines, and the half of the shape on the side away from $O$ is strictly smaller than half.

The triangle, the trapezoid and the kite have only finitely many lines that cut them into congruent halves. For the equilateral triangle: a line not through a vertex cuts it into a triangle and a quadrilateral, which are not congruent. A line through a vertex gives two triangles of equal area only if it is the median, so the only good lines are the three axes of symmetry. Similarly, the isosceles trapezoid and the kite each have just one good line, their axis of symmetry.

So if Amelia picks at least one of these three shapes, her mother can place it so that none of its (finitely many) good lines is a good line of the other shape. If the other shape is the parallelogram or the ellipse, she makes sure that the axes miss its center. If the other shape is also one of the three, she makes sure that no axis of one coincides with an axis of the other, e.g. by tilting it slightly. Then no line works for both shapes.

**Answer: the parallelogram and the ellipse** (both have $180^\circ$ rotational symmetry, so the line through their two centers works).

prompt:
Sugar Station sells $44$ different kinds of candies, packaged one to a box. Each box is priced at a positive integer number of cents, and it costs \$1.51 to buy one of every kind. (There is no discount based on the number of candies in a purchase.) Unfortunately, Anna only has \$0.75.

(a) Show that Anna can buy at least $22$ boxes, each containing a different candy.

(b) Show that Anna can do even better, buying at least $25$ boxes, each containing a different candy.
answer: (a) Split the candies into two groups of $22$; one group costs at most $75$ cents. (b) The $25$ cheapest candies cost at most $75$ cents: look at the $19$th most expensive candy and split into cases on whether it costs at least $4$ cents.

solutions.title: Halves, then the 19th most expensive candy
solutions.body:
All prices are in cents; the total is $151$.

**(a)** Split the $44$ kinds into any two groups of $22$. Their costs add up to $151$, so they cannot both be $76$ or more. One group costs at most $75$ cents, and Anna buys that group.

**(b)** List the candies from most to least expensive, $p_1\ge p_2\ge\dots\ge p_{44}$, and look at $p_{19}$.

- If $p_{19}\ge 4$, then $p_1,\dots,p_{19}\ge 4$, so the $19$ most expensive candies cost at least $76$. The remaining $25$ candies cost at most $151-76=75$.
- If $p_{19}\le 3$, then each of $p_{20},\dots,p_{44}$ is at most $3$, so these $25$ candies cost at most $25\cdot 3=75$.

Either way, the $25$ cheapest candies cost at most $75$ cents, so Anna can buy $25$ different candies. ∎

prompt: Sasha wants to bake $6$ cookies in his $8$ inch $\times$ $8$ inch square baking sheet. With a cookie cutter, he cuts out from the dough six circular shapes, each exactly $3$ inches in diameter. Can he place these six dough shapes on the baking sheet without the shapes touching each other? If yes, show us how. If no, explain why not. (Assume that the dough does not expand during baking.)
answer: Yes. Put the centers at the points $(0,0),(5,0),\left(\tfrac52,\tfrac53\right),\left(0,\tfrac{10}3\right),\left(5,\tfrac{10}3\right),\left(\tfrac52,5\right)$ of the central $5\times5$ square; the closest centers are $\sqrt{325}/6\approx3.005>3$ apart.

solutions.title: Stagger the centers in the middle 5 by 5 square
solutions.body:
A cookie of radius $1.5$ fits on the sheet exactly when its center is at least $1.5$ from every edge. So the centers must lie in the middle $5\times5$ square. Two cookies do not touch exactly when their centers are more than $3$ apart.

Use coordinates on the middle square, $0\le x,y\le 5$. Divide it into halves in one direction and thirds in the other. This gives a grid of six $\tfrac52\times\tfrac53$ rectangles with grid points $x\in\{0,\tfrac52,5\}$, $y\in\{0,\tfrac53,\tfrac{10}3,5\}$. Put the centers at alternate grid points, like the black squares of a checkerboard:
$$(0,0),\ (5,0),\ \left(\tfrac52,\tfrac53\right),\ \left(0,\tfrac{10}3\right),\ \left(5,\tfrac{10}3\right),\ \left(\tfrac52,5\right).$$
Distances between centers:
- diagonal neighbours, e.g. $(0,0)$ and $\left(\tfrac52,\tfrac53\right)$: $\sqrt{\left(\tfrac52\right)^2+\left(\tfrac53\right)^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac{225+100}{36}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{325}}{6}\approx 3.005>3$ (because $325>324=18^2$);
- vertical neighbours, e.g. $(0,0)$ and $\left(0,\tfrac{10}3\right)$: $\tfrac{10}{3}>3$;
- all other pairs are even farther apart ($5$ or more horizontally, or $\tfrac{10}{3}$ vertically together with $\tfrac52$ horizontally).

So the six cookies fit and no two touch, although just barely.

**Answer: Yes** (with the arrangement above). ∎

prompt:
Let $S_n$ be the sum of the first $n$ prime numbers. For example,
$$S_5 = 2+3+5+7+11 = 28.$$
Does there exist an integer $k$ such that $S_{2023} < k^2 < S_{2024}$?

solutions.title: Squares as sums of odd numbers
solutions.body:
**Yes.** Let $p_n$ be the $n$-th prime, and let $k$ be the smallest integer with $k^2>S_{2023}$. Recall that $k^2=1+3+5+\dots+(2k-1)$.

**Claim: $2k-1\le p_{2023}$.** Compare $S_{2023}=2+3+5+\dots+p_{2023}$ with the sum $1+3+5+\dots+p_{2023}$ of *all* odd numbers up to $p_{2023}$. The second sum contains every odd prime that appears in $S_{2023}$, and also $1$ and $9$, which are not prime. So it is at least $S_{2023}-2+1+9>S_{2023}$:
$$S_{2023}<1+3+5+\dots+p_{2023}=\left(\frac{p_{2023}+1}{2}\right)^2.$$
By minimality of $k$, $k$ is at most the integer $\tfrac{p_{2023}+1}{2}$, i.e. $2k-1\le p_{2023}$.

**Finish.** Again by minimality, $(k-1)^2\le S_{2023}$. Therefore
$$k^2=(k-1)^2+(2k-1)\le S_{2023}+p_{2023}<S_{2023}+p_{2024}=S_{2024}.$$
Together with $k^2>S_{2023}$ this gives $S_{2023}<k^2<S_{2024}$. ∎

(Numerically, $S_{2023}=16{,}676{,}972$, $S_{2024}=16{,}694{,}571$, and $k=4084$, $k^2=16{,}679{,}056$.)

solutions.title: Contradiction
solutions.body:
Suppose no square lies strictly between $S_{2023}$ and $S_{2024}$. Let $r=\lfloor\sqrt{S_{2023}}\rfloor$, so $r^2\le S_{2023}<(r+1)^2$. By assumption $(r+1)^2$ is not less than $S_{2024}$, so
$$r^2\le S_{2023}<S_{2024}\le (r+1)^2.$$
Hence $p_{2024}=S_{2024}-S_{2023}\le 2r+1$. So every prime $p_1,\dots,p_{2023}$ is less than $2r+1$, and every odd one among them is at most $2r-1$. Then $S_{2023}$ is at most $2$ plus the odd numbers $3,5,\dots,2r-1$, leaving out $9$ (here $2r-1\ge9$ because $p_{2024}>9$):
$$S_{2023}\le \bigl(1+3+\dots+(2r-1)\bigr)-1-9+2=r^2-8<r^2.$$
This contradicts $r^2\le S_{2023}$. ∎

prompt:
Imagine a language that uses the Latin alphabet and in which all words consist of six letters. Let us define the *distance* between any two words in that language as follows. If the letters in the two words are $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_6$ and $b_1, b_2, \dots, b_6$, then the distance between them is the number of values of index $i$, for $i = 1, \dots, 6$, such that $a_i \ne b_i$. For example, the distance between these two words:

`zmootq`

`zoeutq`

is $3$, because their letters differ in three positions — the 2nd, 3rd and the 4th.

(a) Find three words such that the distance between any pair of these words equals $2$.

(b) Find three words such that the distances between the three pairs of these words are $5$, $4$ and $3$.

The words do not have to make sense in English.
answer: For example (a) `aaaaaa`, `bbaaaa`, `ccaaaa`; (b) `aaaaaa`, `bbbbba`, `aabbbb` (distances $5$, $4$, $3$). Many other answers work.

solutions.title: Build the words position by position
solutions.body:
**(a)** Make the three words agree everywhere except in two chosen positions, and in those two positions use three different letters:
$$W_1=\texttt{aaaaaa},\quad W_2=\texttt{bbaaaa},\quad W_3=\texttt{ccaaaa}.$$
Any two of them differ exactly in positions $1$ and $2$, so every distance is $2$. (A version with English words: `search`, `snatch`, `stanch`, which differ only in positions $2$ and $4$.)

**(b)** Start with two words at distance $5$: $W_4=\texttt{aaaaaa}$ and $W_5=\texttt{bbbbba}$ (they differ in positions $1$–$5$). We want $W_6$ at distance $4$ from $W_4$ and $3$ from $W_5$. Try $W_6=\texttt{aabbbb}$:

- $W_4$ vs $W_6$: they differ in positions $3,4,5,6$, so the distance is $4$;
- $W_5$ vs $W_6$: they differ in positions $1,2,6$, so the distance is $3$.

So $\texttt{aaaaaa},\ \texttt{bbbbba},\ \texttt{aabbbb}$ have pairwise distances $5,4,3$. (Another example: `abcdef`, `aghijk`, `ablmjk`.)

prompt:
Jessica has five distinct integers. She can form ten distinct pairs of these integers if she ignores the order within each pair. The sums of all ten pairs are known and they are:
$$-17,\ -14,\ -9,\ -6,\ -1,\ 2,\ 7,\ 12,\ 15,\ 23.$$
What are the five integers?

solutions.title: Total, then the extreme sums
solutions.body:
Call the integers $a<b<c<d<e$. The smallest pair sum is $a+b=-17$ and the largest is $d+e=23$. The second smallest must be $a+c=-14$ (any other sum except $a+b$ is at least $a+c$), and similarly the second largest is $c+e=15$.

Each integer appears in exactly $4$ of the ten pairs, so the sum of all ten pair sums is $4(a+b+c+d+e)$. The ten sums add to $12$, so $a+b+c+d+e=3$.

Then $c=3-(a+b)-(d+e)=3+17-23=-3$. From $a+c=-14$ we get $a=-11$, and from $c+e=15$ we get $e=18$. Then $b=-17-a=-6$ and $d=23-e=5$.

**Check:** the pair sums of $-11,-6,-3,5,18$ are $-17,-14,-6,7,-9,-1,12,2,15,23$, which is exactly the given list. ✓

**Answer: $-11,\ -6,\ -3,\ 5,\ 18$**

prompt:
Fifteen balls labeled $1, 2, \dots, 15$ are stored in two boxes, so that each box contains at least two balls and the average of the numbers on the balls in one box is not equal to the average of the numbers on the balls in the other box.

Show that it is possible to move one ball from one box to the other so that either both boxes' averages increase or both boxes' averages decrease.
answer: The overall average $8$ lies strictly between the two box averages; moving ball $8$ (from whichever box it is in to the other) moves both averages the same way.

solutions.title: Move the ball labeled 8
solutions.body:
**Key fact.** If a ball with value $v$ is removed from a set whose average is $m$ (leaving at least one ball), the average goes up if $v<m$ and down if $v>m$. If a ball with value $v$ is added to a set with average $m$, the average goes up if $v>m$ and down if $v<m$.

**The boxes straddle 8.** The average of all $15$ numbers is $\tfrac{1+15}{2}=8$. This overall average is a weighted average of the two box averages, which are different, so it lies strictly between them. Call $A$ the box with average below $8$ and $B$ the box with average above $8$.

**Case 1: ball 8 is in box $A$.** Move it to $B$. In $A$, $8$ was above the average, so removing it lowers $A$'s average ($A$ still has at least one ball). In $B$, $8$ is below the average, so adding it lowers $B$'s average. Both averages decrease.

**Case 2: ball 8 is in box $B$.** Move it to $A$. Removing it from $B$, where it was below average, raises $B$'s average; adding it to $A$, where it is above average, raises $A$'s average. Both averages increase.

In either case moving ball $8$ works. ∎

prompt: Let $S$ be a finite, nonempty set of points in the plane such that, for every point $A \in S$, there exist points $B, C \in S$ (distinct from $A$) such that $\angle BAC = 125^\circ$. What is the smallest possible number of points in $S$?

solutions.title: Convex hull bound and a heptagon
solutions.body:
**At least 7 points.** The points of $S$ are not all on one line (on a line, every angle $\angle BAC$ is $0^\circ$ or $180^\circ$). So the convex hull of $S$ is a convex polygon $P$ whose vertices belong to $S$. Let $A$ be a vertex of $P$. All points of $S$ lie in $P$, so for any $B,C\in S$ the angle $\angle BAC$ fits inside the interior angle of $P$ at $A$. Since some $\angle BAC=125^\circ$, every interior angle of $P$ is at least $125^\circ$. Then every exterior angle is at most $55^\circ$. The exterior angles of a convex polygon add up to $360^\circ$, so $P$ has at least $\tfrac{360}{55}\approx 6.5$ vertices, i.e. at least $7$. Hence $|S|\ge 7$.

**7 points suffice.** Draw four equal segments $AB, BC, CD, DE$ end to end, turning the same way at each joint so that $\angle ABC=\angle BCD=\angle CDE=125^\circ$. At $A$ draw a ray $AX$ with $\angle BAX=125^\circ$, and at $E$ a ray $EY$ with $\angle DEY=125^\circ$, both on the same side of the path as the other angles. Walking around, the direction has turned by $5\cdot 55^\circ=275^\circ<360^\circ$, so the two rays meet at a point $F$ (on the symmetry axis of the path). This makes a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$ with five angles of $125^\circ$, so $\angle EFA=720^\circ-5\cdot125^\circ=95^\circ$. Finally, build a triangle $FGA$ on the outside of side $FA$ with $\angle AFG=30^\circ$, $\angle FAG=25^\circ$, and therefore $\angle FGA=125^\circ$.

For $S=\{A,B,C,D,E,F,G\}$:
$$\angle FAB=\angle ABC=\angle BCD=\angle CDE=\angle DEF=125^\circ,$$
$$\angle EFG=95^\circ+30^\circ=125^\circ,\qquad \angle FGA=125^\circ.$$
So every point of $S$ is the vertex of a $125^\circ$ angle formed with two other points of $S$.

**Answer: 7**

prompt:
A *string* is a finite ordered sequence of one or more letters. For example, `apple` and `qvdkxo` are strings consisting of English letters. If one string appears as a consecutive sequence of letters inside another string, we say the first string is a *substring* of the second. (A string is considered to be a substring of itself.)

A *palindrome* is a string that remains the same regardless of whether its letters are read from left to right or from right to left. Given a string, we may count its distinct palindrome substrings. For example, the string `propeller` contains $7$ distinct palindromes as substrings: `p`, `r`, `o`, `e`, `l`, `ll`, and `elle`.

What is the maximum number of distinct palindromes that can appear as substrings in a string of length $2025$?

solutions.title: At most one new palindrome ends at each position
solutions.body:
We show that a string of length $n$ contains at most $n$ distinct palindromes, and that $n$ is possible.

**Example.** The string `aaa…a` ($n$ letters) contains the $n$ palindromes `a`, `aa`, …, and all $n$ of them are different. (A string of $n$ different letters also works.)

**Upper bound.** For each distinct palindrome in the string, mark its *first* occurrence, i.e. the one that ends furthest to the left. (All occurrences have the same length, so this is also the one that starts furthest left.)

*Claim: no two marked occurrences end at the same position.* Suppose palindromes $Q$ (shorter) and $P$ (longer) have marked occurrences that both end at position $j$. Then $Q$ is a suffix (final part) of $P$. Reverse everything: $Q$ reversed is a prefix of $P$ reversed. But $P$ and $Q$ are palindromes, so $Q$ is a prefix of $P$. This copy of $Q$ at the start of $P$ ends at position $j-(|P|-|Q|)<j$, so it is an earlier occurrence of $Q$. Then the occurrence ending at $j$ was not the first one and was not marked. This contradiction proves the claim.

There are only $n$ possible ending positions, so there are at most $n$ marked occurrences, i.e. at most $n$ distinct palindromes. For $n=2025$, the maximum is $2025$.

**Answer: 2025**

solutions.title: Add one letter at a time
solutions.body:
Build the string letter by letter. When a new letter is appended, any *new* palindrome must end at the new last position, so it is a palindromic suffix. Suppose two palindromic suffixes $Q$ and $P$ (with $Q$ shorter) both appeared for the first time. Then $Q$, being a suffix of the palindrome $P$, is also a prefix of $P$. That prefix ends earlier, so $Q$ had appeared before, which is a contradiction. So each new letter adds at most one new palindrome, and $n$ letters give at most $n$. The string `a…a` reaches $n$.

**Answer: 2025**

prompt:
Let $\mathcal{T} = ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezoid with side lengths $1, 1, 1$, and $2$. ("Isosceles" means that angles $A$ and $B$ in the figure are equal.)

(a) Draw a diagram that illustrates how to dissect $\mathcal{T}$ into four congruent trapezoids, each similar to $\mathcal{T}$. In other words, we divide $\mathcal{T}$ into four congruent trapezoids that do not overlap and have no gaps between them, and each is a scaled-down version of $\mathcal{T}$.

(b) Do the same as (a), but now dissect $\mathcal{T}$ into nine congruent trapezoids, each similar to $\mathcal{T}$.

Draw your diagrams carefully, so that it is clear how your dissections work.
answer: (a) Cut along the midline and place two points $\tfrac12$ apart on it: one half-size trapezoid on top (upside down), its mirror image below, and two tilted ones at the sides. (b) Split $\mathcal{T}$ into three unit equilateral triangles and cut each into three trapezoids of side $\tfrac13$ meeting at its center.

solutions.title: Work on the triangular grid
solutions.body:
Put the trapezoid on coordinates: $A=(0,0)$, $B=(2,0)$, $C=\left(\tfrac32,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$, $D=\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)$. Then $AB=2$ and $BC=CD=DA=1$, and the angles at $A$ and $B$ are $60^\circ$. In fact $\mathcal{T}$ is made of three unit equilateral triangles, so it is natural to draw everything on a grid of equilateral triangles. A trapezoid similar to $\mathcal{T}$ at scale $s$ has sides $s, s, s, 2s$ and angles $60^\circ, 60^\circ, 120^\circ, 120^\circ$.

**(a) Four pieces at scale $\tfrac12$.** Let $\ell$ be the midline $y=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}$; it meets $AD$ at $M=\left(\tfrac14,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$ and $BC$ at $N=\left(\tfrac74,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$. On $\ell$ mark $E=\left(\tfrac34,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$ and $F=\left(\tfrac54,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}\right)$, which are $\tfrac12$ apart and symmetric about the axis $x=1$. On $AB$ mark $P=\left(\tfrac12,0\right)$ and $Q=\left(\tfrac32,0\right)$. Draw the segments $EF$, $DE$, $CF$, $PE$, $QF$. The four pieces are:

- $DCFE$ (upside down): $DC=1$, $EF=\tfrac12$, $DE=CF=\tfrac12$.
- $PQFE$ (its mirror image in $\ell$): $PQ=1$, $EF=\tfrac12$, $PE=QF=\tfrac12$.
- $APED$ (tilted): $AD=1$ is parallel to $PE$, which has length $\tfrac12$, and $AP=ED=\tfrac12$.
- $QBCF$ (the mirror image of $APED$ in the line $x=1$): $BC=1$, $QF=\tfrac12$, $QB=FC=\tfrac12$.

Each piece has sides $\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,1$, with the side of length $1$ parallel to the opposite side, so each is congruent to $\mathcal{T}$ scaled by $\tfrac12$. The pieces fill $\mathcal{T}$ without overlap.

**(b) Nine pieces at scale $\tfrac13$.** Let $E=(1,0)$ be the midpoint of $AB$ and draw $ED$ and $EC$. This cuts $\mathcal{T}$ into three unit equilateral triangles $ADE$, $DCE$, $ECB$.

Now cut one unit equilateral triangle, say $ADE$ with center $O=\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}\right)$, into three pieces. Mark the points one third of the way along each side, going around the triangle: $A_1$ on $AD$ with $AA_1=\tfrac13$, $D_1$ on $DE$ with $DD_1=\tfrac13$, and $E_1$ on $EA$ with $EE_1=\tfrac13$. Join each of $A_1$, $D_1$, $E_1$ to $O$. The segment $A_1O$ is horizontal (parallel to $AE$) and has length $\tfrac13$, and the same holds for the other two segments after rotating by $120^\circ$. The piece $AA_1OE_1$ has $AE_1=\tfrac23$ parallel to $A_1O=\tfrac13$, and $AA_1=OE_1=\tfrac13$. So it is $\mathcal{T}$ scaled by $\tfrac13$, and the other two pieces $A_1DD_1O$ and $E_1OD_1E$ are its rotations by $\pm120^\circ$ about $O$.

Do the same in each of the three triangles. This gives nine congruent trapezoids, each similar to $\mathcal{T}$ at scale $\tfrac13$. (This dissection is not the only one.) ∎

prompt:
Suppose that

- $a$ is a positive real number,
- $b$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $a$,
- $c$ is the greatest integer less than or equal to $ab$, and
- $ac = 42$.

Is there any value of $a$ for which this occurs? If so, what are all such value(s), and how do you know there are no others?

(If you are familiar with "floor" notation, this problem is asking you to solve the equation $a\lfloor a\lfloor a\rfloor\rfloor = 42$.)

solutions.title: Monotonicity, then pin down b and c
solutions.body:
If $a<1$ then $b=0$ and $c=0$, so $ac=0\ne 42$. So $a\ge 1$.

**At most one solution.** If $a$ increases, then $b=\lfloor a\rfloor$ cannot decrease, so $ab$ increases and $c=\lfloor ab\rfloor$ cannot decrease. Hence $ac$ strictly increases with $a$ (because $c\ge 1$ for $a\ge 1$). So $ac=42$ has at most one solution.

**Bracketing.** For an integer $a$ we get $b=a$, $c=a^2$, so $ac=a^3$. Since $3^3=27<42<64=4^3$, the solution must satisfy $3<a<4$. Then $b=3$ and $9<3a<12$, so $c\in\{9,10,11\}$. Since $a=\dfrac{42}{c}<4$, we need $c>10.5$, so $c=11$ and $a=\dfrac{42}{11}$.

**Check.** With $a=\tfrac{42}{11}\approx 3.82$: $b=3$, $ab=\tfrac{126}{11}=11\tfrac{5}{11}$, $c=11$, and $ac=42$. ✓

**Answer: $a=\dfrac{42}{11}$, and this is the only value.**

solutions.title: Case on b directly
solutions.body:
As before $a\ge1$, so write $b=n\ge1$. Then $n\le a<n+1$, so $n^2\le ab<n^2+n$ and therefore $n^2\le c\le n^2+n-1$. This gives $42=ac\ge n\cdot n^2=n^3$, so $n\le 3$, and $42=ac<(n+1)(n^2+n)=n(n+1)^2$, so $n(n+1)^2>42$, which forces $n\ge 3$ ($2\cdot 9=18$). So $n=3$, $c\in\{9,10,11\}$, and $a=42/c$ has to lie in $[3,4)$. The candidates are $42/9\approx4.67$, $42/10=4.2$, and $42/11\approx3.82$, so only $c=11$ works. Checking $a=\tfrac{42}{11}$ shows that $c$ really is $11$.

**Answer: $a=\dfrac{42}{11}$**

prompt: Let $B$ be a brick (that is, a rectangular prism). This particular brick has the property that a single cut can split $B$ into two congruent bricks that are similar to $B$. In other words, these smaller bricks are scaled-down copies of the original brick. Find possible dimensions for $B$ (length, width, height) and explain your answer.
answer: For example $\sqrt[3]{4}\times\sqrt[3]{2}\times 1$: the edges must form a geometric progression with ratio $\sqrt[3]{2}$, and the cut halves the longest edge.

solutions.title: Which edge is halved, then compare edges
solutions.body:
Let $B$ have edges $\ell\ge w\ge h$.

**The cut.** Each piece is a box, and the cut face is one face of each piece. The face of a piece opposite its cut face is not the cut, so it lies in a face of $B$. Hence the cut plane is parallel to a pair of opposite faces of $B$. Each piece keeps the two edges of $B$ that run parallel to the cut, and the remaining edge of $B$ is split into two parts. For the pieces to be congruent, the two parts must be equal, so the cut halves one edge of $B$.

**It must halve the longest edge.** Each piece has half the volume of $B$, so it is $B$ scaled by some factor $\tfrac1r$ with $r>1$, and all its edges are shorter than the corresponding edges of $B$. In particular its longest edge is $\tfrac{\ell}{r}<\ell$. If we halved $w$ or $h$, each piece would still have an edge of length $\ell$, which is impossible. So the pieces are $w\times h\times\tfrac{\ell}{2}$.

**Matching the edges.** The shortest edge of a piece must be $\tfrac hr<h$, so $\tfrac{\ell}{2}<h$. Thus the edges of a piece, from longest to shortest, are $w\ge h>\tfrac{\ell}{2}$, and they must equal $\tfrac{\ell}{r},\tfrac{w}{r},\tfrac{h}{r}$:
$$\ell=rw,\qquad w=rh,\qquad h=\frac{r\ell}{2}.$$
Multiplying the three equations gives $\ell wh=\tfrac{r^3}{2}\,\ell wh$, so $r^3=2$ and $r=\sqrt[3]{2}$. (This also follows from the volume: each piece has volume $\tfrac12$ of $B$, so $\tfrac1{r^3}=\tfrac12$.)

**Construction.** Take $h=1$, $w=\sqrt[3]{2}$, $\ell=\sqrt[3]{4}$. Halving the longest edge gives pieces $\sqrt[3]{2}\times 1\times\tfrac{\sqrt[3]{4}}{2}$. Since $\tfrac{\sqrt[3]4}{2}=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]2}$, these edges are exactly $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt[3]2}\left(\sqrt[3]4,\ \sqrt[3]2,\ 1\right)$, so the pieces are similar to $B$. Any brick $\sqrt[3]{4}\,t\times\sqrt[3]{2}\,t\times t$ works, and these are the only ones. (This is the idea behind the A-series paper sizes, whose sides are in ratio $\sqrt2$; here a box needs ratio $\sqrt[3]2$.)

**Answer: e.g. $\sqrt[3]{4}\times\sqrt[3]{2}\times1$.** ∎

prompt: Two distinct squares overlap to form an octagon and eight right triangles (as shown in the diagram). The squares each have side length $4$ and have the same center. If one of those right triangles has side lengths $a, b, c$, where $c$ is the hypotenuse, show that the area of that triangle is $a+b-c$.
answer: All eight triangles are congruent, and each side of a square is split into $a, c, b$, so $a+b+c=4$. Then $4(a+b-c)=(a+b)^2-c^2=2ab$, so $a+b-c=\tfrac12ab$.

solutions.title: Use a + b + c = 4 and Pythagoras
solutions.body:
**All eight triangles are congruent.** The figure does not change under a $90^\circ$ rotation about the common center (each square maps to itself). It also does not change under the reflection in the line through the center and a crossing point of the two squares, which swaps the two squares. Using these symmetries, any one of the eight triangles can be moved onto any other.

**Each side has length $a+b+c$.** Look at one side of a square. The other square cuts it into three segments: the end pieces are legs of two of the small triangles, and the middle piece is a side of the octagon, which is the hypotenuse of the triangle that sticks out beyond this side. The $90^\circ$ rotation carries the corner triangle at one end of this side to the corner triangle at the other end, and it turns the leg on this side into the leg on the neighbouring side. So the two end pieces are the two *different* legs of congruent triangles, of lengths $a$ and $b$, and the side has length $a+c+b=4$.

**Finish.** Using $a+b+c=4$ and $a^2+b^2=c^2$:
$$4(a+b-c)=(a+b+c)(a+b-c)=(a+b)^2-c^2=a^2+2ab+b^2-c^2=2ab.$$
So $a+b-c=\tfrac12ab$, which is the area of the right triangle. ∎

solutions.title: Compute the octagon's area
solutions.body:
As in the first approach, the eight triangles are congruent and $a+b+c=4$. All eight sides of the octagon have length $c$, and each side lies on a side of one of the squares, at distance $2$ from the center. Joining the center to the eight vertices splits the octagon into eight triangles with base $c$ and height $2$, so the octagon has area $8\cdot\tfrac12\cdot c\cdot 2=8c$.

One square (area $16$) consists of the octagon and four of the small triangles. So each small triangle has area
$$\frac{16-8c}{4}=4-2c=(a+b+c)-2c=a+b-c.$$ ∎

prompt:
Lou is in a logic class with six other students. Their teacher assigned each of them the role of Truth-Teller or Liar. The Truth-Tellers must make only truthful statements, and the Liars must make only false statements. Each student—except Lou, who was daydreaming when the roles were assigned—knows their own role and that of all the other students. The teacher asks the students to sit in a circle, where they will be asked a question, and they must answer "in character." Lou doesn't know her own role nor anybody else's.

The teacher asks each student in the circle, one after another, "Is the person sitting to your left a Truth-Teller?" to which they must answer "Yes" or "No." Lou happens to be the last person to be called. She heard "Yes" three times and "No" three times from the other students, in some order.

Suddenly Lou realizes that she can act out her role correctly, even though she doesn't know what her role is! When the teacher asks Lou the same question as the others, what should her answer be, and why?

solutions.title: Yes means same team, No means different team
solutions.body:
Suppose person $P$ is asked about the person $Q$ on their left:

| $P$ | $Q$ | $P$ answers |
|---|---|---|
| Truth-Teller | Truth-Teller | Yes |
| Truth-Teller | Liar | No |
| Liar | Truth-Teller | No |
| Liar | Liar | Yes |

So "Yes" means exactly that $P$ and $Q$ have the **same** role, and "No" means they have **different** roles. This is true for Lou too, whatever her role is.

Walk once around the circle, from each person to the person on their left. Every "No" marks a switch between the two roles. Since we come back to the starting person, we must switch an even number of times. So when everyone (Lou included) has answered, the total number of "No" answers must be even.

The other six students gave three "No"s. So the correct answer from Lou, whatever her role, is a fourth "No". (Answering "Yes" would leave an odd number of "No"s, which is impossible for correct answers.)

**Answer: Lou should say "No".**
